12. What is the difference between UMP and the MIDI 2.0 Protocol?
13. Why does opening a UMP endpoint not complete MIDI 2.0 support?
14. Which information can be lost when mapping MIDI 2.0 to MIDI 1.0?
15. What does MIDI Clock synchronize, and what does it not?
16. Why is MTC not a word clock?
17. How is Link phase synchronization different from one shared timeline?
18. Why should an external-sync callback publish observations rather than mutate the project?
19. Why should piano-roll notes be objects rather than paired bytes?
20. Which policies are required when same-pitch notes overlap?
21. Why is clip plus track automation not universally additive?
22. What state must Touch mode preserve after release?
23. Why must an arpeggiator track generated Note Off events explicitly?
24. Why should groove randomization be seedable?
25. What is the difference between an articulation map and per-note expression transport?
26. Why must articulation references use stable IDs?
27. What does SMF Type 2 mean for an importer?
28. How can malformed running status corrupt the remainder of a track?
29. Why are meta events still positioned by the file timebase?
30. Why should an SMF importer preserve raw order and also support canonical playback order?
31. What makes SMF export lossy for a modern DAW project?
32. Which tests demonstrate block-size independence in APEX?

### Section 6 misconceptions check

- **Misconception:** All DAW time can be stored safely as seconds.  
  **Correction:** Musical, device, timeline, timecode, and block-local domains have different semantics and invalidation rules.

- **Misconception:** A smaller device buffer automatically makes automation sample-accurate.  
  **Correction:** Precision should be independent of device block size and use local offsets or splitting.

- **Misconception:** MIDI 2.0 makes MIDI 1.0 obsolete.  
  **Correction:** MIDI 2.0 extends MIDI 1.0 and prioritizes compatibility.

- **Misconception:** MPE always supports exactly fifteen independently expressive notes.  
  **Correction:** Capacity depends on configured zones and Member Channels.

- **Misconception:** Link makes every app use the same transport timeline.  
  **Correction:** Link aligns relationships among autonomous timelines.

- **Misconception:** MIDI Clock, MTC, and word clock are interchangeable.  
  **Correction:** They synchronize different properties.

- **Misconception:** Track and clip automation should always be added together.  
  **Correction:** Composition is parameter- and product-specific.

- **Misconception:** An arpeggiator only needs the currently held keys.  
  **Correction:** It owns generated notes, phase, discontinuity state, and deterministic pattern state.

- **Misconception:** Swing 66% has one universal mathematical meaning.  
  **Correction:** Products use different percentage conventions; actual offsets are authoritative.

- **Misconception:** Articulation maps are the same as VST3 Note Expression.  
  **Correction:** The map chooses output actions; Note Expression is one transport mechanism.

- **Misconception:** SMF Type 1 requires one track per MIDI channel.  
  **Correction:** That is a common product policy, not the format requirement.

- **Misconception:** Unknown SMF bytes can be recovered by scanning until a plausible status appears.  
  **Correction:** Recovery must respect declared chunk bounds and remain deterministic.

### Section 6 mastery rubric

| Level | Demonstrated capability |
|---|---|
| Foundation | Identifies time domains, basic MIDI layers, tempo versus meter, major sync mechanisms, and SMF chunk/event concepts |
| Engineering | Implements typed conversion, block-size-invariant scheduling, note lifecycle, automation modes, groove/arpeggiator state, and defensive SMF parsing |
| Architecture | Defines APEX policies for ownership, synchronization, protocol neutrality, loss reporting, tempo changes, loops, and external-source failure |
| Research | Verifies current specifications and implementations, constructs adversarial tests, measures conversion error and jitter, and distinguishes normative protocol rules from product conventions |

### 6.12 Primary sources

- [MIDI Association Specifications](https://midi.org/specs): official specification index and distinction between specifications and developer guidance.
- [MIDI Association File Formats](https://midi.org/file-formats): official statement of the Standard MIDI File interchange purpose.
- [MIDI Association MIDI 2.0](https://midi.org/midi-2-0): official overview of MIDI 2.0, MIDI-CI, Profiles, Property Exchange, UMP, and compatibility goals.
- [Universal MIDI Packet and MIDI 2.0 Protocol specification page](https://midi.org/universal-midi-packet-ump-and-midi-2-0-protocol-specification): official specification identity and UMP/MIDI 2.0 scope.
- [MIDI Polyphonic Expression specification summary](https://midi.org/midi-polyphonic-expression-mpe-specification-adopted): official Zone, Master Channel, Member Channel, and note-allocation summary.
- [Ableton Link documentation](https://ableton.github.io/link/): official tempo, beat, phase, quantum, session-state, autonomous-timeline, and start/stop model.
- [Ableton Link source](https://github.com/Ableton/link): official cross-platform implementation and API reference.
- [Cubase/Nuendo Automation Modes](https://www.steinberg.help/r/cubase-pro/15.0/en/cubase_nuendo/topics/automation/automation_automation_modes_c.html): official example of product-specific Touch, Auto-Latch, and punch-out behavior.
- [Cubase/Nuendo Touch mode](https://www.steinberg.help/r/nuendo/15.0/en/cubase_nuendo/topics/automation/automation_touch_c.html): official return-to-underlying-value behavior and configurable return time.
- [Tracktion PlayHead](https://github.com/Tracktion/tracktion_engine/blob/develop/modules/tracktion_graph/tracktion_graph/tracktion_PlayHead.h): public reference/timeline mapping and split-range implementation evidence.
- [Tracktion TempoSequence](https://github.com/Tracktion/tracktion_engine/blob/develop/modules/tracktion_engine/model/edit/tracktion_TempoSequence.h): public tempo/meter conversion and remapping API evidence.
- [Ardour MIDI model](https://github.com/Ardour/ardour/blob/master/libs/ardour/ardour/midi_model.h): public higher-level note/event model evidence.
- [VST3 parameter automation](https://steinbergmedia.github.io/vst3_dev_portal/pages/Technical%2BDocumentation/Parameters%2BAutomation/Index.html): official sample-offset parameter-queue behavior.
- [CLAP events](https://github.com/free-audio/clap/blob/main/include/clap/events.h): official event, note identity, parameter value, modulation, transport, MIDI, SysEx, and MIDI 2 event structures.

## 7. Time-Stretch, Pitch-Shift, and Sample-Rate Conversion

### Section 7 guide

#### Section 7 prerequisites

Before starting this section, the learner should be able to:

- Distinguish project time, beat time, timeline samples, reference samples, and block-local sample offsets from §6.
- Explain the audio callback deadline, bounded work, worker ownership, and buffer-capacity planning from §2.
- Explain requested versus actual device sample rate, clock drift, and adaptive sample-rate conversion from §3.
- Explain plugin latency, block processing, sample-offset events, state reset, and offline versus real-time processing from §4.
- Read a frequency spectrum, identify the Nyquist frequency, and explain why frequencies above Nyquist cannot be represented without aliasing.
- Distinguish a signal's fundamental frequency from its spectral envelope and transients.
- Work with ratios, monotonic maps, piecewise-linear interpolation, and integer frame counts.

A learner does not need to implement a production phase vocoder before reading this section. The goal is to understand the separate problems, their contracts, and the evidence required before choosing an algorithm or third-party library.

#### Why time and pitch transformation matters

A DAW routinely imports audio recorded at one sample rate, places it into a project running at another rate, follows tempo changes, transposes samples, preserves vocal duration while changing pitch, and renders a final file at a delivery rate. These operations sound similar to a user because all of them can make audio appear faster, slower, higher, or lower. Internally they are different transformations with different mathematics, artifacts, latency, licensing, and failure behavior.

A weak design exposes one control called `speed`, applies an arbitrary interpolator, and lets clip duration, pitch, and timeline placement drift according to implementation accidents. A strong design states which property the user asked to preserve:

```text
sampling grid
pitch
musical duration
timeline duration
formant character
transient position
channel coherence
exact final frame count
```

The engineering problem is therefore not simply “stretch this file.” It is:

```text
user intent
→ explicit transformation semantics
→ algorithm and quality policy
→ stateful variable-rate processing contract
→ deterministic timeline mapping
→ measured artifacts, latency, and CPU cost
→ exact publication and project persistence
```

This distinction is especially important for APEX because tempo changes must not unexpectedly alter imported beats or recorded vocals. The clip model must decide whether audio follows musical time, absolute time, tape-style repitch behavior, or an explicit warp map. The engine must never infer that policy merely from the current project BPM.

#### Section 7 learning outcomes

After completing this section, the learner should be able to:

1. **Distinguish** sample-rate conversion, rate transposition, time-scale modification, pitch shifting, and formant shifting.
2. **Predict** how each transformation changes pitch, duration, sample count, and timeline placement.
3. **Derive** a same-duration pitch shift as a coordinated time-stretch and resampling operation while stating the ratio convention.
4. **Explain** why anti-alias filtering is required for high-quality sample-rate conversion.
5. **Compare** WSOLA, TD-PSOLA, phase-vocoder, granular, and hybrid approaches by signal assumptions, latency, CPU cost, and characteristic artifacts.
6. **Trace** a variable-rate processor using independent input-consumed and output-produced counts.
7. **Design** a monotonic warp map and derive local stretch ratios from adjacent anchors.
8. **Handle** latency, pre-roll, seek/reset, dynamic-ratio changes, final drain, and exact output-length correction.
9. **Preserve** stereo, surround, and spatial coherence through shared analysis and linked timing decisions.
10. **Define** explicit APEX clip policies for unwarped audio, tempo-following audio, repitch behavior, one-shot samples, loops, vocals, and rendered assets.
11. **Select** a library only after checking quality, real-time behavior, API contract, licensing, platform support, and benchmark evidence.
12. **Build** a test corpus that measures spectral error, aliasing, transient behavior, output length, latency, CPU percentiles, determinism, and subjective quality.

#### Section 7 evidence of mastery

A learner demonstrates mastery by producing:

- A transformation table that predicts pitch and duration for several independent rate, time, and pitch ratios.
- A stateful SRC wrapper that handles partial input consumption, partial output generation, reset, and drain.
- A monotonic warp-map evaluator with exact endpoint tests and no negative local slope.
- A linked-stereo test proving that both channels use identical timing decisions.
- A clip-semantics document showing what happens when project BPM changes before and after import.
- A benchmark comparing at least two SRC quality levels and two time-stretch algorithm families on representative material.
- A failure report for at least one aliasing, transient-smear, repeated-grain, formant, or exact-length defect.
- An APEX migration plan that separates the clip model, time map, processing backend, cache, and render path.

### 7.1 Separate the operations

#### Why the operations must be named separately

The words *speed*, *tempo*, *stretch*, *pitch*, and *rate* are often used loosely in product interfaces. An engine cannot afford that ambiguity. Each control must have a documented invariant.

| Operation | Primary change | Intended invariant | Common use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sample-rate conversion | Sampling grid | Continuous-time interpretation | Import, device conversion, export |
| Rate transposition | Playback rate | No independent pitch or duration preservation | Tape/varispeed, sampler playback |
| Time-scale modification | Duration | Pitch | Tempo following, dialogue timing |
| Pitch shifting | Pitch | Duration | Vocal/instrument transposition |
| Formant shifting | Spectral envelope character | Product-defined; often pitch and duration | Voice character effects |

The same resampling kernel may participate in both transparent sample-rate conversion and creative rate transposition, but the surrounding semantics are different.

#### Sample-rate conversion

Sample-rate conversion reconstructs a signal represented on one sampling grid and evaluates it on another grid. For example:

```text
source: 44,100 frames per second
project: 48,000 frames per second
```

A transparent converter aims to preserve the represented audio duration and pitch while changing the number of samples per second. One second of source audio remains one second after conversion, but it contains a different frame count.

For a source duration `D`:

```text
inputFrames  ≈ D × inputSampleRate
outputFrames ≈ D × outputSampleRate
```

The output count must use a documented rounding and endpoint policy. A long file cannot repeatedly round each block independently because accumulated error can shift the final length.

##### Why filtering is necessary

Downsampling lowers the output Nyquist frequency. Energy above that new limit must be attenuated before decimation or it folds into lower frequencies as aliasing. High-quality SRC therefore combines interpolation with low-pass filtering rather than merely selecting or linearly connecting input samples.

Upsampling also requires interpolation. Inserting zeros or duplicating values without an appropriate reconstruction filter creates spectral images or obvious high-frequency error.

The practical quality dimensions include:

- Passband width.
- Passband ripple.
- Stopband rejection.
- Transition-band width.
- Phase response.
- Group delay and latency.
- CPU and memory cost.
- Behavior under time-varying ratios.

There is no universal “best” setting. A mastering export can tolerate more latency than live monitoring. A device-drift corrector may require a smoothly variable ratio and tightly bounded callback cost.

#### Rate transposition

Rate transposition consumes source samples at a rate different from the nominal playback rate. Let:

```text
r = input frames consumed per output frame
```

Then, ignoring filter latency and endpoint rounding:

```text
outputDuration = inputDuration / r
pitchRatio     = r
```

Examples:

| `r` | Duration | Pitch |
|---:|---:|---:|
| `0.5` | Twice as long | One octave lower |
| `1.0` | Unchanged | Unchanged |
| `2.0` | Half as long | One octave higher |

This is the digital equivalent of changing tape speed. It is useful when the user intentionally wants pitch and timing to move together.

A product must state its ratio orientation. Some APIs use input-per-output; others use output-per-input or a named sample-rate ratio. Inverting the ratio by mistake produces the opposite transformation and can also overrun buffers.

#### Time-scale modification

Time-scale modification changes duration while attempting to preserve perceived pitch.

Define:

```text
t = output duration / input duration
```

Then:

| `t` | Result |
|---:|---|
| `< 1` | Audio becomes shorter/faster while pitch is intended to remain stable |
| `1` | Identity |
| `> 1` | Audio becomes longer/slower while pitch is intended to remain stable |

The phrase “preserve pitch” describes the target, not a guarantee of transparency. Real algorithms may alter transients, phase relationships, noise texture, formants, or the apparent pitch of difficult material.

#### Pitch shifting

Pitch shifting changes pitch while aiming to preserve duration. Let:

```text
p = output fundamental-frequency scale / input scale
```

For equal-tempered semitone transposition:

```text
p = 2^(semitones / 12)
```

A conventional same-duration implementation can coordinate time stretching and resampling:

```text
1. Time-stretch by t = p.
2. Rate-transpose by r = p.
```

The first stage makes the audio `p` times longer without intentionally changing pitch. The second stage consumes it `p` times faster, restoring the original duration and raising pitch by `p`.

The stages may be ordered differently by a particular implementation, and a modern algorithm may perform an integrated spectral transformation. The host contract should describe the desired result rather than assuming one internal method.

#### Formants are not the same as pitch

A voiced source has a fundamental-frequency pattern and a spectral envelope shaped by the source and resonances. Moving every spectral component upward can make a voice sound smaller or “chipmunk-like” even when the musical pitch shift is mathematically correct.

Formant preservation or formant shifting attempts to manage that spectral envelope separately. It requires assumptions about source structure and is not universally meaningful for drums, dense mixes, noise, or every instrument.

APEX should therefore expose formant behavior as an explicit algorithm capability or mode, not as a guaranteed property of every pitch shift.

#### Clip timebase and tempo-following semantics

A project BPM change must not decide audio behavior by accident. Every audio clip needs an explicit timebase and transformation policy.

A recommended clip model distinguishes:

| Policy | Timeline ownership | Audio behavior when project BPM changes |
|---|---|---|
| Absolute/unwarped | Seconds or timeline samples | Start and duration remain in absolute time; no automatic stretch |
| Musical placement, unwarped content | Beat start; absolute source duration | Clip start follows beats, but audio duration does not stretch |
| Tempo-following/warped | Beat anchors and source-time map | Audio is time-scaled to preserve beat relationships |
| Repitch/varispeed | Beat or time placement | Pitch and duration move together according to rate |
| One-shot sampler | Trigger event plus source playback policy | Usually no automatic stretch unless the instrument enables it |
| Rendered/frozen asset | Original render timeline | Must preserve the render contract; no implicit reinterpretation |

This separation prevents the bug where setting the project to a detected BPM before import causes the imported beat to change pitch or speed even though the source and project sample rates match.

#### Worked example: importing a 91 BPM beat

Assume a stereo beat was produced at 91 BPM and stored at 44.1 kHz.

##### Case A: absolute import

```text
project BPM: 91
clip policy: absolute/unwarped
```

The importer decodes the file and performs SRC only if the project sample rate differs. The file's pitch and duration remain unchanged. BPM metadata may be displayed, but it does not authorize stretching.

##### Case B: tempo-following import

```text
source tempo: 91 BPM
project tempo: 100 BPM
clip policy: tempo-following
```

The clip's beat anchors map the source to the faster project grid. The target duration ratio is approximately:

```text
t = sourceTempo / projectTempo
  = 91 / 100
  = 0.91
```

The audio becomes shorter while the algorithm attempts to preserve pitch.

##### Case C: repitch mode

Using the same tempo relationship with repitch behavior changes both duration and pitch. The clip plays about `100 / 91` times faster. That is a creative tape-style policy, not a transparent tempo-following policy.

##### APEX requirement

Import must never silently switch among these cases. The UI can offer a default, but the project must persist the actual choice.

#### Recommended APEX clip fields

```cpp
struct AudioClipTimePolicy {
    StableId policyId;
    ClipTimebase placementTimebase;       // Absolute or Musical
    StretchMode stretchMode;              // Off, PreservePitch, Repitch
    AlgorithmProfile algorithmProfile;    // Speech, Percussive, Polyphonic, etc.
    std::optional<double> sourceTempoBpm;
    SourceTempoConfidence tempoConfidence;
    bool formantPreservationRequested;
    std::vector<WarpAnchor> warpAnchors;
    std::uint64_t analysisGeneration;
};
```

The source sample rate belongs to the media asset. The current project sample rate belongs to the render configuration. Neither field should be reused as a stretch policy.

### 7.2 Algorithm families

#### Why multiple algorithm families exist

Time-scale modification is underdetermined. Many different output waveforms can have the requested duration and roughly the same perceived pitch. An algorithm must decide which waveform segments, spectral phases, transients, and noise characteristics to preserve.

Different source types violate different assumptions:

- Speech and monophonic voice have pitch periods and formants.
- Drums contain sharp transients and noise.
- Sustained instruments require stable partial relationships.
- Dense mixes contain simultaneous transient, harmonic, and stochastic components.
- Reverberation contains diffuse decays whose phase and texture matter.

No family is transparent for every source and every ratio.

#### WSOLA

Waveform Similarity Overlap-Add is a time-domain approach. It selects analysis segments near predicted positions, searches within a bounded region for a waveform that aligns well with the previous synthesis context, windows the chosen segments, and overlap-adds them.

Conceptual flow:

```text
predict next source position
→ search nearby candidates
→ score waveform similarity in overlap region
→ choose best bounded candidate
→ window and overlap-add
→ advance synthesis position
```

The search allows the algorithm to avoid joining badly mismatched waveform phases.

##### WSOLA good-fit signals

- Speech.
- Moderate tempo changes.
- Percussive or mixed content when a short, responsive time-domain method is preferred.
- Real-time operation with controlled search bounds.

##### WSOLA failure modes

- Repeated or skipped texture when the search repeatedly chooses similar regions.
- Flutter when candidate positions jump inconsistently.
- Doubled or softened attacks when a transient appears in overlapping segments.
- Incorrect matches in dense polyphonic or noisy material.
- Stereo-image instability if channels choose different candidates.

##### Implementation implication

Linked channels should share the candidate offset chosen from a combined or designated analysis signal. Searching each channel independently can change interchannel timing.

#### TD-PSOLA

Time-Domain Pitch-Synchronous Overlap-Add segments voiced speech around estimated pitch epochs. By changing the spacing and repetition of pitch-synchronous segments, it can modify pitch or duration efficiently while retaining speech naturalness under suitable conditions.

Conceptual flow:

```text
classify voiced/unvoiced regions
→ estimate pitch epochs
→ window around epochs
→ choose synthesis epochs
→ repeat, omit, or reposition frames
→ overlap-add
```

##### TD-PSOLA good-fit signals

- Clean monophonic voiced speech.
- Speech synthesis and prosody modification.
- Cases where reliable pitch marking is available.

##### TD-PSOLA failure modes

- Buzzing or discontinuities from incorrect epoch detection.
- Poor results in polyphonic audio.
- Unstable behavior across unvoiced consonants or rapidly changing pitch.
- Voice-character changes when the pitch/formant relationship is mishandled.

A DAW should not label TD-PSOLA a universal “vocal mode.” It is strongest when the source matches its pitch-synchronous assumptions.

#### Phase vocoder

A phase vocoder analyzes overlapping short-time Fourier transform frames, estimates how sinusoidal phases progress, changes the synthesis hop relative to the analysis hop, and reconstructs the signal with an inverse transform and overlap-add.

Simplified flow:

```text
window input frame
→ FFT
→ measure magnitude and phase
→ estimate phase advance
→ apply new synthesis timing
→ reconstruct phase
→ inverse FFT
→ overlap-add
```

If the analysis hop is `Ha` and synthesis hop is `Hs`, a simplified constant stretch ratio is:

```text
t ≈ Hs / Ha
```

Real implementations must also handle instantaneous-frequency estimation, window normalization, phase wrapping, transients, and changing ratios.

##### Phase-vocoder good-fit signals

- Polyphonic material.
- Sustained tones.
- Larger or offline transformations where more analysis latency is acceptable.
- Spectral transformations that naturally operate on frequency-domain components.

##### Characteristic artifacts

- Phasiness or loss of presence.
- Transient smearing.
- Reverberant or “underwater” texture.
- Loss of vertical phase coherence among bins belonging to one partial.
- Stereo-image damage when channels are analyzed independently.

##### Common improvements

- Identity or peak phase locking.
- Phase propagation from spectral peaks to neighboring bins.
- Transient detection and phase reset.
- Multi-resolution analysis.
- Separate handling of harmonic, percussive, and residual components.
- Shared multichannel analysis.

These improvements reduce specific artifacts; they do not create a universally transparent processor.

Rubber Band's published technical notes describe its R2 engine as a block-based phase vocoder with transient phase resets, adaptive stretch between reset points, and a method intended to improve vertical phase coherence. That is implementation evidence for Rubber Band, not a universal description of all phase vocoders.

#### Granular time scaling

Granular methods divide audio into short grains and schedule them with changed spacing, overlap, position, or playback rate.

Conceptual flow:

```text
select grain start
→ apply grain window
→ schedule overlapping grains
→ vary source advance independently from output advance
```

##### Granular good-fit signals

- Interactive creative effects.
- Texture design.
- Responsive low-complexity transformations.
- Sources where a grain character is acceptable.

##### Granular failure modes

- Grain flutter.
- Repetition.
- Roughness at low overlap.
- Loss of low-frequency stability when grains are too short.
- Transient multiplication or softening.

A granular engine can be musically valuable even when it is not the most transparent option. The product should distinguish *creative texture* from *transparent stretch*.

#### Hybrid and content-adaptive systems

Commercial-quality processors often combine multiple methods or change parameters according to detected content. Examples include:

- Time-domain treatment near attacks and spectral treatment for sustained regions.
- Different windows for transient and harmonic content.
- Source separation into harmonic, percussive, and residual components.
- Speech-specific formant handling.
- Multi-resolution spectral analysis.
- Ratio-dependent quality modes.

A detector can also fail. Abrupt algorithm switching may create discontinuities, and misclassification can sound worse than one consistent method. Therefore, hybrid systems need confidence measures, smoothing, deterministic state transitions, and tests around classification boundaries.

#### Real-time versus offline processing

Real-time and offline modes are not merely the same algorithm with a faster loop.

| Constraint | Real-time | Offline |
|---|---|---|
| Future knowledge | Limited lookahead | Entire file or planned map may be available |
| Latency | Must be bounded and reported | Can be larger if result quality improves |
| Ratio changes | May occur during streaming | Can be planned globally |
| Analysis passes | Usually one streaming pass | May use study/analysis plus render pass |
| CPU | Must meet device deadline | Can run faster or slower than real time |
| Exact output length | Must manage streaming error | Can correct endpoints globally |

Rubber Band's documented API explicitly separates real-time single-pass processing from offline study-plus-process operation. The host should expose that distinction through its backend adapter rather than pretending every library has one uniform mode.

#### Algorithm profile is a hint, not truth

A user-facing profile such as `Percussive`, `Voice`, or `Complex` is a requested strategy. It should not overwrite the original asset or become an unsupported factual claim about the signal.

Recommended persisted fields include:

```text
requested profile
detector result and confidence
algorithm backend/version
quality mode
analysis-cache generation
manual overrides
```

The project should remain loadable when the original backend is unavailable. It may fall back with an explicit warning or use a previously rendered cache, but it must not silently substitute a different sound and report the project as exact.

### 7.3 Processing contract

#### Variable-rate processing cannot assume one block in equals one block out

A fixed-rate insert often receives and returns the same frame count. A resampler or time stretcher may consume a different amount of input for every output block and may temporarily retain samples internally.

A minimum result contract is:

```cpp
struct ProcessResult {
    std::uint32_t inputFramesConsumed;
    std::uint32_t outputFramesProduced;
    ProcessStatus status;
};
```

The caller must advance pointers and counters using the returned values. The libsamplerate documentation specifically warns that streaming callers must use `input_frames_used` and `output_frames_gen`; using a whole-file convenience function on successive chunks breaks filter continuity.

#### Push, pull, and hybrid adapters

##### Push model

```text
caller supplies available input
processor consumes some input
processor queues produced output
caller retrieves available output
```

This matches APIs such as Rubber Band's `process()` plus `retrieve()` model.

##### Pull model

```text
caller requests N output frames
processor calculates required input
processor pulls or reports source demand
```

This can fit a graph that is driven by the device's required output block size.

##### Adapter requirement

A DAW may need to wrap a push-style library in a pull-style render graph. The adapter requires bounded input and output FIFOs, explicit maximum ratios, latency accounting, and a policy for underrun or unavailable future samples.

It must not allocate a larger buffer from the callback when an extreme ratio arrives.

#### Ratio orientation must be explicit

Never expose an unnamed `ratio` field. Prefer names that encode direction:

```cpp
struct StretchCommand {
    double outputDurationPerInputDuration;
    double outputPitchPerInputPitch;
};

struct ResampleCommand {
    double inputFramesPerOutputFrame;
};
```

Adapters for libraries using another convention perform the inversion at one boundary and test it with known tones and lengths.

#### Latency, start delay, and pre-roll

Variable-rate processors often require context before producing valid output. Sources include:

- FIR or FFT filter delay.
- Analysis windows.
- Similarity-search lookahead.
- Transient detection.
- Pitch-period estimation.
- Internal buffering.

The processor must report or allow measurement of:

```text
algorithmic latency
required input before first output
output start delay
lookahead requirement
final drain behavior
```

These quantities are not always identical.

For timeline playback, the host may pre-roll the processor so the first retained output frame corresponds to the requested timeline start. For live input, that latency becomes audible monitoring delay and must be reported to PDC where appropriate.

#### Drain and finalization

A stateful converter may hold samples after the final input frame. Libsoxr's documentation notes that the application must signal end-of-input and continue reading until no more output remains. A time stretcher may have a similar finalization or `flush` contract.

A safe end-of-stream state machine is:

```text
Feeding
→ EndOfInputSignaled
→ Draining
→ Exhausted
```

Calling finalization repeatedly should be either documented as idempotent or rejected deterministically. The host should not invent behavior.

#### Seek and discontinuity

A seek invalidates analysis history. Continuing with old overlap, phase, filter, or pitch-tracker state can leak audio from the previous location or create a large transient.

Recommended sequence:

```text
stop consuming old timeline range
→ reset processor state
→ seek source and analysis caches
→ provide required pre-roll
→ discard preparation output
→ begin retained output at requested position
```

Looping may use a prepared loop-specific state or crossfade policy, but it must not accidentally reuse unrelated history.

#### Dynamic ratios and smoothing

A real-time processor may allow ratio changes during streaming. The host still needs a policy for:

- Control-rate versus sample-accurate updates.
- Maximum slope of ratio changes.
- Parameter smoothing.
- Automation point interpolation.
- Backend-specific update granularity.
- Reanalysis or cache invalidation.

Abrupt ratio changes can create pitch jumps, timing discontinuities, buffer-level shocks, or transient artifacts. Over-smoothing can make automation late. The correct policy depends on whether the control represents an intentional step, a continuous curve, or a drift-correction estimate.

#### Monotonic warp maps

A warp map relates source positions to output timeline positions.

```cpp
struct WarpAnchor {
    std::int64_t sourceFrame;
    BeatPosition destinationBeat;
    StableId anchorId;
};
```

For adjacent anchors `A` and `B`:

```text
sourceFrameB > sourceFrameA
destinationBeatB > destinationBeatA
```

The map must remain monotonic unless the product explicitly supports reverse or scrub segments as a different feature.

Within a piecewise-linear section, the local source-frame consumption per destination beat is:

```text
(sourceFrameB - sourceFrameA)
---------------------------------
(destinationBeatB - destinationBeatA)
```

The tempo map then converts destination beats to output samples. A curved warp map can use another interpolation model, but it must preserve monotonicity and define endpoint derivatives.

#### Why warp anchors need stable identity

Users edit anchors, undo changes, copy clips, and merge project states. An array index is not stable across insertion and deletion. Each anchor should have a persistent ID, with a deterministic policy for linked copies and independent copies.

#### Exact output-length ownership

For a fixed render region, the timeline owns the desired output frame count. The processor may produce slightly more or fewer frames because of ratio approximation, latency, and rounding.

A recommended offline policy is:

1. Compute the exact target output interval from timeline boundaries.
2. Render with sufficient pre-roll and tail context.
3. Consume the processor until the target is covered.
4. Trim preparation frames.
5. Retain exactly the requested count.
6. Record any endpoint correction in diagnostics.

Do not distribute independent rounding errors across every block. Use a continuous phase or accumulated fractional position.

#### Shared analysis for multichannel audio

Stereo and spatial channels often encode timing and phase relationships. Independent transient detection, similarity search, or warp decisions can move one channel relative to another.

Recommended policy:

```text
one time map
+ one linked timing decision
+ channel-coherent analysis
→ all channels transformed together
```

Channel samples remain separate, but timing decisions are shared. A product may offer independent-channel creative processing, but it must be explicit.

#### Cache architecture

Time-stretch analysis can be expensive. A cache key should include every property that changes the analysis result:

```text
asset content hash
source sample rate
channel layout
algorithm backend and version
analysis profile
quality mode
relevant detector settings
warp-map generation where required
```

Do not key only by filename. Replacing a file in place or changing algorithm version can otherwise reuse invalid analysis.

The cache is derived data. The project must remain recoverable without it.

#### Recommended backend-neutral interface

```cpp
class VariableRateAudioProcessor {
public:
    virtual ~VariableRateAudioProcessor() = default;

    virtual PrepareResult prepare(const VariableRatePrepareSpec&) = 0;
    virtual void reset() noexcept = 0;

    virtual void setPlannedTimeMap(std::span<const TimeMapPoint>) = 0;
    virtual void setRealtimeRatios(double timeRatio,
                                   double pitchScale) noexcept = 0;

    virtual InputRequirement inputRequiredFor(std::uint32_t outputFrames) const = 0;
    virtual ProcessResult process(const AudioBusView<const float>& input,
                                  AudioBusView<float>& output,
                                  bool endOfInput) noexcept = 0;

    virtual std::uint32_t availableOutputFrames() const noexcept = 0;
    virtual DrainResult drain(AudioBusView<float>& output) noexcept = 0;

    virtual LatencyDescription latency() const noexcept = 0;
    virtual BackendIdentity backendIdentity() const = 0;
};
```

Not every backend supports every function. Capability discovery must be explicit:

```text
supports offline study pass
supports dynamic time ratio
supports dynamic pitch ratio
supports planned key-frame map
supports formant control
supports multichannel linked processing
supports deterministic rendering
```

#### APEX execution policy

**Recommendation:** APEX should separate five objects:

```text
AudioClipTimePolicy       user intent and persisted semantics
WarpMap                   stable source↔timeline anchors
StretchAnalysisCache      derived, replaceable analysis
VariableRateBackend       algorithm/library adapter
ClipRenderNode            real-time or offline graph integration
```

This preserves the existing timeline, UI, routing, and automation while allowing the processing backend to change.

The render node must not read media files or run an offline analysis pass inside the audio callback. Source decoding and analysis occur on workers; prepared PCM and analysis state are consumed by the render path.

### 7.4 Library comparison

#### Why library selection is an architecture decision

A library choice affects more than sound quality. It determines:

- Real-time and offline API shape.
- Latency and buffering.
- Dynamic-ratio support.
- Exact-length behavior.
- Channel limits.
- CPU and platform support.
- Determinism and version drift.
- Licensing and distribution obligations.
- Long-term project compatibility.

A thin adapter prevents these details from becoming the project file format.

#### Current dependency register

All licensing statements in this subsection are **Time-sensitive**. Verify the exact source release, commit, and commercial agreement selected for shipping. This is engineering research, not legal advice.

| Product | Primary function | Published processing model | Current license/status | APEX concern |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rubber Band | Independent time and pitch transformation | Real-time streaming; offline study and process; planned key-frame maps | GPL version 2 or later, or proprietary commercial license | Proprietary APEX distribution requires an appropriate commercial arrangement or a GPL-compliant product decision |
| SoundTouch | Tempo, pitch, and playback-rate controls | Streaming time-domain processing | LGPL-2.1; commercial non-LGPL option advertised | Verify exact library version, relinking/source obligations, latency, and quality on target material |
| libsamplerate | Stateful and variable SRC | Whole-file convenience API plus stateful streaming/callback APIs | BSD-2-Clause for current main library source | SRC only; wrapper must honor consumed/produced counts, state, transport delay, and drain |
| libsoxr | High-quality constant or variable SRC | Stateful one-dimensional SRC with configurable quality and phase | LGPL-2.1 in upstream repository | SRC only; high-quality modes may add substantial latency; verify distribution obligations |
| zplane élastique | Proprietary time and pitch SDK | Vendor-defined | Negotiated proprietary terms | Obtain written scope for platforms, redistribution, support, patents, updates, and offline/server use |
| iZotope Radius | Historical proprietary offline technology | Historical product integration | Current SDK availability not publicly established | Treat as unavailable until current written vendor confirmation |

#### Rubber Band integration implications

Rubber Band's current documentation distinguishes:

- Offline mode with `study()` followed by `process()` and `retrieve()`.
- Real-time mode with one streaming pass.
- Dynamic time and pitch changes in real-time mode.
- Planned variable stretching through a key-frame map in offline mode.
- Separate faster and finer engines.

The adapter should not call offline study work from the callback. It should also record engine, options, and library version because those choices can change output.

Rubber Band's technical notes state that pitch shifting may be implemented by combining resampling and time stretching in opposite duration directions. That supports the conceptual model in §7.1, while the library's exact internal behavior remains its own implementation.

#### libsamplerate integration implications

libsamplerate provides a simple whole-buffer API and stateful streaming APIs. The official FAQ warns against applying the simple API independently to successive chunks because the higher-quality converters require preserved state.

The wrapper must test:

```text
input_frames_used
output_frames_gen
end_of_input
initial transport delay
final drain
reset between unrelated streams
```

A linear or zero-order mode may be useful for deliberately low-quality or diagnostic comparison, but it is not a substitute for a production-quality converter where alias rejection matters.

#### libsoxr integration implications

libsoxr exposes configurable passband, phase response, alias rejection, and quality presets, including a variable-rate mode. Its own repository warns that FFT-based high-quality configurations can have higher real-time latency than non-FFT approaches.

Therefore:

- Do not select the highest preset blindly for live monitoring.
- Query or measure delay.
- Signal end-of-input and continue draining.
- Benchmark the exact sample-rate pair and channel count.
- Treat phase and bandwidth configuration as part of the render identity.

#### SoundTouch integration implications

SoundTouch publishes separate tempo, pitch, and rate controls. A backend adapter must document how those controls compose and what latency is produced under the selected sequence and seek settings.

The product website advertises both LGPL-2.1 and a commercial non-LGPL option. The shipping decision must be reviewed against the exact distributed artifacts and product packaging.

#### Selection matrix

| Use case | First properties to prioritize |
|---|---|
| Device sample-rate mismatch | Bounded stateful SRC, low latency, channel support, exact drift control |
| Offline mastering SRC | Stopband rejection, passband, phase policy, deterministic final length |
| Live vocal pitch shift | Low and stable latency, formant behavior, pitch tracking, dropout policy |
| Tempo-synced drum loop | Transient preservation, exact loop length, dynamic ratio behavior |
| Dense full mix | Polyphonic quality, stereo coherence, CPU, offline option |
| Creative grain effect | Responsiveness, modulation range, character, deterministic seeding |
| Dialogue conformance | Speech intelligibility, moderate-ratio quality, exact duration |

No table can replace listening and measurement on the product's actual corpus.

#### APEX backend strategy

**Recommendation:** APEX should begin with one high-quality offline/tempo-follow backend and one dedicated SRC backend behind stable interfaces. It should not expose library-specific enums directly in the project schema.

Persist a semantic profile such as:

```text
PreservePitch.Percussive
PreservePitch.Polyphonic
PreservePitch.Voice
Repitch
TransparentSRC
CreativeGranular
```

A versioned backend policy resolves the profile to a specific implementation. When opening an older project, APEX can preserve the prior backend version, use a cached render, or warn that a re-render may differ.

### 7.5 Test corpus and validation

#### Why one quality score is insufficient

A time-stretch algorithm can perform well on speech and poorly on cymbals. An SRC can have excellent steady-state rejection but undesirable latency for monitoring. A pitch shifter can preserve musical interval while changing formants. Testing must therefore combine structural, numerical, timing, spectral, and perceptual evidence.

#### Required source corpus

Include at least:

- Clean speech with voiced and unvoiced transitions.
- Solo vocal with vibrato, breath, and consonants.
- Piano or guitar with sharp attacks and sustained decay.
- Kick, snare, hi-hat, and complete drum loops.
- Bass with low fundamentals.
- Dense stereo mix.
- Reverberant ambience.
- White and pink noise.
- Silence and near-silence.
- Impulses.
- Single sine tones near low, mid, and high frequencies.
- Logarithmic sweeps.
- Linked stereo signals with known phase offsets.
- Multichannel and spatial material where supported.
- Very short clips and clips shorter than the algorithm window.

#### Ratio matrix

Test constant and changing ratios:

```text
time ratios: 0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.5, 2.0
pitch shifts: -12, -7, -1, +1, +7, +12 semitones
SRC pairs: 44.1↔48, 48↔96, 96↔44.1 kHz
```

Also test product-defined extremes, but do not let extreme settings obscure defects in the common range.

#### Structural and length tests

Verify:

- Exact target frame count for offline regions.
- No frame loss at the beginning or end.
- Correct drain after end-of-input.
- No duplication across block boundaries.
- Identical result across reasonable input chunk sizes where the backend promises chunk invariance.
- Deterministic result across repeated renders when deterministic mode is promised.
- Correct reset after seek, clip reuse, and source change.
- Monotonic warp-map evaluation.
- Stable endpoint behavior at every anchor.

#### SRC spectral tests

Measure:

- Passband ripple.
- Stopband rejection.
- Aliasing under downsampling.
- Imaging under upsampling.
- Frequency and phase response.
- Impulse response and group delay.
- DC behavior.
- NaN/Inf propagation policy.
- Clipping and headroom.

A sine above the destination Nyquist limit should not reappear as a strong lower-frequency alias after a high-quality downsample.

#### Time-stretch artifact tests

Listen and inspect for:

- Transient smear or duplication.
- Phasiness.
- Flutter.
- Grain repetition.
- Pitch wobble.
- Formant shift.
- Stereo-image movement.
- Reverberation texture changes.
- Boundary clicks.
- Loop discontinuity.

Spectrograms and waveforms help diagnose causes, but a visually smooth result is not proof of perceptual quality.

#### Real-time performance tests

Measure on target hardware:

```text
callback p50
p95
p99
p99.9
maximum
xrun count
processor FIFO minimum/maximum fill
ratio update cost
seek/reset cost outside callback
analysis-worker time
```

Test every supported block size and sample rate. Average CPU alone is insufficient.

#### Tempo-semantics regression tests for APEX

1. Import an unwarped 91 BPM beat into a 91 BPM project: pitch and duration remain unchanged.
2. Set project BPM before import: no change unless tempo-following is explicitly selected.
3. Enable tempo-following and change project BPM: beat anchors remain aligned and pitch follows the selected preserve/repitch policy.
4. Disable tempo-following after edits: define whether the clip preserves current duration or returns to source duration.
5. Record a vocal at one BPM and change project BPM: behavior follows the persisted clip policy.
6. Save, close, and reopen: algorithm profile, warp anchors, and policy remain unchanged.
7. Freeze or render the clip: the rendered asset does not receive a second implicit stretch.
8. Change project sample rate with unchanged BPM: only SRC occurs unless another policy is active.

#### Subjective evaluation

Use blind, level-matched comparisons where practical. Evaluate by content class and ratio rather than asking for one universal winner.

Record:

- Listener experience.
- Playback system.
- Source category.
- Ratio and algorithm settings.
- Randomized presentation order.
- Confidence and comments.

A subjective preference does not replace exact-length, aliasing, or crash tests. Numerical measurements also do not replace listening.

#### Laboratory 7A — Transformation semantics calculator

Build a tool that accepts:

```text
source duration
source sample rate
destination sample rate
rate ratio
time ratio
pitch semitones
```

It must predict output duration, nominal frame count, and pitch ratio for SRC, repitch, preserve-pitch stretch, and combined pitch shift. Include tests that catch inverted ratios.

**Acceptance criteria:** Every transformation names its invariant and matches hand-calculated cases.

#### Laboratory 7B — Stateful SRC wrapper

Wrap libsamplerate or another stateful SRC backend.

Requirements:

- Arbitrary input chunk sizes.
- Bounded output buffer.
- Correct consumed/produced accounting.
- Reset.
- End-of-input signaling.
- Complete drain.
- Exact final duration within the selected rounding policy.

**Acceptance criteria:** The output is continuous across chunk boundaries and contains no missing tail.

#### Laboratory 7C — Aliasing demonstration

Generate a swept sine, downsample it using:

1. Naive sample dropping.
2. Linear interpolation or another simple baseline.
3. A high-quality bandlimited converter.

Compare spectrograms and identify folded components.

**Acceptance criteria:** The report explains why interpolation alone does not remove frequencies above the destination Nyquist limit.

#### Laboratory 7D — WSOLA prototype

Implement a bounded WSOLA prototype with:

- Configurable analysis and synthesis hops.
- Bounded candidate search.
- Normalized similarity score.
- Windowed overlap-add.
- One shared candidate offset for linked stereo.

**Acceptance criteria:** The learner identifies at least two source types where quality fails and explains why.

#### Laboratory 7E — Basic phase vocoder

Implement or instrument a basic phase-vocoder time stretcher.

Measure the effect of:

- FFT size.
- Analysis hop.
- Synthesis hop.
- Phase propagation.
- Transient reset.

**Acceptance criteria:** The report connects parameter changes to time/frequency resolution and audible artifacts.

#### Laboratory 7F — Warp-map engine

Implement a monotonic piecewise-linear map from source frames to destination beats.

Test:

- Anchor insertion and deletion.
- Undo/redo using stable IDs.
- Duplicate destination positions.
- Reversed source anchors.
- Tempo-map changes.
- Exact endpoint evaluation.

**Acceptance criteria:** Invalid maps are rejected without mutating the last valid render snapshot.

#### Laboratory 7G — Multichannel coherence

Create a stereo test where one channel is a delayed or phase-shifted version of the other. Process it using linked and intentionally independent timing decisions.

**Acceptance criteria:** The learner measures and explains the image or phase change caused by independent timing.

#### Laboratory 7H — Real-time adapter stress test

Wrap a push-based time stretcher in a pull-based graph node using fixed-capacity FIFOs.

Inject:

- Rapid ratio changes.
- Source starvation.
- End-of-input.
- Seek/reset.
- Maximum supported stretch.

**Acceptance criteria:** The callback never allocates or blocks; underrun behavior is bounded and counted.

#### Laboratory 7I — APEX clip-policy migration

Audit the current APEX repository for every place where BPM, source sample rate, clip start, clip duration, playback rate, or stretch mode is stored or inferred.

Produce:

- A field/domain table.
- A list of implicit policies.
- A migration schema for `AudioClipTimePolicy`.
- Tests preserving existing projects.
- A plan to prevent double stretching after freeze/render.

**Acceptance criteria:** The migration preserves unwarped existing clips unless project evidence explicitly proves another intent.

### Section 7 review questions

1. How does transparent SRC differ from rate transposition?
2. Why can one interpolation kernel participate in two operations with different user semantics?
3. What does `input frames per output frame` mean when the value is greater than one?
4. Why does downsampling require low-pass filtering?
5. How is a same-duration pitch shift constructed from time stretching and resampling?
6. Why is formant preservation not identical to pitch preservation?
7. What clip policies should APEX distinguish when project BPM changes?
8. Why must importing a file at the project BPM not automatically authorize stretching?
9. What does WSOLA search for, and why can it fail on dense material?
10. Why does TD-PSOLA depend on reliable pitch epochs?
11. What causes phasiness and transient smear in a basic phase vocoder?
12. Why do phase locking and transient reset reduce but not eliminate artifacts?
13. When is granular processing desirable even if it is not transparent?
14. Why can a content detector make a hybrid algorithm worse?
15. What is the difference between real-time and offline analysis availability?
16. Why must variable-rate processors return both consumed and produced frame counts?
17. Why is a whole-file convenience SRC API unsafe for independent successive streaming blocks?
18. What states are required to drain a processor correctly?
19. Why must a seek reset overlap, phase, filter, and detector history?
20. How is the local ratio derived from adjacent warp anchors?
21. Why must a warp map normally be monotonic?
22. Why do warp anchors require stable identity?
23. Who owns the exact final frame count during offline rendering?
24. Why should linked channels share timing decisions?
25. Which properties belong in an analysis-cache key?
26. Why should the project persist semantic profiles instead of raw library enums?
27. What additional risk does a high-quality FFT resampler introduce for live use?
28. Why are library license claims time-sensitive?
29. Which tests reveal aliasing that a listening test might miss?
30. Why can a spectrogram fail to predict subjective preference?
31. Which performance percentiles matter for real-time stretching?
32. How can APEX prevent a rendered or frozen clip from being stretched twice?

### Section 7 misconceptions check

- **Misconception:** Changing the project sample rate is the same as changing project BPM.  
  **Correction:** Sample rate changes the sampling grid; BPM changes the musical time map.

- **Misconception:** Any speed control preserves pitch.  
  **Correction:** Rate transposition changes pitch and duration together unless a separate time-scale process compensates.

- **Misconception:** Linear interpolation is a complete high-quality downsampler.  
  **Correction:** Downsampling also requires appropriate attenuation above the destination Nyquist limit.

- **Misconception:** A phase vocoder is always better than a time-domain algorithm.  
  **Correction:** Quality depends on content, ratio, latency, implementation, and artifact priorities.

- **Misconception:** A “voice” mode guarantees natural vocals.  
  **Correction:** Speech-specific methods still depend on reliable voicing, pitch, formant, and transient assumptions.

- **Misconception:** One input block should generate exactly one output block.  
  **Correction:** Variable-rate processors consume and produce independent frame counts and may retain state.

- **Misconception:** Signaling end-of-input means the last returned buffer is complete.  
  **Correction:** Stateful filters and stretchers may require continued drain calls.

- **Misconception:** Warp markers can be sorted after the fact without consequence.  
  **Correction:** Invalid non-monotonic edits must be rejected or resolved under an explicit product rule before publication.

- **Misconception:** Processing stereo channels independently improves quality.  
  **Correction:** Independent timing decisions can destroy interchannel phase and image stability.

- **Misconception:** The highest quality preset is always correct for monitoring.  
  **Correction:** Higher-quality modes can add latency and CPU cost that violate the real-time deadline.

- **Misconception:** An open-source license automatically clears every patent or distribution concern.  
  **Correction:** Copyright license, patent rights, platform terms, and product distribution are separate review domains.

- **Misconception:** Detecting a source BPM means the clip should follow project tempo.  
  **Correction:** Detection provides metadata and confidence; the user or product policy selects the transformation.

### Section 7 mastery rubric

| Level | Demonstrated capability |
|---|---|
| Foundation | Distinguishes SRC, repitch, time stretch, pitch shift, formants, major algorithm families, and clip timebase policies |
| Engineering | Implements stateful consumed/produced processing, drain/reset, monotonic warp evaluation, linked channels, and exact-length tests |
| Architecture | Defines APEX clip semantics, backend abstraction, cache identity, quality tiers, latency ownership, migration, and fallback policy |
| Research | Reproduces algorithm behavior from primary sources, measures artifacts and performance, audits current licenses, and separates documented facts from product recommendations |

### 7.6 Primary sources

- [libsamplerate API](https://libsndfile.github.io/libsamplerate/api.html): official whole-file, stateful streaming, and callback API descriptions.
- [libsamplerate FAQ](https://libsndfile.github.io/libsamplerate/faq.html): official guidance on streaming state, consumed/produced counts, transport delay, and debugging.
- [libsamplerate quality documentation](https://libsndfile.github.io/libsamplerate/quality.html): official converter-quality measurement definitions.
- [libsamplerate upstream repository and license](https://github.com/libsndfile/libsamplerate): current source and BSD-2-Clause licensing evidence.
- [SoX Resampler upstream repository](https://github.com/chirlu/soxr): official implementation description, configurable quality/phase behavior, variable-rate support, latency note, and license files.
- [SoX Resampler documentation](https://sourceforge.net/p/soxr/wiki/Home/): official end-of-input and drain guidance.
- [Rubber Band class documentation](https://breakfastquay.com/rubberband/code-doc/classRubberBand_1_1RubberBandStretcher.html): official offline study/process and real-time streaming contracts.
- [Rubber Band technical notes](https://breakfastquay.com/rubberband/technical.html): published R2 phase-vocoder, transient-reset, adaptive-stretch, phase-coherence, and pitch-shift implementation notes.
- [Rubber Band licensing](https://breakfastquay.com/rubberband/license.html): official GPL-2.0-or-later and commercial licensing description.
- [SoundTouch official site](https://www.surina.net/soundtouch/): official tempo, pitch, rate, platform, latency, and LGPL/commercial-option statements.
- [Roelands and Verhelst, WSOLA structures and evaluation](https://www.isca-archive.org/eurospeech_1993/roelands93_eurospeech.html): primary WSOLA method and online-operation evidence.
- [Moulines and Charpentier, pitch-synchronous waveform processing](https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-6393(90)90021-Z): primary PSOLA family, speech assumptions, and distortion discussion.
- [Laroche and Dolson, improved phase-vocoder time-scale modification](https://doi.org/10.1109/89.759041): primary phase-coherence and phase-locking research.
- [Laroche and Dolson, new phase-vocoder pitch-shifting techniques](https://www.ee.columbia.edu/~dpwe/papers/LaroD99-pvoc.pdf): primary explanation of pitch shifting through time scaling plus SRC and direct spectral alternatives.
- [Ableton Live manual — Audio Clips, Tempo, and Warping](https://www.ableton.com/en/manual/audio-clips-tempo-and-warping/): official documented product behavior separating warping, pitch-preserving timing changes, and repitch behavior.
- [DawDreamer paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.09931): public implementation evidence for source-time/beat warp-marker pairs driving Rubber Band; not evidence of closed-source Ableton internals.

## 8. Mixing, Routing, Metering, and Rendering

### Section 8 guide

#### Section 8 prerequisites

Before beginning this section, the learner should be able to:

- Explain the project-model, render-snapshot, device, and persistence boundaries from §1.
- Calculate an audio callback deadline and identify work that cannot block from §2.
- Distinguish device latency, stream configuration, clock drift, and hardware monitoring from §3.
- Explain plugin buses, latency reporting, bypass, tails, sample-offset events, and offline process modes from §4.
- Trace a Tracktion or comparable edit model into a playback graph from §5.
- Distinguish timeline samples, reference samples, beat time, block-local offsets, and external synchronization from §6.
- Explain sample-rate conversion, variable-rate processing, pre-roll, drain, and exact frame-count ownership from §7.
- Use decibels, linear gain, mean square, RMS, and basic graph terminology.

A learner does not need professional mixing experience before reading this section. The purpose is not to teach artistic taste. The purpose is to explain how a DAW represents, schedules, measures, monitors, and renders the signal paths on which creative decisions depend.

#### Why mixing and routing architecture matters

A DAW mixer is not merely a collection of faders. It is a directed processing graph whose visible controls create, remove, or modify paths through audio, MIDI, control, and monitoring systems. A user sees tracks, buses, sends, sidechains, solo buttons, meters, and a master output. The engine must turn those gestures into a graph that is valid, latency-aligned, real-time safe, persistent, testable, and reproducible enough for the product's promises.

The same routing decision can affect several independent results:

```text
what the performer hears while recording
what the control room hears
what is written to a recording file
what is heard during playback
what a stem contains
what an offline export contains
what a meter measures
what a sidechain processor receives
```

Confusing these results is a common source of DAW defects. A send may feed a reverb return without replacing the track's main output. A subgroup normally replaces or redirects the main path. A sidechain key controls a processor but is not automatically part of the processor's audible output. A monitor dim switch must not reduce the exported file. Plugin delay compensation must align converging paths without adding the same latency twice. A meter must state where it taps the graph and which measurement it displays.

For APEX, this domain is central because Bubblegum routing is a product-defining interface. The visual cables, bubbles, colors, and animation may be expressive, but the underlying routing state must remain exact. The engine needs one authoritative routing graph; the UI is a projection and editor of that graph, not a second source of truth.

#### Section 8 learning outcomes

After completing this section, the learner should be able to:

1. **Diagram** a mixer as typed nodes, ports, taps, and edges rather than as an assumed left-to-right channel strip.
2. **Distinguish** a main output, subgroup, auxiliary send, return, sidechain key, external insert, VCA-style control relationship, cue mix, and monitor route.
3. **Compile** user-facing routing into an immutable execution graph with explicit channel layouts, fan-in, fan-out, and cycle policy.
4. **Derive** plugin delay compensation for converging paths and explain why sidechains, bypass paths, oversampling, sandbox pipelines, and hardware inserts participate.
5. **Separate** device latency, graph latency, presentation latency, monitored latency, and recording-placement policy.
6. **Implement** click-free gain, pan, mute, bypass, send, and dry/wet transitions while preserving scheduled automation timing.
7. **Compare** linear, constant-power, balance, and width semantics and defend a documented product policy.
8. **Explain** sample peak, true peak, RMS, Momentary, Short-term, Integrated loudness, and Loudness Range without treating them as interchangeable.
9. **Design** a meter pipeline whose numerical results are independent of device block size and whose UI cannot block the audio thread.
10. **Preserve** routing, transport, PDC, state, tails, and publication safety during offline render, freeze, bounce, and stem generation.
11. **Separate** the control-room path from the mix and delivery paths, including PFL, AFL, solo-in-place, cue mixes, talkback, dim, speaker management, and calibration.
12. **Apply** these models to APEX while preserving Bubblegum visual routing and preventing UI state from becoming render state.
13. **Validate** the architecture with impulse tests, null comparisons, loudness test signals, failure injection, route-state tests, and repeatable render reports.

#### Section 8 evidence of mastery

A learner demonstrates mastery with evidence such as:

- A typed routing graph for a session containing tracks, a drum subgroup, parallel compression, a shared reverb, a sidechain compressor, a cue mix, and a monitor path.
- A compiler test proving that an inactive send remains persistent but contributes silence, while a deleted send no longer exists in the graph.
- An impulse-alignment test across unequal plugin, sidechain, sandbox, and hardware-insert latencies.
- A smoothing test showing no discontinuity when gain, pan, mute, bypass, or dry/wet values change at arbitrary sample offsets.
- A meter test showing equivalent Integrated loudness for the same programme processed at several device block sizes.
- A render test showing that monitor dim, room correction, talkback, and PFL/AFL do not enter the exported mix.
- An APEX design memo mapping Bubblegum cable states to stable route identities, graph generations, validation rules, and render-snapshot adoption.

### 8.1 Routing graph

#### What a routing graph is

A routing graph is the host-owned representation of signal producers, processors, destinations, control dependencies, and the connections between them. A visible mixer strip is one useful view of that graph, but it is not the complete graph.

A minimal typed model may contain:

```cpp
enum class PortKind {
    audio,
    midi,
    note,
    sidechainAudio,
    control,
    transport,
    monitor
};

struct PortDescriptor {
    StableId portId;
    PortKind kind;
    ChannelLayout layout;
    Direction direction;
};

struct RouteEdge {
    StableId routeId;
    StableId sourcePort;
    StableId destinationPort;
    TapIdentity tap;
    RouteGain gain;
    RouteState state;
};
```

The exact classes are a product choice. The important properties are:

- Every route has stable identity.
- Source and destination types are explicit.
- Channel layout is validated.
- The tap point is explicit.
- Active, inactive, missing, and invalid are distinguishable states.
- User-facing names and colors do not substitute for engine identity.
- The editable graph is compiled into a real-time execution snapshot.

JUCE's `AudioProcessorGraph` demonstrates the basic public idea of processors as nodes and channel-to-channel connections as edges. Ardour's documented routing shows why a production mixer must go further: tracks can change channel width through processors, auxiliary sends branch from specific locations, inserts interrupt and return to the path, and patching may connect tracks, buses, hardware, and external applications.

#### Why the graph must be explicit

An implicit mixer often assumes a fixed sequence:

```text
input → inserts → fader → pan → master
```

That model fails as soon as the user requests:

- A pre-insert cue send.
- A post-fader reverb send.
- Parallel compression.
- A sidechain from another track.
- A hardware insert.
- A multi-output instrument.
- A bus feeding more than one destination.
- A monitor path that is excluded from export.
- A surround or spatial channel layout.

The graph therefore needs explicit nodes and branch points. A channel strip can still present a familiar ordered interface, but the engine must know that a send is an edge leaving a defined tap, not an adjective attached to a track.

#### Main path, send, subgroup, return, and VCA-style control

These relationships are different:

| Relationship | Audio behavior | Does the original main route remain? | Typical purpose |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Main output | Delivers the primary track or bus output | N/A | Main mix, subgroup, hardware output |
| Auxiliary send | Copies or branches signal from a defined tap | Usually yes | Shared FX, cue mix, parallel processing |
| Subgroup route | Redirects main output through another summing bus | Usually no direct duplicate to master | Common processing and level control |
| Return bus | Sums one or more sends and processes their result | Separate branch | Shared reverb, delay, parallel processing |
| Sidechain key | Supplies control audio to a processor input | Main route is independent | Compression, gating, dynamic EQ triggering |
| External insert | Interrupts a path and expects a return | Path depends on return | Outboard processing |
| VCA-style control | Changes one or more gains without summing audio | Yes | Group level control without a new audio bus |

A VCA-style group is not a bus. It changes control values or effective gains; it does not create a new summing point. This distinction matters for processing, metering, latency, solo, and stem semantics.

#### Tap points

A send needs a precise source identity. Labels such as `pre-fader` and `post-fader` are useful but can be insufficient when a strip contains movable processors.

A robust route references a stable tap or processor boundary:

```text
input trim output
before insert slot 1
after insert slot 3
before fader
after fader
before panner
after panner
post channel-format conversion
```

If a plugin is reordered around a send, the product must define whether the send stays attached to a semantic tap or moves with a neighboring processor. That choice must persist through save/load and undo.

#### Sidechains are control dependencies

A sidechain key is an input dependency that can affect the audible result of another node. It must therefore participate in graph ordering and timing. It is not automatically summed into the target node's audible output.

Example:

```text
Kick audible path ───────────────→ drum bus
      └─ hidden key branch ─────→ bass compressor sidechain input
Bass audible path → compressor ─→ music bus
```

The exported bass includes the compressor's reaction to the kick. It does not include audible kick unless another route explicitly mixes the kick into that stem.

#### Channel layouts and adapters

A connection is valid only if source and destination layouts are compatible or an explicit adapter exists. Never assume that channel count alone defines meaning.

```text
2 channels may mean stereo L/R
2 channels may mean dual mono
4 channels may mean first-order ambisonics
6 channels may mean 5.1 with a declared order
```

The compiler may insert explicit operations for:

- Mono-to-stereo duplication.
- Stereo-to-mono downmix under a documented coefficient policy.
- Channel reordering.
- Bus-layout conversion.
- Format adapters for plugins with fixed layouts.

Silent implicit conversion is dangerous because the user cannot reason about level, phase, or channel identity.

#### Fan-out and fan-in

Fan-out occurs when one source feeds several consumers. The source buffer must remain valid until every consumer that needs the original value has completed.

Fan-in occurs when several sources feed one destination. The engine must define:

- The channel mapping for each input.
- The gain applied before summation.
- The order of accumulation when determinism matters.
- Whether an inactive source contributes explicit silence or is absent.
- The numeric format and headroom policy.

Floating-point addition is not mathematically associative. Reordering many additions may produce small numerical differences. Most creative sessions do not require bit-identical summation across machines, but deterministic render modes should stabilize source order, worker reduction order, processor state, and other relevant variables.

#### Feedback and cycles

A zero-delay cycle has no well-defined evaluation order:

```text
A output → B input
B output → A input
```

A DAW should reject it or require an explicit delay element that defines state from a previous sample or block. The delay becomes part of the route, latency model, persistence, and render result.

Do not create an undocumented one-block feedback delay merely because the graph executor processes in blocks. Block size would then change the sound.

#### Editable graph versus render graph

The user edits a mutable project graph. The audio callback consumes an immutable compiled graph.

```text
UI command
→ validate model edit
→ update undoable routing state
→ compile topology, layouts, buffers, PDC, taps, and execution order
→ publish new render snapshot
→ audio thread adopts at a safe boundary
→ reclaim old snapshot off the real-time path
```

Value-only changes may use bounded event or parameter paths when topology does not change. Creating a send, deleting a route, changing a bus layout, moving a processor across a tap, or altering plugin latency usually requires a graph rebuild.

#### APEX Bubblegum routing policy

**Recommendation:** APEX should treat `RoutingGraph` as the authoritative source of truth and Bubblegum cables as a visual projection of stable routes.

The product already distinguishes useful send states:

```text
route absent
route exists and active
route exists and inactive
```

Those states should remain distinct in persistence and undo:

- **Absent:** no route object; no graph edge.
- **Active:** route exists and contributes according to gain, tap, and mapping.
- **Inactive:** route exists, keeps identity and settings, but contributes bounded silence or is omitted by a compile optimization that preserves semantics.

The cable renderer may animate thickness, color, sag, droplets, spectrum, or activity. None of those visual states should be read by the audio engine. Meter snapshots may drive animation through a one-way UI data path.

Suggested ownership:

```text
ProjectRoutingModel
    stable route identities, names, states, taps, layouts, undo

RoutingCompiler
    validation, cycle policy, adapters, PDC, buffer plan, execution graph

RoutingSnapshot
    immutable operations adopted by audio workers

BubblegumRoutingView
    reads project model + meter snapshots
    emits commands
    never becomes render state
```

#### Worked example: routing graph

A vocal session contains:

- Lead vocal track.
- Vocal subgroup.
- Shared reverb return.
- Delay return.
- Parallel-compression return.
- Headphone cue bus.
- Music bus feeding a sidechain key to the vocal compressor.
- Master bus.
- Monitor bus with room correction and dim.

The graph contains separate branches:

```text
Lead input
→ input trim
→ corrective inserts
├─ pre-fader cue send ─────────────────────────────→ Cue bus → headphones
├─ post-fader reverb send ─────────────────────────→ Reverb return ─┐
├─ post-fader delay send ──────────────────────────→ Delay return ──┤
├─ post-insert parallel send ──────────────────────→ Parallel comp ─┤
└─ main path → fader → pan → Vocal subgroup ────────────────────────┤
                                                                  Music mix
Music bus hidden key ─────────→ Vocal subgroup compressor sidechain │
Music mix → Master ─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Master export tap → offline/export graph
Master monitor tap → Monitor bus → room correction → speaker output
Talkback → Cue bus only
```

The exported master excludes room correction, monitor dim, speaker selection, and talkback. The performer hears the cue branch, not necessarily the master branch. The sidechain key remains available to the compressor but is not audibly added to the vocal subgroup.

#### Routing failure modes

- A send is represented only by a UI cable, so reopening the mixer silently removes it.
- A deleted route leaves a dangling node or buffer pointer in the render snapshot.
- An inactive send loses its saved level and cannot be restored.
- A sidechain is ignored by dependency ordering and arrives one block late.
- A monitor route enters the export graph.
- A subgroup is implemented like an aux send, duplicating the signal to the master.
- A channel-count match is mistaken for a channel-layout match.
- A cycle is accepted and gains an accidental block-size-dependent delay.
- A worker reorders fan-in nondeterministically while the product promises repeatable renders.

### 8.2 Plugin delay compensation

#### What plugin delay compensation solves

Some processors cannot produce an output that corresponds to the current input sample immediately. Look-ahead dynamics, linear-phase filters, oversampling, convolution, resampling, sandbox pipelines, and external hardware can add delay. When delayed and non-delayed paths converge, their musical events and waveforms no longer align.

Plugin delay compensation, or PDC, inserts delay on shorter paths so that signals intended to meet at a summing or control point arrive together.

VST3 exposes `IAudioProcessor::getLatencySamples()` and requires a plugin to notify the host when that latency changes. Comparable plugin APIs provide their own latency mechanisms. Reported plugin latency is one input to the host's graph calculation; it is not the complete device or recording latency model.

#### Latency vocabulary

Keep these concepts separate:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Node latency | Delay introduced by one processor or adapter |
| Path latency | Sum of relevant node and transport delays along a route |
| Compensation delay | Delay inserted on a shorter path to align a convergence |
| Device input latency | Delay from the physical input to samples delivered to the host |
| Device output latency | Delay from host samples to physical output |
| Presentation latency | Timing context reported or supplied around a processor's connection to real devices |
| Monitoring latency | Delay perceived by a performer through the selected monitor path |
| Recording placement offset | Policy used to place captured material on the project timeline |
| Hardware-insert round trip | Measured send, converter, hardware, return, and buffering delay |

PDC aligns graph paths. It does not automatically calibrate physical recording placement, compensate unknown driver error, or make a high-latency monitor path comfortable for a performer.

#### Canonical path calculation

For a directed acyclic graph, define:

```text
T_out(source) = source_latency

T_in(n) = max(T_out(p)) for every predecessor p of n
Delay(p, n) = T_in(n) - T_out(p)
T_out(n) = T_in(n) + L(n)
```

Where:
