2. Attempt normal companion discovery.
3. Attempt ARA factory acquisition through the companion integration.
4. Apply a deadline and attribute a crash or timeout to the candidate.
5. Record protocol/capability metadata.
6. Destroy in legal order.
7. Persist a versioned result keyed by binary fingerprint.

A factory-probe failure should not necessarily blacklist the ordinary plug-in. It may remain usable as a conventional companion processor while ARA capability is disabled with a diagnostic.

### 38.5 Canonical host model versus ARA projection

#### Authority rule

**Recommendation:** The APEX project model remains canonical. ARA receives a projection of relevant objects and relationships.

```text
APEX Asset / AudioSource
APEX SourceUse / ClipSourceBinding
APEX Clip / CompSegment / Region
APEX Track or Lane Sequence
APEX Tempo/Meter/Key map
APEX command transaction
        ↓ mapping layer
ARA AudioSource
ARA AudioModification
ARA PlaybackRegion
ARA RegionSequence
ARA MusicalContext
ARA edit scope / notification batch
```

This is a conceptual mapping, not a claim that every APEX object maps one-to-one in every workflow.

#### Why a projection is necessary

The DAW must still open a project when:

- The ARA plug-in is missing.
- A different plug-in version cannot restore old analysis.
- A source is offline.
- The user disables ARA processing.
- ARA data is corrupt.
- The project is opened on an unsupported platform.

APEX therefore must preserve source, clip, edit, and timeline truth independently. ARA-specific data augments the project and can be represented by placeholders when unavailable.

### 38.6 Stable identity model

ARA integration fails easily when object identity is inferred from array position, pointer address, display name, or timeline start.

Recommended stable identities:

```text
AraDocumentId
AraPluginInstanceId
AraAudioSourceId
AraAudioModificationId
AraPlaybackRegionId
AraRegionSequenceId
AraMusicalContextId
AraStateArchiveId
AraAnalysisGeneration
```

Mappings should be persisted explicitly:

```cpp
struct AraObjectBinding {
    StableId apexObject;
    StableId araObject;
    StableId araDocument;
    std::uint64_t hostObjectRevision;
    std::uint64_t araRevision;
};
```

#### Identity rules

- Moving a clip does not change its identity.
- Trimming may update one playback-region range while preserving the region identity if the semantic object remains the same.
- Splitting creates new host clip identities and normally requires explicit new playback-region identities or a documented reuse policy.
- A copied clip may share the same source and audio modification or create an independent modification, depending on linked-copy semantics.
- “Make Unique” must create the identities required for independent ARA edits.
- Consolidation creates a new source asset and invalidates bindings that depended on the old source topology.
- Save As preserves project identity policy according to §9 and does not silently reseed or regenerate every ARA identity.

### 38.7 ARA document scope

#### Scope alternatives

| Scope | Benefit | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| One ARA document per project per plug-in implementation | Shared analysis/context and coherent document edits | Large lifetime, state, and failure blast radius |
| One document per track | Simpler ownership and isolation | Cross-track context and shared analysis may be limited; more instances/state |
| One document per clip | Very simple local mapping | Excessive duplication, weak sequence context, costly analysis/state |
| Hybrid document groups | Can match product workflows | More complex persistence and movement between groups |

**Recommendation:** APEX should begin with one ARA document per project per ARA plug-in class/instance group only if the selected plug-in and integration contract support that model cleanly. The actual grouping decision must be validated against the SDK, target plug-ins, project state size, editor behavior, and failure isolation.

The host must not create one universal ARA document shared by unrelated plug-in implementations.

### 38.8 Audio sources

#### Meaning

An ARA audio source represents host-provided audio material and descriptive properties. It is not the same as one timeline clip. Multiple edits or playback regions can refer to one source.

For APEX, a source binding should include:

```text
stable asset/source ID
content fingerprint and revision
sample rate
sample count or duration
channel count/layout
source origin and ownership policy
availability state
random-access reader factory
content-change generation
```

#### Source revision

A path and filename are insufficient. If the underlying media changes while retaining the same path, cached analysis can become invalid.

Recommended source revision inputs:

- Content hash where available.
- File size and modification evidence as a fast precheck, not sole authority.
- Imported/decoded canonical media identity.
- Channel-layout and sample-rate revision.
- Destructive source-replacement generation.
- Proxy-to-original relation.

#### Missing source policy

When a source is missing:

- Preserve the ARA and host object identities.
- Do not silently bind a different same-named file.
- Prevent random-access reads from returning stale unrelated content.
- Report explicit unavailable status.
- Permit hash-aware relink.
- Revalidate or invalidate analysis after relink according to content identity.

### 38.9 Random-access audio delivery

#### Contract

Random audio access must define:

```text
source identity and revision
sample rate and channel layout
requested start and frame count
destination representation
out-of-range policy
thread and reentrancy policy
cancellation and shutdown
read error behavior
lifetime of returned data
```

A robust host does not hand a third-party plug-in raw pointers into mutable caches whose lifetime it cannot guarantee.

#### Read architecture

```text
ARA plug-in requests source range
→ host validates source and revision
→ source service resolves canonical media/proxy
→ decoder/cache fulfills range on allowed thread
→ samples copied into caller-owned or contract-owned buffer
→ status reports complete/partial/unavailable/cancelled
```

Whether a particular callback is synchronous and which thread may call it are SDK-contract questions that must be verified against the pinned ARA version. The host must prepare for reentrancy where permitted and must not take locks whose ownership can invert with plug-in callbacks.

#### Realtime boundary

Random-access reading for analysis must not make the active device callback wait for disk or decode. ARA playback rendering may occur under realtime constraints through prepared renderer roles; arbitrary source reads and analysis belong to permitted non-realtime contexts.

#### Out-of-range policy

A request partially outside the source must follow one documented policy:

- Return silence for unavailable frames and report the valid range.
- Clamp and report a shorter result.
- Reject the request.

The policy must match the SDK contract and cannot be improvised independently by each media backend.

### 38.10 Audio modifications

#### Meaning

An audio modification represents a derived interpretation or edit state associated with an audio source. Multiple playback regions can reference a modification.

This separation enables workflows such as:

```text
one vocal source
→ modification A: corrected lead tuning
→ modification B: alternate timing edit
→ playback regions from A and B placed independently
```

#### Host mapping questions

APEX must explicitly decide:

- Does duplicating a clip share the audio modification?
- Does “Make Unique” clone or recreate modification state?
- Does a comp segment reference one modification across takes?
- What happens when a source is replaced beneath a modification?
- Can one modification be used on multiple tracks?
- How are freeze and Render-in-Place traced back to the modification?

There is no universal product answer. The UI must expose linked versus independent behavior where it changes future edits.

### 38.11 Playback regions

#### Meaning

A playback region maps a portion of a modification/source into a timeline context for rendering and editing. It carries the relationship between source-time and playback-time ranges required by the ARA document model.

The host must keep distinct:

```text
source sample range
modification timeline/reference range
project playback range
musical position/context
time-stretch or warp relation
clip fades and gain outside or inside ARA policy
```

#### Clip-edit mapping

| Host edit | ARA action concept |
|---|---|
| Move clip | Update playback placement/context without changing source content |
| Trim start/end | Update playback-region range and source relation |
| Slip | Change source-relative range while preserving project placement |
| Split | Create two host clips and corresponding playback-region relationship |
| Duplicate linked | New playback region, potentially shared modification |
| Make unique | New modification identity and new playback-region binding |
| Delete | Destroy playback region after renderer/editor assignments are released |
| Reverse | Requires explicit support strategy; may demand derived source or host-side processing |
| Warp/stretch | Requires ownership decision between host and ARA processor to prevent double transformation |

#### Fade/gain ownership

APEX should not automatically push every clip fade, envelope, or gain into ARA. A practical layering can be:

```text
ARA edited source render
→ host clip gain/fades
→ track inserts/routing
```

If an ARA plug-in needs those properties as content/context, provide them through the supported model without duplicating audible processing.

### 38.12 Region sequences and track/lane semantics

A region sequence groups playback regions into an ordered musical/editor context. It should not be equated blindly with one visible track because APEX may have:

- comp lanes;
- takes;
- playlists;
- track versions;
- hidden lanes;
- shared clips;
- nested containers;
- frozen replacements.

**Recommendation:** APEX should define a stable `SequenceIdentity` representing the edit/playback context that ARA should perceive. A visible track can expose one or more sequences according to comp and lane policy.

Questions requiring explicit policy:

- Do inactive takes remain in the ARA document for editing?
- Does comp selection alter one sequence or create a derived playback view?
- Can the editor display multiple sequences simultaneously?
- How are region colors, names, order, and visibility synchronized?
- What happens when a clip moves between tracks or lanes?

### 38.13 Musical contexts

#### Purpose

Musical contexts communicate host knowledge such as tempo, meter, key, and scale relationships associated with regions or sequences. The host should expose authoritative context without pretending that all musical interpretation is objective.

#### Tempo and meter

APEX must map its canonical tempo representation into ARA with:

- Stable context identity.
- Ordered tempo events.
- Meter events.
- Conversion between project time and musical position.
- Explicit handling of ramps/curves according to supported semantics.
- Revision generation.
- Boundary behavior before the first and after the last event.

#### Key and scale

Key/scale information can be:

- User-authored authoritative project metadata.
- Imported metadata.
- Plug-in-derived analysis.
- Unknown.

Do not silently promote plug-in analysis into canonical project truth. A bidirectional update should identify origin, confidence, scope, and whether the user accepted the change.

#### Conflict policy

If host and plug-in content disagree:

```text
preserve both claims with provenance
→ apply product-defined authority
→ display conflict where relevant
→ never silently overwrite user-authored context with analysis
```

### 38.14 Content exchange and confidence

ARA content exchange can include information derived from audio or supplied by the host. APEX should use a neutral internal schema:

```cpp
struct ContentClaim {
    ContentType type;
    StableId subject;
    TimeRange range;
    ContentOrigin origin;
    float confidence;
    std::uint64_t revision;
    Payload payload;
};
```

The exact ARA payload and support flags remain adapter concerns. Internally, the host should distinguish:

- Authoritative user data.
- Host-computed analysis.
- Plug-in-computed analysis.
- Imported metadata.
- Unknown or unavailable content.

#### Why confidence matters

Detected notes, chords, tempo, and key are interpretations. A result may be useful while uncertain. A UI that displays analysis as indisputable truth makes correction and collaboration difficult.

### 38.15 Analysis lifecycle

ARA allows plug-ins to perform sophisticated analysis, but the host still needs a lifecycle model:

```text
Unrequested
→ Queued
→ ReadingSource
→ Analyzing
→ PartialResult
→ Complete
→ Stale
→ Failed / Cancelled
```

#### Invalidation reasons

- Source bytes changed.
- Source sample rate/channel interpretation changed.
- Plug-in version changed.
- Analysis algorithm/settings changed.
- Audio modification changed.
- Musical context changed where analysis depends on it.
- State archive failed validation.
- User requested reanalysis.

#### Progress

Progress callbacks must not flood the UI. APEX should throttle/coalesce updates and preserve:

- Analysis job identity.
- Source/modification identity.
- Revision being analyzed.
- Completed/total estimate where valid.
- Cancellation state.
- Failure reason.

A stale job must not publish results into a newer source or modification generation.

### 38.16 Change notification and edit scopes

#### Why batching exists

One user gesture can modify many related objects. A clip split may create two regions, adjust sequences, update selections, modify fades, and change undo state. Sending each mutation as an unrelated immediate notification can expose invalid intermediate models.

Recommended flow:

```text
begin host edit transaction
→ enter required ARA edit scope/guard
→ create/update/destroy related objects in legal order
→ complete ARA notifications
→ validate mapping invariants
→ commit host undo transaction
→ publish new render generation
```

The pinned SDK defines exact editable-state and notification rules. JUCE exposes an `ARAEditGuard` helper to keep a document controller in editable state around host changes.

#### Reentrancy

Host-to-plug-in calls may trigger plug-in-to-host callbacks where the API permits. Avoid holding:

- Project-model mutexes.
- UI locks.
- Plug-in registry locks.
- Graph publication locks.
- File-cache locks.

across calls into third-party ARA code unless the pinned contract and lock ordering are proven safe.

#### Ordering principle

Create parents before children; detach renderer/editor assignments before destroying referenced model objects; destroy children before parents where required. Tests must enforce actual SDK ordering rather than relying on C++ destructor coincidence.

### 38.17 Undo and redo

#### Authority

The host owns the user-visible undo history for project operations. ARA-aware plug-ins may initiate or report edits that must be represented coherently.

A completed transaction should identify:

```text
transaction ID
human-readable action
host objects affected
ARA objects affected
before/after host revisions
before/after ARA archive or command state
render invalidation reason
```

#### Undo design alternatives

| Strategy | Benefit | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| Host command replay | Efficient and semantically clear | Every ARA mutation must be reversible and version-safe |
| Snapshot ARA archive per transaction | Simple recovery model | Large storage and serialization cost |
| Plug-in-managed undo mirrored by host | Preserves plug-in semantics | Two histories can diverge; lifecycle complexity |
| Hybrid checkpoints plus commands | Bounded recovery and efficient common edits | More implementation complexity |

**Recommendation:** Begin with host-owned transactions and plug-in-supported edit grouping. Use versioned checkpoints at safe intervals if required for robust recovery. Do not create an invisible second undo stack that the user cannot reconcile with APEX.

#### Undo acceptance rule

After undo and redo:

- Host object graph matches the intended prior/next revision.
- ARA object relationships match.
- Renderer assignments are valid.
- Audible output matches the corresponding saved reference under defined tolerance.
- No stale analysis/result is displayed as current.

### 38.18 Persistence architecture

#### State layers

A project may need to persist:

| Layer | Owner |
|---|---|
| APEX project objects and stable IDs | Host |
| ARA object bindings and grouping policy | Host |
| ARA document/archive data | ARA plug-in/document controller through host storage contract |
| Companion plug-in processor/controller state | Companion host adapter |
| Derived host caches | Host, regenerable |
| Plug-in analysis cache embedded in ARA state | Plug-in-defined opaque data |
| Dependency manifest | Host |

Do not concatenate opaque blobs without boundaries. Use a container with typed entries, lengths, hashes, versions, and ownership metadata.

Conceptual manifest:

```text
ara/document/<id>/binding.json
ara/document/<id>/archive.bin
plugins/<instance>/companion-state.bin
plugins/<instance>/descriptor.json
assets/<source>/identity.json
manifest.json
```

#### Atomic save

```text
capture stable host revision
→ request/serialize ARA state on allowed thread
→ serialize companion state
→ validate sizes and checksums
→ write temporary project package
→ fsync/close according to durability level
→ atomically publish
→ advance saved revision only after success
```

A failed ARA archive write must not overwrite the previous valid project.

#### Restore order

A typical restore plan is:

1. Parse and validate host project schema.
2. Resolve plug-in descriptors and compatibility policy.
3. Create module/factory/companion/document-control resources off realtime.
4. Recreate host canonical objects and stable bindings.
5. Restore ARA document objects/archive in legal order.
6. Restore companion plug-in state according to companion contract.
7. Assign playback/editor renderer roles.
8. Validate source identities and availability.
9. Compile/publish a prepared render graph.
10. Open editor only after a coherent document exists.

The pinned SDK and specific companion integration determine exact processor/controller state ordering. Test real target plug-ins rather than generalizing one product's behavior.

### 38.19 Archive validation and defensive loading

Opaque does not mean trusted. Treat ARA archives and companion state as untrusted length-delimited data.

Validate:

- Maximum total archive size.
- Integer lengths and offsets.
- Entry counts.
- Stable-ID syntax and uniqueness.
- Plugin class/factory identity.
- SDK/protocol compatibility.
- Hashes where stored.
- Source-binding references.
- Decompression limits.
- Recursion/depth limits.
- Timeout and cancellation.

If restoration fails:

- Preserve the original project file.
- Keep canonical APEX clips and sources.
- Create a failed/missing ARA placeholder.
- Do not report the project as fully restored.
- Offer retry, alternate plug-in version, reanalysis, or removal while preserving user audio edits.

### 38.20 Companion state and ARA state synchronization

The ordinary plug-in state and ARA document state can be related but are not interchangeable. APEX should save and restore both under one transaction and track their revisions.

Potential mismatch cases:

- Companion state restores parameters but ARA archive is absent.
- ARA archive restores edits but companion state uses incompatible algorithm settings.
- Plug-in version migrates one state layer but rejects the other.
- A user changes a companion parameter after an ARA checkpoint.

Recommended manifest fields:

```text
companionStateRevision
araArchiveRevision
pluginBinaryFingerprint
pluginSemanticVersion if available
factoryIdentity
hostBindingSchemaVersion
sourceRevisionSet
saveTransactionId
```

The host should never silently combine state layers from different save transactions.

### 38.21 Playback renderer role

#### Purpose

The playback renderer produces the ARA-edited result during normal playback. The host assigns playback regions to the appropriate renderer/extension instance and supplies the normal process context through the companion integration.

JUCE's host-side ARA model documentation notes that hosts commonly create one or more ARA extension instances for playback and editor rendering and assign playback regions to those renderer interfaces.

#### Graph integration

```text
prepared ARA playback renderer node
→ optional host clip gain/fades
→ track inserts
→ sends/buses
→ master
```

The actual ordering is an APEX product decision and must avoid processing the same correction twice.

#### Node contract

An ARA renderer node should expose:

```text
prepare(actual sample rate, max block, layout)
assign immutable region-set generation
process bounded block
dynamic latency notification
tail/silence behavior
reset/discontinuity behavior
offline mode capability
failure state
```

Mutable document edits should compile into a prepared renderer assignment generation adopted at a safe boundary.

### 38.22 Editor renderer and editor view

ARA distinguishes playback rendering, editor rendering, and editor-view responsibilities. Editor rendering may be required for audition, preview, or editor-specific visualization/workflows that are not identical to the main transport renderer.

#### UI ownership

- The ARA plug-in owns its editor implementation.
- APEX owns the parent window, docking/floating policy, focus integration, accessibility fallback, lifecycle, and project association.
- The editor must not become the canonical owner of model objects.
- Closing the editor must not destroy playback state.
- Destroying or replacing the document must detach the editor view safely first.

#### DPI/focus/modal policy

Reuse the native-editor contracts from §10 and §21:

- Per-monitor DPI awareness.
- Host/plugin resize negotiation.
- Focus and keyboard-command arbitration.
- IME and text input.
- Modal-loop restrictions.
- Z-order and floating-window ownership.
- Accessibility and generic status fallback.

An ARA editor can be much more document-centric than an ordinary parameter panel; closing/reopening it must restore selection and view state without changing audio truth.

### 38.23 Selection and view synchronization

Selection is not canonical audio state, but it strongly affects editing UX.

APEX should distinguish:

```text
project selection
ARA editor selection
playback cursor
edit cursor
loop range
time selection
visible region range
focused sequence
```

Synchronization must avoid feedback loops:

```text
origin = APEX timeline
→ update ARA view with transaction/origin token
→ plug-in callback echoes selection
→ host recognizes token and suppresses redundant command
```

Selection updates should be throttled where high frequency and excluded from undo unless they are part of an explicit product operation.

### 38.24 Tempo-map and transport changes

#### Tempo edits

A tempo change can alter musical context without changing source samples. The host should:

1. Commit the canonical tempo-map edit.
2. Increment musical-context revision.
3. Notify affected ARA contexts in a batch.
4. Determine whether analyses become stale.
5. Rebuild playback-region timing/render assignments.
6. Publish the new render generation.

#### Transport discontinuities

Seek, loop, stop, punch, and scrubbing must be represented to the playback renderer according to companion/ARA process-context contracts. ARA does not justify bypassing the transport discontinuity policy in §6, §8, and §31.

#### Tempo ownership with time correction

If both APEX warp/stretch and the ARA plug-in alter timing, the host must define one order. A safe default is to avoid double time transformation:

- ARA owns correction; host warp is disabled or baked before ARA.
- Host owns warp; ARA receives the resulting source/context relation.
- A derived source boundary separates the transformations.

The choice must be visible and reversible.

### 38.25 Clip edits and transaction mapping

#### Move

Preserve source and modification; update playback placement and sequence/context.

#### Trim

Update region bounds. Decide whether hidden trimmed content remains available to the ARA editor and how re-expansion behaves.

#### Slip

Change source-relative mapping without changing project range. Verify whether ARA edits follow source-time, region-time, or modification-time semantics.

#### Split

Create two persistent clip IDs and update playback regions atomically. Preserve shared modification only if linked-edit behavior is intended.

#### Duplicate

The duplicate command must state:

```text
shared source?
shared modification?
shared analysis?
independent future edits?
new playback-region identity?
new sequence membership?
```

#### Consolidate/bounce

Create a new asset/source and a trace record. The original ARA state may remain behind an unfreeze/revert boundary; it must not be silently rebound to different audio bytes.

### 38.26 Comping and take lanes

Comping introduces many source fragments and changing active selections.

Architecture options:

| Model | Benefit | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| ARA per raw take | Preserves source analysis and edits | Comp playback assembly remains host responsibility |
| ARA on derived comp source | Simple single sequence | Recomping invalidates/bakes analysis |
| Shared document with take sequences | Rich editor access | More model/selection complexity |
| Hybrid raw-take analysis plus derived playback | Efficient reuse | Complex mapping and persistence |

**Recommendation:** APEX should initially apply ARA to stable clips/takes, not to a continuously mutating virtual comp unless the integration is proven. A comp commit can create a derived source for the first shipping vertical slice while preserving the raw-take project model for undo.

### 38.27 Freeze, bounce, and Render-in-Place

These operations must include the ARA renderer in the same graph semantics as live playback.

#### Freeze

- Capture immutable project/ARA state.
- Render the correct ARA playback regions.
- Include or exclude downstream inserts according to freeze boundary.
- Preserve source/modification/archive state for unfreeze.
- Reconcile latency, tails, sends, and sidechains.

#### Bounce/Render-in-Place

- Create a traceable derived asset.
- Record whether ARA edits are baked.
- Preserve handles and publication atomicity.
- Decide whether the new clip has no ARA state, cloned state, or a fresh source eligible for reanalysis.

#### Null/equivalence testing

A null comparison is valid only after matching:

- Range.
- PDC.
- Tail.
- Random state.
- Realtime/offline mode.
- Host fades/gain.
- ARA renderer assignment.
- Sample rate and SRC.

A residual demonstrates difference under those conditions; it does not prove which subsystem is wrong.

### 38.28 Offline export

Offline export should use an immutable export snapshot that includes the required ARA document/renderer state.

Potential behaviors:

- Faster-than-realtime ARA rendering supported.
- Realtime-only mode required by a plug-in.
- Background preanalysis required before render.
- Deterministic render unavailable.

APEX policy should:

1. Query capabilities.
2. Freeze export state.
3. Complete required analysis or fail explicitly.
4. Select offline/realtime/hybrid policy.
5. Prevent live input or editor audition from entering the export graph.
6. Validate duration, frames, errors, and publication.

If a plug-in cannot provide a valid offline result, APEX must not silently export unprocessed source audio as success.

### 38.29 Latency, PDC, bypass, and tails

ARA playback still participates in the path latency contract.

- Dynamic latency changes request a control-plane PDC rebuild.
- Bypass must define whether it outputs original source, companion bypass, or ARA-unprocessed audio.
- Dry/wet combinations require aligned paths.
- Tail policy must be queried or conservatively represented.
- Editor audition may use a different route and must not corrupt main-graph PDC.

A bypass transition can require crossfade and state continuity. For pitch/time editing, dry bypass may jump in timing and phase; the UI should communicate the semantic change.

### 38.30 Realtime safety and prepared publication

The ARA document model is mutable control-plane state. The audio thread should not traverse it.

Recommended publication:

```text
host/ARA edit completes
→ validate bindings and renderer assignments
→ prepare immutable AraRenderAssignment generation
→ graph compiler integrates latency/buffers
→ publish completed render snapshot
→ callback adopts at block boundary
→ retire old assignment after all readers finish
```

Prohibited callback behavior includes:

- Serializing ARA state.
- Creating/destroying model objects.
- Reading source files arbitrarily.
- Waiting for analysis.
- Opening editor resources.
- Resizing assignment containers.
- Formatting ARA diagnostics.

### 38.31 Threading and reentrancy contract

A host implementation should document every ARA entry point with:

```text
allowed calling threads
whether call may reenter host
whether call may block
lifetime preconditions
edit-scope requirement
error/timeout behavior
```

Thread roles:

| Thread | Allowed responsibilities |
|---|---|
| Main/control | Model creation/update, editor lifecycle, legal document calls, command integration |
| Audio callback | Prepared playback rendering only under realtime contract |
| Analysis workers | Source reading and analysis where API permits |
| Disk/media workers | Decode/cache/random-access fulfillment |
| Persistence worker/control coordination | State/archive save and restore where contract permits |
| Scanner/helper | Factory probing and validation |

Do not infer thread safety from C++ constness. The pinned SDK documentation and target plug-in behavior are authoritative.

### 38.32 Lifetime and destruction ordering

The host must coordinate:

```text
module
factory
companion instance
ARA document controller
model objects
renderer extension instances
editor view/editor window
prepared graph node
state archive
```

A safe teardown concept:

1. Stop new edits and analysis requests.
2. Detach editor view and close UI.
3. Publish graph without the ARA renderer and wait for old readers to retire.
4. Cancel/join non-realtime jobs under bounded shutdown policy.
5. Detach playback/editor region assignments.
6. Destroy child model objects in legal order.
7. Destroy document controller.
8. Destroy companion instances.
9. Release factory wrapper and module.

Never perform this chain in the device callback.

### 38.33 Sandboxing and crash isolation

ARA complicates sandboxing because it adds document calls, source reads, model notifications, archive transfer, and editor integration beyond normal block IPC.

#### IPC planes

```text
control/model messages
random-access audio requests
realtime audio/events
state/archive streams
analysis progress/content
editor/window messages
health/heartbeat
```

#### Random-access IPC

Options:

- Copy requested ranges through bounded shared-memory windows.
- Maintain a read-only media proxy accessible to the worker under broker policy.
- Decode in host and publish prepared pages.

Never expose arbitrary filesystem access merely because the plug-in requests source samples.

#### Failure policy

If the isolated ARA worker dies:

- Reject stale shared-memory output by generation/sequence.
- Move renderer node to explicit silence or unprocessed-source fallback according to role and user policy.
- Preserve placeholder latency when required for graph alignment.
- Keep ARA archive and canonical APEX clips.
- Offer controlled restart and state restore.
- Mark analysis/editor state unavailable until validated.

A helper process improves containment but does not automatically solve security, state correctness, or deadline completion.

### 38.34 Editor failure and headless operation

The playback renderer should continue when the native editor closes or fails, unless the specific plug-in contract makes that impossible and the host reports failure.

APEX should support:

- Project open without creating the ARA editor.
- Offline export in a headless process where supported.
- Missing GUI resources with preserved playback.
- Generic status panel showing analysis/progress/failure even when the native editor is unavailable.
- Safe recreation of the editor view after DPI/device/project changes.

### 38.35 Source replacement, relink, and content mutation

#### Replacement classes

| Change | Policy |
|---|---|
| Same verified content at new path | Preserve source revision and analysis where contract permits |
| Different content with same format | New source revision; invalidate dependent analysis |
| Channel/sample-rate reinterpretation | New source revision and remapping/reanalysis |
| Proxy replaced by original | Validate time/channel equivalence before preserving analysis |
| Destructive external edit | Detect fingerprint change and require explicit reconciliation |

The host must not tell the ARA plug-in “nothing changed” when the underlying samples changed.

### 38.36 Project migration and plug-in updates

A plug-in update may change:

- Factory identity or capabilities.
- Archive format.
- Analysis algorithm.
- Companion state schema.
- Renderer latency.
- Supported content types.

Migration policy:

```text
open project in isolated/controlled restore path
→ identify exact prior/current binary
→ attempt documented migration
→ preserve original archive
→ validate object counts/bindings/source revisions
→ render comparison or smoke test
→ publish migrated project only after explicit save
```

Never overwrite the only old state during migration.

### 38.37 Collaboration and document merging

ARA document state is not automatically CRDT/OT mergeable. Opaque plug-in archives cannot be field-merged safely without plug-in support.

For collaboration:

- Host project operations remain stable-ID transactions.
- ARA archive changes can be treated as versioned opaque revisions.
- Concurrent edits to the same ARA modification may require lock/lease, branch, or explicit conflict resolution.
- Source assets remain content-addressed/resumable according to §22.
- Collaborators without the plug-in receive placeholders and rendered proxies where policy permits.

A “last writer wins” replacement of the entire ARA archive can discard another user's edits and should not be silent.

### 38.38 Accessibility and localization

ARA native editors may have their own accessibility quality. APEX remains responsible for the surrounding workflow:

- Keyboard command to add/open/remove ARA processing.
- Accessible status for analysis progress, stale data, source missing, and renderer failure.
- Non-color-only distinction for active/bypassed/failed states.
- Localized host messages without translating opaque plug-in-provided identifiers incorrectly.
- Focus restoration when the editor closes.
- Generic action to bypass/remove/reanalyze when the native UI is inaccessible.

APEX should not claim the native editor is accessible merely because its container is exposed through UI Automation.

### 38.39 Privacy and security

ARA tools may analyze voice, speech, pitch, timing, and musical content. If any plug-in or host feature can transmit data externally:

- Require explicit disclosure and consent.
- Broker network access where sandbox policy supports it.
- Identify which audio ranges and metadata leave the machine.
- Provide offline policy and enterprise disable controls.
- Avoid including raw audio in support bundles by default.
- Redact paths/user names from diagnostics where possible.

The ARA API itself does not grant permission to upload user audio.

### 38.40 Diagnostics

Recommended event families:

```text
AraFactoryProbeStarted/Completed/Failed
AraDocumentCreated/Destroyed
AraObjectCreated/Updated/Destroyed
AraEditScopeBegin/End
AraSourceReadRequested/Completed/Failed
AraAnalysisStarted/Progress/Completed/Stale/Failed
AraRendererAssigned/Detached
AraLatencyChanged
AraStateSaveStarted/Completed/Failed
AraStateRestoreStarted/Completed/Failed
AraBindingMismatch
AraWorkerDeadlineMiss/Hang/Crash/Restart
AraEditorCreated/Closed/Failed
```

Each record should include stable IDs, plugin fingerprint, project/render generation, source revision, operation sequence, and bounded error code. Text formatting occurs off realtime.

Metrics:

- Analysis duration and cancellation count.
- Source bytes/frames read.
- Cache hit/miss.
- Stale-result rejection count.
- Archive size/save/restore time.
- Renderer callback p50/p99/p99.9/max.
- Deadline misses.
- Object/binding counts.
- Worker restarts.
- Missing-source and migration failures.

### 38.41 Failure matrix

| Failure | Bounded/degraded behavior | Recovery owner |
|---|---|---|
| Factory creation fails | Disable ARA capability; retain ordinary companion plug-in where valid | Scanner/control |
| Document creation fails | Keep canonical clips; create failed placeholder | Control |
| Random source read fails | Return contract-defined failure/silence; mark analysis failed | Media/control |
| Analysis fails | Preserve previous valid result if clearly labeled stale or retain unprocessed audio | Control/plugin worker |
| Stale job completes | Reject by source/modification generation | Control |
| Editor crashes | Close editor; preserve playback if process remains trustworthy | UI/control |
| In-process native crash | Treat process as untrusted; rely on crash recovery | Application recovery |
| Isolated worker dies | Reject stale output; silence/bypass policy; offer restart | Sandbox manager |
| Archive corrupt | Preserve project and canonical clips; disable affected ARA state | Loader/control |
| Plug-in missing | Placeholder plus dependency report; optional rendered proxy | Project loader |
| Source missing | Preserve identity; no silent replacement; relink workflow | Asset service |
| Dynamic latency change | Request PDC/graph rebuild | Control/graph compiler |
| Undo mismatch | Abort transaction/restore checkpoint; report project inconsistency | Command system |
| Disk full during save | Keep previous project; do not advance saved revision | Project storage |

### 38.42 Testing architecture

#### Model tests

- Create/destroy every object type in legal/illegal order.
- Stable-ID uniqueness and mapping persistence.
- Parent/child reference validity.
- Move, trim, slip, split, duplicate, make unique, delete, undo, redo.
- Clip movement across tracks/sequences.
- Tempo/context revision propagation.

#### Random-access tests

- Arbitrary aligned and unaligned ranges.
- Start before zero/end after source.
- Mono/stereo/multichannel.
- Multiple sample rates.
- Missing/corrupt/truncated source.
- Concurrent reads where permitted.
- Cancellation and shutdown.
- Source revision change during queued job.

#### State tests

- Save/reload identical build.
- Missing plug-in.
- Newer/older plug-in version.
- Corrupt/truncated/oversized archive.
- Mismatched companion and ARA transaction IDs.
- Unknown future host schema.
- Disk full and interrupted write.

#### Render tests

- Realtime versus offline under documented determinism policy.
- Variable block sizes allowed by backend lifecycle.
- Seek, loop, stop, restart, scrub, and punch.
- PDC and dynamic latency.
- Freeze/bounce/Render-in-Place.
- Host fades/gain and downstream inserts.
- Bypass and failure transitions.

#### Failure injection

- Factory timeout/crash.
- Analysis worker crash/hang.
- Source read latency and failure.
- Editor destruction during analysis.
- Document teardown during pending jobs.
- Rapid edit publication.
- Old-generation callback after rebuild.
- Sandbox shared-memory corruption and sequence mismatch.

### 38.43 Target plug-in compatibility corpus

A production host cannot validate ARA against one implementation only.

The corpus should vary:

```text
companion formats
ARA SDK generations supported
single/multiple renderer roles
large/small archives
mono/stereo/multichannel sources
short/long sources
analysis-heavy/light behavior
dynamic latency behavior
editor open/closed
sandbox/in-process policy
```

Because product availability and supported combinations are Time-sensitive, APEX should maintain a versioned internal compatibility matrix rather than embedding a timeless product list in canonical architecture.

### 38.44 Performance and scale

Test projects with:

- Hundreds of playback regions.
- Many modifications sharing sources.
- Long multichannel recordings.
- Repeated split/duplicate/undo operations.
- Large tempo maps.
- Multiple ARA documents/plug-ins.
- Concurrent analysis jobs.
- Low device block sizes during editing.

Measure:

- Object-update transaction time.
- Analysis throughput and memory.
- Source-cache pressure.
- State archive size and save time.
- Graph compile/adoption latency.
- Editor frame time.
- Callback tail latency.

Do not optimize by bypassing correctness. Add incremental update/coalescing only after reference behavior is proven.

### 38.45 APEX internal interfaces

Conceptual interfaces:

```cpp
class AraHostService {
public:
    virtual AraCapability queryCapability(PluginClassStableId) = 0;
    virtual Future<AraDocumentHandle> createDocument(const AraDocumentSpec&) = 0;
    virtual Result applyProjectTransaction(const AraTransaction&) = 0;
    virtual Future<AraStatePackage> captureState(AraDocumentId) = 0;
    virtual Future<Result> restoreState(AraDocumentId, const AraStatePackage&) = 0;
};

class AraSourceProvider {
public:
    virtual SourceDescriptor describe(AraAudioSourceId) const = 0;
    virtual ReadResult read(const AraReadRequest&, AudioBufferView destination) = 0;
};

struct AraRenderAssignment {
    AraDocumentId document;
    AraRendererId renderer;
    std::span<const AraPlaybackRegionId> regions;
    std::uint64_t generation;
    std::uint32_t latencySamples;
};
```

These examples express boundaries, not exact SDK signatures. The adapter layer owns conversion to the pinned ARA API.

### 38.46 APEX architecture decision

**Recommendation:** APEX should treat ARA as an optional deep-editing subsystem with these non-negotiable rules:

1. APEX project/source/clip/tempo/undo state remains canonical.
2. ARA objects use stable persisted bindings, never UI pointers or container indices.
3. Random-access source delivery never depends on the device callback or mutable UI state.
4. Document edits are batched into legal host transactions.
5. The audio callback sees only prepared renderer assignments.
6. ARA and companion state are saved atomically in one project transaction.
7. Missing/corrupt ARA state never destroys canonical clips or the previous valid project.
8. Dynamic latency enters normal graph/PDC invalidation.
9. Native editor lifetime is independent from playback lifetime.
10. Every target plug-in/version/format is validated; “ARA supported” is not one universal behavior.
11. ARA may be disabled without making the project structurally unreadable.
12. Public builds pin a tagged ARA SDK and complete all companion-license obligations.

### 38.47 Staged APEX roadmap

#### Stage 0 — Repository readiness audit

Before compiling the SDK, verify:

- Canonical asset/source versus clip separation.
- Stable IDs for clips, tracks, lanes, assets, plug-ins, and project commands.
- Undo transaction boundaries.
- Tempo-map generation and conversion API.
- Random-access media reader independent of playback.
- Plugin module/factory lifetime ownership.
- Prepared render-node publication.
- Project package support for typed opaque state.

**Stop condition:** If clip identity depends on UI objects, if project save cannot atomically preserve opaque state, or if the audio callback reads mutable clip containers, repair those foundations first.

#### Stage 1 — SDK and factory probe

- Pin tagged ARA SDK and submodule commits.
- Integrate license/NOTICE.
- Enable JUCE/native ARA host support in a dedicated branch.
- Add isolated factory probing and capability cache.
- No user-facing ARA editing yet.

#### Stage 2 — One-source headless vertical slice

- One project.
- One ARA document.
- One audio source.
- One modification.
- One playback region.
- One target plug-in.
- No native editor required.
- Realtime playback and save/reload.

Acceptance: correct audio, no callback allocation, stable state after reload, and graceful missing-plugin behavior.

#### Stage 3 — Basic editor integration

- Open/close native editor.
- Selection and transport synchronization.
- Analysis progress.
- DPI/focus/resize.
- Playback continues with editor closed.

#### Stage 4 — Core clip editing

- Move, trim, slip, split, linked duplicate, make unique, delete.
- Undo/redo.
- Cross-track movement and sequence mapping.
- Stale analysis rejection.

#### Stage 5 — Production render paths

- PDC and dynamic latency.
- Offline export.
- Freeze, bounce, and Render-in-Place.
- Failure and cancellation.
- Realtime/offline comparison reports.

#### Stage 6 — Comping and advanced context

- Take lanes/comp policy.
- Tempo/meter/key contexts.
- Content exchange and confidence.
- Multiple documents or plug-in instances.

#### Stage 7 — Isolation and compatibility expansion

- Sandboxed runtime if product policy requires it.
- Broader target plug-in/format corpus.
- Migration tests across versions.
- Collaboration/proxy policy.

### 38.48 Common failure modes and misconceptions

- **“ARA is just Melodyne support.”** ARA is a general integration contract; product behavior is implementation-specific.
- **“ARA replaces VST3/CLAP/AU/AAX.”** It extends a companion API.
- **“One Boolean from the scanner proves compatibility.”** Factory creation, protocol generation, state, renderer roles, editor behavior, and target versions require validation.
- **“The ARA document can become the project model.”** The DAW must survive missing or failed third-party state.
- **“A clip is an audio source.”** Multiple clips/playback regions can reference one source and modification.
- **“Copying a clip obviously copies its edits.”** Linked versus independent modification semantics must be explicit.
- **“Random access can read the project file directly.”** The host must provide validated audio through a controlled source contract.
- **“Analysis results remain valid when the filename is unchanged.”** Content and interpretation revisions matter.
- **“The editor must stay open for playback.”** Editor and playback roles should be independent where supported.
- **“Opaque state is safe because the host does not understand it.”** It still requires size, identity, transaction, and corruption boundaries.
- **“Undo can be handled inside the plug-in only.”** The host's project history must remain coherent.
- **“Freeze automatically includes the ARA edit.”** The render boundary and assignment must be tested.
- **“Sandboxing ARA is the same as sandboxing a simple insert.”** Random source access, state, model, analysis, and editor IPC add major complexity.
- **“The latest SDK branch is suitable for release.”** Public releases should pin a tagged public SDK.

### 38.49 Worked example — vocal pitch editing in APEX

Assume a user imports `LeadVocal.wav`, places two clips from the source, adds an ARA pitch editor, corrects several notes, splits the second clip, moves the new part, saves, closes, reloads, and exports stems.

#### Host/model flow

```text
1. Import creates AssetId A17 and canonical AudioSourceId S44.
2. Two clips C100 and C101 reference S44.
3. ARA insertion creates Document D3 and plugin bundle P8.
4. Host maps S44 → AraAudioSource AS1.
5. Host creates AudioModification AM1 for the intended linked edit policy.
6. C100 and C101 become playback regions PR1 and PR2 in sequence RS1.
7. Plugin requests arbitrary samples from AS1 through AraSourceProvider.
8. Analysis job J12 publishes only if sourceRevision(S44) still matches.
9. User pitch edits are grouped into host transaction T90 and ARA edit scope.
10. Prepared renderer assignment generation 55 replaces generation 54.
11. Split C101 creates C102/C103 and PR3/PR4 atomically; AM1 remains shared by policy.
12. Moving C103 updates placement/context, not source bytes.
13. Save transaction captures APEX objects, mappings, ARA archive, companion state, and hashes.
14. Reload recreates sources and document before assigning renderers.
15. Stem export freezes generation 61, completes required analysis, renders ARA playback, then track inserts/sends according to stem policy.
16. Temporary stem files are validated and atomically published.
```

#### Failure variant

If the ARA plug-in is absent on reload:

```text
APEX restores S44 and clips C100/C102/C103
→ loads ARA placeholder with D3/P8 metadata and preserved archive
→ displays dependency failure
→ can play unprocessed source or stored proxy according to project policy
→ never discards the archive or rewrites the project as successfully resolved
```

### Section 38 laboratories and assessment

#### Laboratory 1 — Model mapping

Design a mapping from APEX assets, sources, clips, tracks, lanes, tempo maps, and plug-in instances to ARA objects.

**Acceptance criteria:**

- Stable IDs survive move, trim, save, reload, and UI reconstruction.
- Source and clip identity are not conflated.
- Linked and independent duplicate semantics are explicit.
- Missing ARA state leaves canonical clips intact.

#### Laboratory 2 — Random-access reader

Implement a source provider for arbitrary ranges over WAV/FLAC-backed canonical media or test fixtures.

Test:

- Negative/out-of-range requests.
- Partial final blocks.
- Mono/stereo/multichannel.
- Concurrent reads where allowed.
- Cancellation.
- Source revision replacement.
- No audio-thread file I/O.

#### Laboratory 3 — Factory scanner

Probe one or more test candidates in a helper process.

Record:

- Companion identity.
- ARA factory result.
- SDK/protocol capability.
- Timeout/crash.
- Module lifetime.
- Cache invalidation after binary change.

#### Laboratory 4 — Edit transaction suite

Implement or simulate:

- Move.
- Trim.
- Slip.
- Split.
- Linked duplicate.
- Make Unique.
- Delete.
- Undo/redo.

**Pass condition:** Host and ARA object graphs remain valid after every operation and after randomized command sequences.

#### Laboratory 5 — State round trip

Save and restore project, companion state, ARA archive, and bindings.

Inject:

- Truncated archive.
- Mismatched transaction revision.
- Missing plug-in.
- Changed source.
- Plug-in update.
- Disk full.

**Pass condition:** Previous valid project remains available and canonical audio edits are never discarded.

#### Laboratory 6 — Realtime/offline render

Compare live playback, offline export, freeze, bounce, and Render-in-Place.

Align range, latency, tail, fades, SRC, and deterministic state. Produce a qualified residual report.

#### Laboratory 7 — Editor lifecycle

Repeatedly open, resize, move across DPI scales, close, recreate, and destroy the native editor during analysis and playback.

**Pass condition:** Playback and project state remain valid; focus and selection do not enter feedback loops.

#### Laboratory 8 — Failure isolation

Inject:

- Factory crash.
- Analysis hang.
- Random-read failure.
- Renderer deadline miss.
- Worker death.
- Invalid state.
- Source disappearance.

Document degraded output, recovery owner, preserved artifacts, and diagnostics.

#### Laboratory 9 — Tempo and context

Create tempo steps, ramps where supported by host model, meter changes, key changes, and clip movement across contexts.

Verify conversions, revisions, notification batching, analysis invalidation, and playback alignment.

#### Laboratory 10 — APEX readiness audit

Using the actual APEX repository, report exact files/classes for:

```text
canonical source and clip identity
random-access media reading
undo commands
project state container
tempo map
plugin module lifetime
native editor ownership
render graph publication
PDC invalidation
background job cancellation
```

Classify each as:

```text
ready
partially ready
incompatible
unknown
```

Do not implement ARA until every incompatible foundation has a bounded remediation plan.

### 38.50 Review questions

1. Why is ARA an extension rather than a replacement plug-in format?
2. Which responsibilities remain in the companion API?
3. Why must the host keep its project model canonical?
4. How do audio source, modification, playback region, region sequence, and musical context differ?
5. Why can multiple playback regions share one modification?
6. Which identity changes during move, split, linked duplicate, and Make Unique?
7. What must a random-access audio contract define?
8. Why must arbitrary source reads stay outside the device callback?
9. How does source revision protect analysis validity?
10. Why should model changes be batched inside an edit scope?
11. What reentrancy risks exist when calling third-party document code?
12. Why is host undo authority essential?
13. Which state layers must be saved separately?
14. Why must companion and ARA state belong to the same save transaction?
15. What restore ordering risks exist?
16. How does a playback renderer enter the graph?
17. Why may editor rendering differ from playback rendering?
18. How should selection synchronization avoid feedback loops?
19. How can tempo edits invalidate or reinterpret ARA data?
20. Why must warp/time-correction ownership be explicit?
21. What should freeze preserve for unfreeze?
22. When is a realtime/offline null comparison meaningful?
23. How do dynamic latency and bypass affect PDC?
24. Why is sandboxed ARA harder than sandboxing a simple insert?
25. What should survive an isolated worker crash?
26. How should missing sources and missing plug-ins appear?
27. Why are opaque archives still untrusted input?
28. Why can collaboration not safely field-merge arbitrary ARA archives?
29. Which diagnostics identify stale result publication?
30. What is the safest first APEX vertical slice?

#### Common misconceptions check

Classify each statement as accurate, incomplete, or unsafe and defend the answer:

- “ARA is a replacement for VST3.”
- “One clip should always equal one ARA audio source.”
- “Moving a clip should create a new source analysis.”
- “The plug-in can own project undo because it owns the editor.”
- “A filename proves analysis is still valid.”
- “The ARA editor must stay open for corrected playback.”
- “Saving the companion plug-in blob is enough.”
- “An isolated process can read any project file safely.”
- “A successful factory probe proves every ARA workflow works.”
- “Freeze and export automatically use the same renderer assignment as playback.”

#### Practical examination

Design an ARA host integration for APEX and submit:

1. Companion/ARA plane diagram.
2. Stable identity and binding schema.
3. Document-scope decision.
4. Source/modification/region/sequence/context mapping.
5. Random-access audio contract.
6. Edit-scope and notification ordering.
7. Undo/redo architecture.
8. Persistence and restore package.
9. Renderer/editor lifecycle.
10. Graph, latency, bypass, and offline-render integration.
11. Sandboxing design or documented in-process boundary.
12. Failure matrix.
13. Compatibility and test corpus.
14. Repository-readiness report.
15. Staged implementation roadmap with stop conditions.

#### Mastery rubric

| Dimension | Foundation | Engineering | Architecture/Research |
|---|---|---|---|
| Conceptual model | Explains why ARA exists and names model objects | Builds coherent source/modification/region mapping | Defends document scope and authority against alternatives |
| Identity/edits | Distinguishes move/trim/split/copy semantics | Implements transaction and undo tests | Designs linked/independent policy across comping and collaboration |
| Audio access | Explains random versus realtime access | Implements bounded validated source provider | Measures cache, cancellation, reentrancy, and failure behavior |
| Persistence | Names host/ARA/companion state layers | Builds atomic round-trip and corruption tests | Designs migration, placeholders, and long-term provenance |
| Rendering | Explains playback/editor roles | Integrates PDC, offline, freeze, and bypass | Validates multiple plugins/formats and isolation strategies |
| Realtime/lifetime | Identifies forbidden callback work | Publishes prepared generations and proves teardown order | Audits reentrancy, sandbox IPC, and worker recovery |
| APEX application | Maps existing product concepts | Produces one working vertical slice | Creates phased roadmap preserving product assets and project integrity |
| Evidence | Uses official tagged SDK documentation | Reproduces examples and target behavior | Records unknowns, version drift, and falsifiable assumptions |

### 38.51 Primary sources

- [Celemony ARA SDK umbrella repository](https://github.com/Celemony/ARA_SDK): official SDK composition, companion APIs, licensing, tagged-release policy, and examples.
- [ARA API repository](https://github.com/Celemony/ARA_API): core C API headers, integration headers, audio-file chunks, and normative documentation.
- [ARA Library repository](https://github.com/Celemony/ARA_Library): official C++ wrappers and host/plugin utility architecture.
- [ARA Examples repository](https://github.com/Celemony/ARA_Examples): official host and plug-in examples.
- [Celemony ARA product/developer overview](https://www.celemony.com/en/ara): official conceptual overview and ecosystem entry point.
- [Apache License 2.0](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0): license used by the public ARA SDK; companion SDK terms remain separate.
- [JUCE ARA host model classes](https://docs.juce.com/master/namespacejuce.html): host-side ARA model, renderer, editor, factory, stream, and edit-guard surfaces.
- [JUCE `AudioPluginFormat::createARAFactoryAsync`](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1AudioPluginFormat.html): asynchronous factory creation surface.
- [JUCE `ARAFactoryWrapper`](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1ARAFactoryWrapper.html): factory and module lifetime wrapper.
- [JUCE `ARAHostModel::PlaybackRegionRegistry`](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1ARAHostModel_1_1PlaybackRegionRegistry.html): playback-region assignment to playback/editor renderer roles.
- [JUCE ARA module configuration](https://docs.juce.com/develop/juce__audio__processors__headless_8h.html): `JUCE_PLUGINHOST_ARA` integration and SDK-path requirements; verify exact JUCE branch/version before implementation.
- [Steinberg VST 3 SDK](https://github.com/steinbergmedia/vst3sdk): one supported ARA companion API; pin exact SDK and license.
- [CLAP specification repository](https://github.com/free-audio/clap): one supported ARA companion API; pin exact SDK and extension integration.
- [Apple Audio Unit documentation](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/audiotoolbox/audio_unit_v3_plug-ins): Audio Unit companion architecture and lifecycle.
- [Avid developer portal](https://developer.avid.com/): AAX SDK and optional ARA integration access; terms and availability are Time-sensitive.

## 39. Note-Based Audio Analysis, Editing, and Resynthesis

### Section 39 guide

#### Section 39 prerequisites

Before starting this section, the learner should be able to:

- Explain source/clip separation, stable identity, nondestructive editing, and project persistence from §9 and §32.
- Explain sample time, musical time, tempo maps, warp maps, pitch shift, time stretch, SRC, formants, and realtime/offline processing from §§6–7.
- Explain immutable render generations, worker-thread analysis, RT-safe publication, and evidence capture from §§2, 14, 28, 34, and 37.
- Explain ARA document integration, audio-source/modification/playback-region identity, random-access audio, and companion plug-in boundaries from §38.
- Distinguish fundamental frequency, perceived note, harmonic spectrum, spectral envelope, aperiodic energy, transients, and unvoiced material.
- Understand that note boundaries inferred from audio are hypotheses with confidence, not inherent ground-truth objects inside the waveform.

The implementation laboratories assume C++20, FFT/STFT fundamentals, asynchronous job systems, persistent schemas, undo transactions, and the ability to compare analysis/resynthesis against controlled reference material.

#### Why this domain matters

Traditional waveform editing operates on ranges of samples. Musical editing operates on notes, timing intent, pitch contours, formants, attacks, vibrato, dynamics, and phrase structure. A note-based deep editor attempts to bridge those two representations.

A product in the Melodyne class demonstrates the user-facing concept: analyzed audio is presented note by note, and the user can edit properties including pitch, vibrato/modulation, timing, duration, amplitude, sibilant balance, and formants. Celemony's public documentation describes this as note-based audio editing and exposes distinct concepts such as pitch center, pitch modulation, pitch drift, timing, note separation, and formants. Those public behaviors are evidence for the interaction model, not evidence of Celemony's private internal algorithms.

For APEX, the engineering challenge is therefore not “draw blobs and move them.” It is to construct an explicit, versioned transformation system:

```text
source audio
→ analysis
→ editable musical representation
→ user edit model
→ render plan
→ resynthesis
→ playback / offline render
```

Every arrow has failure modes. Incorrect F0 tracking produces wrong notes. Incorrect segmentation makes one sung syllable become several false notes. Aggressive pitch quantization destroys intentional slides. Poor resynthesis creates phasiness, transient smearing, robotic timbre, doubled attacks, or formant shift. Stale analysis after source replacement can corrupt edits. A UI can look correct while rendering a different generation.

The purpose of this section is to define a product-neutral deep-audio-editing architecture for APEX while preserving evidence boundaries: public products demonstrate possible behavior; open algorithms and academic work provide reproducible references; the final APEX implementation remains a repository fact only after it exists and passes its own tests.

#### Section 39 learning outcomes

By the end of this section, the learner should be able to:

1. **Distinguish** waveform truth, analysis hypotheses, note objects, user edits, and rendered output as separate authorities.
2. **Design** a canonical analyzed-source identity that survives clip moves, copies, trims, save/reload, and cache invalidation.
3. **Compare** monophonic F0 tracking, multipitch estimation, automatic music transcription, and source-specific models.
4. **Construct** a note-segmentation model that represents confidence, ambiguity, and user correction.
5. **Explain** pitch center, pitch contour, drift, modulation/vibrato, transitions, timing, duration, amplitude, sibilance, and formant edits.
6. **Design** a nondestructive edit graph whose operations remain reversible and versioned.
7. **Select** resynthesis strategies for monophonic voice, polyphonic material, percussion/transients, and mixed content.
8. **Separate** realtime preview requirements from offline high-quality rendering.
9. **Integrate** deep editing with ARA without making ARA the owner of the analysis algorithm.
10. **Validate** analysis and resynthesis using controlled corpora, perceptual tests, invariants, regression evidence, and environment identity.
11. **Define** APEX capability maturity without confusing UI presence, analysis presence, and verified production quality.
12. **Defend** which functions belong in §39 versus the realtime automatic-correction responsibilities of §40.

### 39.1 Evidence profile

**Fact:** Celemony's public Melodyne documentation demonstrates a note-based editing workflow with pitch, modulation/drift, timing, note separation, amplitude, sibilant, and formant controls. Spotify Basic Pitch publicly provides polyphonic note/multipitch transcription with pitch-bend output. pYIN is a published probabilistic monophonic F0 estimator. WORLD publicly separates F0, spectral-envelope, aperiodicity, and synthesis roles. Rubber Band publicly documents realtime/offline pitch/time processing and formant-preservation options.

**Synthesis:** The canonical analysis/edit/render architecture, stable identities, edit layering, invalidation model, confidence model, and APEX integration described here are engineering syntheses.

**Recommendation:** APEX should begin with a high-quality monophonic vocal path before claiming general polyphonic note editing. It should make confidence and correction of analysis explicit, and it should keep analysis, edit state, and render caches separately versioned.

**Unknown:** Proprietary algorithms used internally by Melodyne, Auto-Tune, or other closed products remain Unknown unless documented by their owners. Similar visible behavior does not prove similar implementation.

**Time-sensitive:** Product editions, supported features, licenses, model versions, and SDK integrations must be pinned at implementation time.

### 39.2 Five authorities in deep audio editing

The system must not collapse these concepts:

```text
SOURCE AUDIO
what samples exist

ANALYSIS
what the analyzer believes exists

NOTE MODEL
the editable musical abstraction

EDIT MODEL
what the user wants changed

RENDERED AUDIO
what the synthesis path produced
```

A wrong analysis must be correctable without rewriting the source.

A user edit must not mutate the original analysis silently.

A render cache must be disposable.

A clip move on the arrangement timeline must not force source analysis to be recomputed unless the analysis depends on timeline context.

### 39.3 Source identity versus clip identity

A single audio asset may appear in many clips.

Recommended identities:

```text
SourceAssetId
AnalysisId
AnalysisGeneration
ClipId
AudioModificationId
EditLayerId
RenderCacheId
```

A source-level pitch contour can be reused by several clips referencing the same unchanged source.

Clip-relative operations may differ:

```text
Clip A → transpose +2
Clip B → timing edit
Clip C → no deep edit
```

Therefore:

```text
analysis identity
≠ clip identity
≠ edit identity
```

This separation aligns with §9 persistence, §32 editing, and §38 ARA source/modification/playback-region semantics.

### 39.4 Analysis is probabilistic

Audio does not contain explicit note-object records.

The analyzer estimates them.

A robust model should be able to represent:

```text
voiced probability
F0 estimate
F0 confidence
multipitch candidates
onset confidence
offset confidence
note-class probability
source-class probability
transient likelihood
aperiodicity/noise likelihood
```

A note boundary should be editable because:

- a consonant can trigger a false onset;
- vibrato can cross semitone boundaries;
- a legato phrase can contain several musical notes with no hard acoustic break;
- one sustained note can contain register changes;
- polyphonic partials can be confused with fundamentals.

### 39.5 Monophonic pitch analysis

For a predominantly monophonic vocal or lead instrument, the primary task is a time-varying F0 contour plus voiced/unvoiced classification.

Possible reference families include:

- YIN/pYIN-style periodicity analysis.
- Autocorrelation or difference-function trackers.
- Cepstral/spectral trackers.
- WORLD DIO/Harvest plus refinement.
- Neural pitch estimators.
- Hybrid candidate generation plus temporal decoding.

pYIN is valuable as a reproducible reference because it produces probabilistic F0 estimates and temporal smoothing rather than treating every frame independently.

The product must define:

```text
analysis sample rate
frame length
hop length
frequency range
candidate count
confidence threshold
temporal smoothing
octave-jump policy
unvoiced handling
```

No one frame size is universally correct. Longer windows improve low-frequency resolution but increase temporal blur and latency.

### 39.6 Polyphonic multipitch and note transcription

Polyphonic audio may contain several simultaneous fundamentals whose harmonics overlap.

This is a different problem from monophonic F0 tracking.

Spotify Basic Pitch is an open reference demonstrating instrument-agnostic polyphonic note transcription and multipitch estimation with pitch-bend output. Its public project also warns that model behavior and code versions matter; APEX must pin any evaluated model revision.

A polyphonic deep editor requires decisions about:

```text
simultaneous note hypotheses
voice assignment
harmonic ownership
shared transient ownership
note confidence
overlapping releases
pedal/resonance
inharmonic instruments
```

A system can support polyphonic transcription without supporting artifact-free independent resynthesis of every detected note.

Those are separate capabilities.

### 39.7 Analysis capability decomposition

Recommended APEX capability IDs:

```text
APEX-CAP-DEEP-F0-MONO
APEX-CAP-DEEP-NOTE-SEGMENT-MONO
APEX-CAP-DEEP-MULTIPITCH
APEX-CAP-DEEP-POLYPHONIC-NOTES
APEX-CAP-DEEP-FORMANT-ANALYSIS
APEX-CAP-DEEP-TRANSIENT-ANALYSIS
APEX-CAP-DEEP-SIBILANT-ANALYSIS
APEX-CAP-DEEP-RESYNTH-MONO
APEX-CAP-DEEP-RESYNTH-POLY
APEX-CAP-DEEP-OFFLINE-HQ
```

The aggregate “Deep Editing” capability must not be marked complete merely because one analyzer works.

### 39.8 Analysis generation identity

Every analysis result should record:

```text
analysisId
analysisGeneration
sourceContentIdentity
algorithmId
algorithmVersion
modelDigest if applicable
configurationDigest
sampleRate
channel policy
createdBuild
```

If a neural model or DSP algorithm changes, old analysis may remain valid for old projects but should not be silently reinterpreted as new-generation output.

### 39.9 Canonical pitch representation

APEX should define one canonical pitch representation usable by §§39 and 40.

A possible conceptual structure:

```cpp
struct PitchPoint {
    SamplePosition sourceSample;
    float semitoneFromA4;
    float confidence;
    bool voiced;
};

struct NoteRegion {
    StableNoteAnalysisId id;
    SampleRange sourceRange;
    float nominalMidiPitch;
    float pitchCenterCents;
    float onsetConfidence;
    float offsetConfidence;
};
```

The actual schema may differ.

The important rule is:

> §§39 and 40 must not create competing canonical pitch truths for the same analyzed material.

### 39.10 Pitch center

Pitch center represents the main perceived pitch emphasis of a note region.

It is not identical to every instantaneous F0 sample.

A note may have:

```text
center = A4
attack scoop below A4
vibrato around A4
release fall below A4
```

Changing the center should not necessarily flatten the vibrato.

That is why public note-based editors expose pitch center separately from modulation/drift.

### 39.11 Pitch modulation and vibrato

Fast intentional oscillation should be represented separately from slow drift where practical.

This allows operations such as:

```text
move center by +23 cents
preserve vibrato depth

reduce vibrato depth by 40%
preserve note center
```

The decomposition is a model, not absolute musical truth. Some pitch gestures fall between “drift” and “vibrato.” The UI should avoid implying impossible certainty.

### 39.12 Pitch drift

Pitch drift describes slower movement of the note's local center over its duration.

Possible edit:

```text
original:
start -18 cents
middle +2 cents
end +27 cents

drift correction:
start -5
middle 0
end +5

micro-modulation preserved
```

An implementation may derive drift using low-pass filtering or another trend estimator, but the cutoff and edge behavior must be versioned because they affect musical result.

### 39.13 Pitch transitions

Transitions between notes carry identity.

A naive editor that independently snaps each note can create discontinuous jumps.

A transition model may represent:

```text
transition start
transition end
transition curvature
portamento amount
transition preservation
```

The renderer must distinguish:

- correcting note centers;
- preserving a natural glide;
- intentionally hard-snapping for an effect.

### 39.14 Note segmentation

Segmentation converts continuous analysis into editable regions.

Inputs can include:

```text
pitch discontinuity
onset strength
energy envelope
spectral change
voiced/unvoiced transitions
phonetic or source-class cues
user scale context
```

Segmentation should remain editable.

A user correction to one boundary should not require destroying the entire analysis.

### 39.15 Analysis correction mode

A professional deep editor needs a distinct mode for correcting what the analyzer believes.

Examples:

```text
merge false split
split missed note
change note assignment
change voiced/unvoiced classification
remove false octave
correct source class
```

This is not the same as creative editing.

Analysis corrections change the interpretation.

Creative edits change the desired result.

Persist them separately.

### 39.16 Time representation

Deep editing needs at least:

```text
source sample time
analysis frame time
clip-local time
project sample time
musical beat time
```

Never store one ambiguous `double time`.

Conversions must use explicit coordinate domains.

### 39.17 Timing edits

A note timing edit may change:

```text
onset position
internal timing
duration
transition timing
attack speed
release
```

Moving a note is not always equivalent to uniform time stretch.

For vocals, consonant/transient regions may need different handling from sustained voiced regions.

### 39.18 Time handles and anchors

A flexible edit model can use anchors:

```text
source anchor
target anchor
protected transient
stretch interval
```

The resulting map must remain monotonic unless the product explicitly supports reversal.

Crossing anchors should be rejected or resolved deterministically.

### 39.19 Formants

Formants are spectral-envelope resonances associated with timbre and vocal-tract characteristics, distinct from the fundamental pitch.

Pitch shifting without spectral-envelope compensation can produce a perceived “chipmunk” or “giant” timbre.

Rubber Band publicly exposes formant-preservation and separate formant-scale behavior; WORLD publicly separates F0, spectral envelope, and aperiodicity in a speech-analysis/synthesis architecture. These are useful references, not universal requirements.

### 39.20 Formant editing

A note-based formant edit should identify:

```text
edit range
formant shift amount
transition shape
whether sibilant/unvoiced regions are included
```

Extreme shifts may be treated as creative effects rather than transparent correction.

### 39.21 Sibilants and unvoiced material

Sibilants do not have the same stable periodic F0 structure as voiced vowels.

Applying voiced pitch transformation blindly can create metallic artifacts.

A vocal editor should detect or allow manual marking of:

```text
sibilants
breaths
fricatives
plosives
unvoiced consonants
```

Possible rendering policy:

```text
voiced core → pitch/formant transform
sibilant region → timing/amplitude processing with limited pitch transform
transition → crossfaded or source-aware blend
```

### 39.22 Transients

Transients define attacks and rhythmic identity.

Time stretching or note movement can smear them.

The analysis should identify high-confidence transient anchors and permit policies such as:

```text
preserve attack timing
move attack with note
stretch sustain only
```

### 39.23 Amplitude and note gain

Note-level amplitude editing should be nondestructive.

It may coexist with:

```text
clip gain
clip envelope
track fader
automation
```

The authority order must be defined so that deep-edit amplitude changes do not silently replace mixer automation.

### 39.24 Editing operation model

Recommended operations:

```text
MovePitch
AdjustPitchCenter
AdjustPitchDrift
AdjustPitchModulation
AdjustTransition
MoveTime
StretchDuration
MoveBoundary
SplitNote
MergeNotes
AdjustFormant
AdjustAmplitude
AdjustSibilantBalance
ResetProperty
```

Each operation references stable analyzed-note or region identities.

### 39.25 Edit layering

Store user intent as edits over analysis.

Conceptually:

```text
Source
→ AnalysisGeneration
→ AnalysisCorrections
→ MusicalEdits
→ ClipOverrides
→ Render
```

This makes re-analysis possible.

If a new analyzer generation is adopted, edits must either:

- map through stable correspondence;
- be migrated with confidence;
- remain pinned to the old analysis;
- require user review.

Never silently attach old note edits to unrelated newly detected notes.

### 39.26 Undo and transactions

A drag gesture that adjusts one property across many notes should normally become one undo transaction.

Preview may update continuously.

Canonical edit publication should occur at bounded transaction boundaries.

Undo must restore:

```text
edit values
selection-independent data
analysis correction where applicable
render-cache invalidation
```

### 39.27 Rendering architecture

Recommended separation:

```text
AnalysisCore
EditModel
RenderCompiler
PreviewRenderer
OfflineHQRenderer
RenderCache
```

The audio callback should never run full source analysis.

It consumes prepared render state.

### 39.28 Preview versus offline HQ

Realtime preview prioritizes bounded latency and responsiveness.

Offline HQ can use:

```text
lookahead
two-pass analysis
larger windows
more expensive phase reconstruction
higher-quality pitch/time modes
```

The project should store edit intent, not the incidental realtime preview waveform.

Offline export should render the same intent under the selected quality policy.

### 39.29 Monophonic resynthesis

Possible families include:

- PSOLA-like pitch-synchronous waveform operations.
- Phase-vocoder/spectral methods.
- Vocoder decomposition/resynthesis.
- Granular methods.
- Hybrid transient/sustain methods.
- Neural resynthesis where licensing, determinism, quality, and deployment permit.

No one method is universally best.

### 39.30 WORLD as a reference decomposition

WORLD publicly exposes a speech-oriented architecture with:

```text
F0
spectral envelope
aperiodicity
synthesis
```

This separation is educationally valuable for vocal tuning because it demonstrates that pitch, spectral shape, and noise-like energy can be modeled separately.

It does not prove that WORLD is the best production engine for APEX music editing.

### 39.31 Rubber Band as a reference backend

Rubber Band publicly documents:

- realtime and offline processing modes;
- dynamic pitch-change options;
- quality/consistency trade-offs;
- formant-preservation options.

APEX may Adopt, Wrap, Reference, or Avoid it according to §25 and §13 licensing analysis.

### 39.32 Polyphonic resynthesis difficulty

Detecting several notes is easier than independently editing them without artifacts.

A shared harmonic partial may plausibly belong to more than one note.

Room reverb, distortion, chorus, and compression entangle sources.

Therefore APEX should separate:

```text
polyphonic note detection
```

from:

```text
independent transparent polyphonic note resynthesis
```

in the Capability Registry.

### 39.33 Source separation boundary

Source separation can improve editability of mixed material but introduces another probabilistic transformation.

If used:

```text
original source
→ separation model/version
→ stems
→ note analysis
```

Every derived stem requires provenance.
