A separation artifact must not be mistaken for original-source truth.

### 39.34 Cache architecture

Useful caches:

```text
analysis cache
pitch contour cache
note segmentation cache
spectrogram tiles
preview render cache
offline render cache
```

Each cache key should include all inputs that affect validity.

### 39.35 Cache invalidation

Invalidate when relevant:

```text
source content changes
analysis algorithm changes
analysis config changes
user corrects note assignment
edit generation changes
render backend changes
quality policy changes
```

A clip position move may not invalidate source analysis.

### 39.36 Threading

Recommended roles:

```text
UI/control
→ edits and transactions

analysis workers
→ expensive source analysis

render-preparation workers
→ compile edit state

audio thread
→ bounded prepared preview render

offline workers
→ HQ render
```

No analysis worker may mutate a live render structure without publication.

### 39.37 Cancellation

Long analysis jobs must be cancellable.

Cancellation should leave:

```text
previous complete analysis valid
partial new analysis unpublished
```

Do not replace a valid analysis with an incomplete job.

### 39.38 Persistence

Persist:

```text
analysis identity
algorithm/model identity
analysis corrections
user edits
stable note/region IDs
quality-independent intent
```

Derived heavyweight caches may be regenerable.

The project should specify whether caches are embedded, sidecar, or content-addressed.

### 39.39 Save/reload invariant

After save/reload:

```text
same source
+
same analysis generation
+
same edits
+
same render policy
```

should reproduce equivalent musical intent.

Bitwise identity may not be guaranteed across backend/platform changes unless explicitly required.

### 39.40 Relink and source replacement

If media is missing and later relinked:

- compare content identity;
- preserve edits only if mapping remains valid;
- re-analyze when content changed;
- never silently apply old note edits to unrelated audio.

### 39.41 Tempo changes

Source analysis is generally source-time based.

A project tempo change may affect:

```text
clip placement
musical-time interpretation
tempo-relative timing edits
```

but should not automatically change detected source F0.

### 39.42 ARA integration

§38 defines ARA integration.

§39 defines APEX deep-editing semantics.

ARA may provide:

```text
random-access audio
host musical context
document model
playback-region integration
```

but it does not become the canonical owner of APEX pitch-analysis algorithms.

### 39.43 §40 integration

§40 realtime tuning may consume the shared canonical pitch representation.

§39 owns deep region editing.

§40 owns realtime target/correction policy.

A manual §39 edit may optionally feed §40 only through an explicit shared-state contract.

### 39.44 Realtime safety

Forbidden in the audio callback:

```text
full source analysis
model loading
file I/O
unbounded note remapping
cache serialization
schema migration
neural-model initialization
```

Prepared preview rendering must follow §2 and §34.

### 39.45 Latency

Deep editing can tolerate more lookahead than live monitoring.

Preview latency must be explicit.

Offline render has no live-device deadline but still requires deterministic state and failure handling.

### 39.46 Quality modes

Possible:

```text
Draft
Realtime
High
OfflineHQ
```

Names are product decisions.

A quality mode must specify what changes:

```text
windowing
backend
lookahead
phase policy
formant policy
analysis refinement
```

### 39.47 Determinism

Any random or neural stochastic component used during rendering must have explicit reproducibility policy.

Analysis model updates can legitimately produce different note boundaries; version them.

### 39.48 Diagnostics

Useful diagnostics:

```text
analysis duration
frames processed
voiced ratio
median confidence
octave-jump count
manual analysis corrections
render cache hit/miss
preview underrun
offline fallback
```

Do not log raw private audio by default.

### 39.49 Privacy

Pitch contours and transcriptions can reveal musical content.

Voice-derived features can be sensitive.

Support bundles should minimize:

```text
raw audio
filenames
usernames
lyrics/transcriptions
```

unless the user explicitly includes them.

### 39.50 Failure matrix

| Failure | Correct response |
|---|---|
| Analysis crash | Keep previous valid analysis; mark job failed |
| Low confidence | Expose uncertainty; permit manual correction |
| Source changed | Invalidate or remap explicitly |
| Preview renderer overload | Use bounded fallback; do not block callback |
| Offline renderer fails | Do not publish incomplete output |
| Model unavailable | Mark capability unavailable; preserve project data |
| Cache corrupt | Regenerate from canonical state |
| Note-ID migration ambiguous | Require review or retain old generation |

### 39.51 Testing corpus

Include:

- clean monophonic vocals;
- vibrato;
- slides and portamento;
- breathy voice;
- sibilants/plosives;
- low male and high female ranges;
- guitar/bass monophonic;
- piano/guitar polyphonic;
- distorted sources;
- reverberant sources;
- silence/noise;
- sample-rate matrix.

Ground truth may be synthetic, annotated, or perceptual depending on test.

### 39.52 Pitch-analysis metrics

Possible metrics:

```text
raw pitch accuracy
raw chroma accuracy
voicing recall
voicing false alarm
cent error
octave error
onset/offset F-measure
note transcription precision/recall/F1
```

Metrics must match the capability.

### 39.53 Resynthesis metrics

Objective metrics alone are insufficient.

Use:

```text
null/difference where applicable
spectral deviation
transient timing
loudness change
artifact detectors
AB/ABX listening
expert perceptual review
```

### 39.54 Block-size invariance

Realtime preview should not change musical result merely because the device callback block size changes, except where an explicitly documented latency/quality mode changes.

Test variable internal subdivision.

### 39.55 Transport discontinuity

Seek, loop, stop/start, and source-jump behavior must reconcile renderer history.

State carried from one unrelated region must not contaminate another.

### 39.56 Worked example — manual vocal correction

```text
1. Vocal source imported.
2. Source receives SourceAssetId.
3. Monophonic analysis job runs off-thread.
4. Pitch contour and note hypotheses published as AnalysisGeneration 12.
5. User corrects one false split in Analysis Correction Mode.
6. User lowers pitch drift on a sustained note.
7. User moves pitch center -18 cents.
8. User preserves vibrato.
9. Render compiler creates preview generation 44.
10. Audio thread adopts generation 44 at block boundary.
11. Offline export renders the same edit intent using OfflineHQ policy.
12. Evidence records analysis/render build identity for regression testing.
```

### 39.57 Worked example — analyzer upgrade

Old project:

```text
analysisGeneration = DEEP-MONO-V1
```

New APEX ships:

```text
DEEP-MONO-V2
```

Correct policy:

```text
load project
→ preserve V1 analysis and edits
→ optionally offer reanalysis
→ compute V2 separately
→ map edits with confidence
→ show ambiguous mappings
→ publish only after user/policy decision
```

Incorrect policy:

```text
silently replace V1 note IDs with V2
→ attach old edits by array index
```

### 39.58 APEX staged roadmap

**Stage 1 — Monophonic analysis**
- source identity;
- F0 + confidence;
- voiced/unvoiced;
- note segmentation;
- correction mode.

**Stage 2 — Monophonic editing**
- pitch center;
- modulation/drift;
- timing;
- split/merge;
- amplitude.

**Stage 3 — Production rendering**
- formant-preserving pitch;
- transient-aware timing;
- realtime preview;
- OfflineHQ.

**Stage 4 — ARA integration**
- §38 model binding;
- persistence;
- playback regions.

**Stage 5 — Polyphonic intelligence**
- multipitch;
- transcription;
- limited edit workflows.

**Stage 6 — Advanced polyphonic resynthesis**
- only after independent capability validation.

### 39.59 Permanent APEX deep-editing invariants

1. Source audio, analysis, note model, user edits, and rendered audio remain separate authorities.
2. Analysis results carry algorithm/model identity and generation.
3. Analysis confidence is preserved where uncertainty matters.
4. User analysis corrections are not silently rewritten as creative edits.
5. §39 and §40 share canonical pitch identity for the same source where they interoperate.
6. Deep analysis never runs on the realtime audio callback.
7. A failed analysis job does not replace the previous valid analysis.
8. Render caches are derived and disposable.
9. Stable IDs, not vector indices, bind persistent note edits.
10. Reanalysis never silently attaches edits to ambiguous new notes.
11. ARA integration does not own APEX's pitch algorithm.
12. Polyphonic transcription does not imply transparent independent-note resynthesis.
13. Offline HQ and realtime preview render the same edit intent under declared quality policies.
14. Source relink validates content identity before reusing analysis.
15. Transport discontinuities reconcile renderer history.
16. Capability maturity is evidence-gated through §42.

### 39.60 Laboratories

**Laboratory 1 — Monophonic F0**
Implement or integrate one monophonic F0 reference. Measure cent error, octave errors, voiced/unvoiced performance, and latency.

**Laboratory 2 — Segmentation**
Convert a pitch contour into editable note regions. Add manual split/merge and prove stable-ID persistence.

**Laboratory 3 — Drift/modulation decomposition**
Create a controllable trend/modulation decomposition. Demonstrate that changing drift does not necessarily erase vibrato.

**Laboratory 4 — Pitch render**
Render ±50 and ±200 cent corrections on vocals. Compare formant-preserved and shifted modes.

**Laboratory 5 — Timing**
Move a vocal note while protecting the attack transient.

**Laboratory 6 — Save/reload**
Save analysis corrections and edits, reload, and verify identity.

**Laboratory 7 — Reanalysis migration**
Change analyzer generation and test safe edit mapping.

**Laboratory 8 — Realtime preview**
Prove no allocation/file I/O in the audio path and test block-size invariance.

**Laboratory 9 — Offline HQ**
Render the same edit with realtime and HQ policies and document expected differences.

**Laboratory 10 — Polyphonic boundary**
Use Basic Pitch or another pinned reference to transcribe polyphonic material, then document why transcription confidence does not prove separable-note resynthesis quality.

### 39.61 Review questions

1. Why is a waveform not inherently a collection of note objects?
2. Why must analysis and user edits have separate identities?
3. What is the difference between pitch center, modulation, and drift?
4. Why can note segmentation be wrong even when F0 is mostly correct?
5. Why are sibilants difficult for voiced pitch transformation?
6. Why does formant preservation matter?
7. Why is polyphonic transcription not the same as polyphonic resynthesis?
8. When should analysis be invalidated?
9. Why must reanalysis be versioned?
10. What belongs to ARA and what belongs to the APEX algorithm?
11. Why should realtime preview and offline HQ share edit intent?
12. How does §42 prevent APEX from claiming Deep Editing is complete too early?

### 39.62 Practical examination

Design an APEX deep vocal editor.

Submit:

1. Source/analysis/edit identity schema.
2. F0 and confidence model.
3. Note-segmentation model.
4. Analysis-correction workflow.
5. Pitch center/modulation/drift representation.
6. Timing and transient model.
7. Formant and sibilant policy.
8. Undo transactions.
9. Realtime preview architecture.
10. Offline HQ architecture.
11. Persistence and migration.
12. ARA integration boundary.
13. Capability decomposition.
14. Failure matrix.
15. Validation corpus and promotion gates.

### 39.63 Mastery rubric

| Level | Required evidence |
|---|---|
| Foundation | Explains F0, note hypotheses, pitch center, drift, modulation, timing, formants, and resynthesis. |
| Engineering | Builds a stable-ID monophonic analysis/edit/render prototype and validates save/reload and realtime boundaries. |
| Architecture | Separates source, analysis, corrections, edits, caches, ARA, realtime preview, and offline rendering. |
| Research | Compares reproducible algorithms, quantifies uncertainty, performs perceptual validation, and maintains provenance across analyzer generations. |

### 39.64 Primary sources

- [Celemony — What is Melodyne?](https://www.celemony.com/en/melodyne/what-is-melodyne): public note-based editing behavior and supported musical edit concepts; do not infer private implementation.
- [Celemony Melodyne Help Center](https://helpcenter.celemony.com/): public documentation for detection/algorithms, note assignment, pitch, modulation/drift, formants, timing, note separation, and Audio-to-MIDI behavior.
- [Celemony — Pitch Tool](https://helpcenter.celemony.com/M5/doc/melodyneStudio5/en/M5tour_ToolPitch_2?env=standAlone): public pitch-center editing behavior.
- [Celemony — Pitch modulation and drift](https://helpcenter.celemony.com/M5/doc/melodyneStudio5/en/M5tour_ToolModulationDrift_2?env=standAlone): public distinction between modulation and drift.
- [Celemony — Formant Tool](https://helpcenter.celemony.com/M5/doc/melodyneStudio5/en/M5tour_ToolFormants?env=standAlone): public formant-edit behavior.
- [Spotify Basic Pitch](https://github.com/spotify/basic-pitch): open polyphonic transcription/multipitch reference with pitch-bend output; pin exact revision/model.
- [Mauch and Dixon — pYIN: A Fundamental Frequency Estimator](https://qmro.qmul.ac.uk/xmlui/bitstream/handle/123456789/6040/MAUCHpYINFundamental2014Accepted.pdf?sequence=2): probabilistic monophonic F0 reference.
- [Tony melody annotation tool](https://code.soundsoftware.ac.uk/projects/tony/wiki/Wiki): pYIN-based computer-assisted monophonic melody annotation reference.
- [WORLD vocoder](https://github.com/mmorise/World): open speech analysis/manipulation/synthesis reference separating F0, spectral envelope, aperiodicity, and synthesis.
- [Rubber Band Library](https://breakfastquay.com/rubberband/): time/pitch-processing backend reference.
- [Rubber Band integration guidance](https://www.breakfastquay.com/rubberband/integration.html): realtime/offline and dynamic-pitch/formant-preservation guidance.
- [RubberBandStretcher API](https://breakfastquay.com/rubberband/code-doc/classRubberBand_1_1RubberBandStretcher.html): documented pitch/formant options and realtime/offline distinctions.
- [aubio](https://github.com/aubio/aubio): open onset, pitch, beat, phase-vocoder, transient/steady-state analysis reference; current maintenance and licensing must be reviewed before adoption.

## 40. Real-Time Automatic Pitch Correction and Vocal Tuning

### Section 40 guide

#### Section 40 prerequisites

Before starting this section, the learner should be able to:

- Explain callback deadlines, prepared-state publication, bounded work, denormals, invalid samples, and transport discontinuities from §2.
- Explain pitch shift, time stretch, SRC, formants, algorithm latency, drain/reset, and dynamic-ratio processing from §7.
- Explain plugin hosting, automation, state persistence, PDC, live monitoring, recording paths, and offline export from §§4, 8, 9, 21, 30, 31, and 33.
- Explain analysis confidence, canonical pitch representation, note segmentation, and deep-edit ownership from §39.
- Explain RT-safe telemetry and regression validation from §§28 and 34.
- Understand that a realtime tuner must decide not only “what pitch is present?” but also “what target is musically legal?”, “how aggressively should correction occur?”, and “how should correction state behave across note changes, transport jumps, silence, and unvoiced material?”

The implementation laboratories assume C++20, realtime DSP, stateful streaming, unit/integration testing, and the ability to measure algorithmic and system latency.

#### Why this domain matters

Automatic pitch correction is deceptively simple at the UI level. The user may select a key, scale, retune speed, and vocal range, then expect the voice to remain musical and responsive. Internally, however, the system must repeatedly solve several coupled problems under a hard deadline:

```text
input audio
→ voiced/unvoiced decision
→ pitch estimate
→ pitch confidence
→ target selection
→ correction trajectory
→ pitch/formant transformation
→ latency alignment
→ output
```

Each stage can fail differently.

A pitch tracker can jump octaves.

A target selector can choose the wrong scale degree.

A fast correction law can destroy intentional scoops and vibrato.

A slow correction law can leave a weak singer audibly flat.

A resynthesizer can shift formants.

A state machine can carry the previous phrase's target across a seek.

A plugin can sound perfect in playback but fail during low-latency monitoring.

A realtime system can also be musically correct yet unusable if its total monitoring latency is too high.

Public Auto-Tune documentation demonstrates user-facing controls such as Retune Speed, Humanize, Flex-Tune, key/scale selection, vocal/instrument ranges, MIDI target control, vibrato controls, and formant processing. These behaviors define useful product concepts, but Antares' proprietary internal algorithms remain unknown. APEX should reproduce the class of capability through independently engineered algorithms and documented architecture, not by inventing knowledge of closed-source internals.

#### Section 40 learning outcomes

By the end of this section, the learner should be able to:

1. **Trace** the complete realtime tuning pipeline from live input to audible corrected output.
2. **Distinguish** pitch estimation, target selection, correction trajectory, resynthesis, and monitoring as separate authorities.
3. **Design** a target-note engine for chromatic, diatonic, custom-scale, and MIDI-directed correction.
4. **Explain** why Retune Speed-like behavior is a correction-state time constant rather than simply “amount of pitch correction.”
5. **Design** Humanize/Flex-Tune-like behaviors without copying proprietary implementation details.
6. **Preserve** intentional vibrato, scoops, note transitions, and unvoiced consonants under configurable correction.
7. **Specify** formant handling and distinguish correction from creative formant shift.
8. **Calculate** and measure total monitoring latency, including detector, shifter, buffering, plugin, PDC, driver, and device contributions.
9. **Integrate** Native Tune with APEX monitoring so exactly one audible monitoring path remains active.
10. **Handle** seek, stop/start, loop, record-arm, sample-rate change, and transport discontinuities correctly.
11. **Define** realtime and offline-HQ modes while preserving one canonical parameter/edit state.
12. **Validate** Native Tune across voices, keys, scales, buffers, sample rates, automation, recording modes, and export.
13. **Represent** capability maturity honestly through §42.

### 40.1 Evidence profile

**Fact:** Current Antares documentation publicly describes controls including Retune Speed, Humanize, Flex-Tune, vocal/instrument range, key/scale, MIDI target control, vibrato controls, and formant processing. Public documentation states that Retune Speed controls how quickly input pitch is tuned toward the target; faster values create stronger/obvious correction and moderate values create subtler correction. Antares support documentation describes Humanize as slowing correction on sustained notes and Flex-Tune as preserving more expressive pitch variation around targets.

**Fact:** Rubber Band publicly documents dynamically changing pitch-shift modes and formant-preservation options. WORLD publicly exposes F0, spectral-envelope, aperiodicity, and synthesis roles. pYIN, aubio, and other open systems provide reproducible pitch-detection references.

**Synthesis:** The APEX Native Tune pipeline, target-state model, correction law, transport reconciliation, monitoring ownership, and validation architecture described here are engineering syntheses.

**Unknown:** Antares' internal detector, target-state implementation, resynthesis algorithm, proprietary formant algorithms, and exact latency architecture remain Unknown unless officially documented.

**Recommendation:** APEX should implement and verify the monophonic vocal case first. Polyphonic automatic correction should be a separate future capability, not an implied extension of monophonic tuning.

### 40.2 Native Tune authority model

Native Tune should contain distinct authorities:

```text
PitchDetector
→ what pitch/confidence is currently estimated

TargetResolver
→ which pitch target is musically allowed

CorrectionPlanner
→ how desired correction evolves over time

PitchRenderer
→ how samples are transformed

TuneState
→ persistent user settings and automation

MonitoringIntegration
→ where corrected signal becomes audible
```

Do not place all behavior in one opaque `processBlock()` function.

### 40.3 Shared pitch identity with §39

Where §39 and §40 operate on the same analyzed source, they should share canonical pitch conventions:

```text
A4 reference
semitone/cents representation
voiced flag
confidence
time domain
note identity where available
```

For live input, §40 may produce ephemeral realtime analysis that has no persistent §39 note object.

For recorded material, offline/deep analysis may provide richer information.

The relationship must be explicit.

### 40.4 Input role

Native Tune may process:

```text
live microphone input
recorded clip playback
frozen/bounced source
offline export
```

These paths can have different latency and lookahead policies.

They should not have different parameter meanings.

### 40.5 Monophonic assumption

The first APEX Native Tune engine should declare its supported input model.

Recommended initial scope:

```text
one dominant pitched voice
limited accompaniment bleed tolerated but not guaranteed
unvoiced consonants allowed
no general polyphonic correction claim
```

If two singers overlap, one F0 tracker may produce unstable or ambiguous output.

### 40.6 Pitch detector

A realtime detector must expose:

```text
estimated pitch
confidence
voiced/unvoiced state
optional candidate set
detector latency
```

Do not force low-confidence frames into a target note.

### 40.7 Detector window and hop

A larger analysis window can improve low-frequency stability but increases temporal latency and smears fast note changes.

A smaller window can respond faster but become noisy.

The correct configuration depends on:

```text
voice range
sample rate
desired latency
CPU
algorithm
```

Therefore vocal range selection can legitimately influence detector search constraints.

### 40.8 Vocal/instrument range

A range control should constrain plausible F0.

Example:

```text
Soprano
Alto/Tenor
Baritone/Bass
Instrument High/Mid
Instrument Bass
```

These are UI categories; the implementation should map them to documented frequency priors or detector limits.

Do not encode gender identity into engine logic.

### 40.9 Confidence gating

A possible state machine:

```text
UNVOICED
CANDIDATE
LOCKED
TRANSITION
RELEASE
```

Low confidence may hold, release, or bypass correction according to policy.

Never interpret random low-confidence F0 as a valid note.

### 40.10 Octave-error control

Common failure:

```text
true pitch = A3
tracker briefly reports A4
→ renderer jumps one octave
```

Mitigations can include:

```text
candidate continuity
harmonic consistency
range priors
temporal decoding
confidence hysteresis
maximum plausible slope
```

Do not clamp legitimate falsetto/register jumps indiscriminately.

### 40.11 Key and scale

Target selection requires a pitch-class set.

Examples:

```text
Chromatic
Major
Natural Minor
Harmonic Minor
Melodic Minor
modes
custom scale
user-enabled notes
```

Scale definitions should be data-driven.

### 40.12 Target pitch identity

Represent a target in an unambiguous pitch domain:

```text
MIDI note integer + cent offset
```

or:

```text
continuous semitones relative to A4
```

The target must remain stable across sample rate.

### 40.13 Nearest-note quantization

Simplest policy:

```text
target = nearest enabled scale pitch
```

But musical behavior may need hysteresis.

Without hysteresis, a singer near the midpoint between C and C# can chatter between targets.

### 40.14 Target hysteresis

Maintain current target until the input crosses a defined boundary or transition criterion.

Conceptually:

```text
current target
candidate new target
confidence
distance
dwell time
```

This reduces target flicker.

### 40.15 Note-transition detection

A new target may be triggered by:

```text
large pitch movement
onset
energy change
confidence reset
MIDI target
scale transition
```

The target resolver should not rely on pitch distance alone.

### 40.16 Retune Speed

Public Antares documentation defines Retune Speed as how quickly input pitch is tuned toward target pitch.

A product-neutral implementation can model this as a time-dependent correction response.

For example:

```text
pitchError = target - detectedPitch
correctionState = smoothed response to pitchError
```

The exact curve may be linear, exponential, critically damped, or another designed response.

### 40.17 Retune Speed is not correction amount

Two independent concepts:

```text
Correction Amount
how far toward target to move

Correction Speed
how quickly to move there
```

A fast 50% correction differs from a slow 100% correction.

The UI may expose one or both.

### 40.18 Hard-tune behavior

A “hard” effect generally uses:

```text
rapid target acquisition
strong correction
minimal tolerance around target
fast note transitions
```

The exact sound also depends on:

```text
detector
target hysteresis
pitch renderer
formant policy
input performance
```

Do not reduce the entire effect to one knob.

### 40.19 Natural correction

Natural correction usually preserves more of:

```text
attack scoop
vibrato
micro-intonation
transition glide
sustained-note movement
```

This requires more than simply increasing the response time.

### 40.20 Flex-Tune-like tolerance

Without copying proprietary internals, APEX can define an expressive tolerance zone.

Concept:

```text
near target
→ preserve more original variation

far from target
→ apply stronger correction
```

Possible transfer:

```text
correctionAmount = f(abs(pitchError))
```

with a soft knee.

Document the exact APEX behavior.

### 40.21 Humanize-like sustained-note behavior

Without copying proprietary implementation details, APEX can expose a sustained-note relaxation policy:

```text
short note
→ base retune response

long stable note
→ gradually relax correction speed or amount
```

This can preserve life in sustained notes while keeping fast passages tight.

### 40.22 Vibrato preservation

A detector may separate:

```text
slow center movement
fast modulation
```

Correction can act mainly on center.

Hard tuning may intentionally reduce modulation.

Natural tuning should allow configurable preservation.

### 40.23 Natural vibrato control

Creative control may scale modulation depth:

```text
0% preserve original
negative reduce
positive increase
```

The exact UI semantics are product-defined.

Avoid unstable modulation synthesis when confidence is low.

### 40.24 Formant preservation

Pitch shifting changes perceived vocal character if the spectral envelope moves with the fundamental.

Native Tune should support a formant policy:

```text
Preserve
ShiftWithPitch
CustomFormantScale
```

The transparent default for vocals should normally preserve formant character where the renderer supports it.

### 40.25 Formant correction versus formant creative effect

Keep separate:

```text
formant preservation
```

and:

```text
intentional formant shift
```

One prevents unwanted timbre change.

The other creates a new timbre.

### 40.26 Unvoiced handling

Do not pitch-correct:

```text
sibilants
breaths
many fricatives
plosives
silence
```

as though they were stable voiced tones.

Use classification/crossfade policies.

### 40.27 Voiced/unvoiced transition

A hard switch between processed and unprocessed audio can click or change phase.

Use bounded transition logic:

```text
voiced renderer state
↔ crossfade
↔ unvoiced pass-through
```

### 40.28 Pitch-renderer choices

Possible implementation families:

- pitch-synchronous waveform methods;
- phase-vocoder/spectral methods;
- vocoder decomposition;
- granular/hybrid methods;
- high-quality library backend;
- neural backend where deployment permits.

Each trades:

```text
latency
CPU
transient quality
formant control
dynamic ratio stability
determinism
```

### 40.29 Dynamic pitch ratio

For detected pitch `p` and target `t` in semitones:

```text
ratio = 2^((t - p) / 12)
```

The actual renderer may receive a smoothed correction state rather than instantaneous target error.

Avoid discontinuous ratio jumps.

### 40.30 Parameter smoothing

Realtime automation can change:

```text
retune speed
correction amount
formant
mix
scale
```

Continuous DSP parameters require smoothing where needed.

Discrete musical-state changes require explicit transition logic.

Do not treat a key change as merely a smoothed float.

### 40.31 Scale automation

If key/scale changes during playback:

```text
publish new scale generation
→ target resolver adopts at defined sample/block boundary
→ current target reconciles
```

A change must not leave an impossible target from the previous scale indefinitely.

### 40.32 MIDI target control

Public Auto-Tune documentation demonstrates MIDI-directed target behavior.

APEX may support:

```text
MIDI note sets allowed targets
MIDI note directly selects target
chord defines target pool
```

The semantics must be explicit.

### 40.33 MIDI timing

MIDI target changes should honor sample offsets where the host event model supports them.

Do not quantize all target changes to arbitrary UI timer boundaries.

### 40.34 Scale/key detection boundary

Automatic key detection is a separate capability.

Native Tune should accept:

```text
manual key/scale
project key track
external analysis result
MIDI control
```

Do not make the realtime audio callback run a full-song key detector.

### 40.35 Live-monitoring path

Native Tune is latency-sensitive in live vocal monitoring.

Correct APEX ownership:

```text
input
→ exactly one monitoring owner
→ Native Tune in chosen monitor path
→ remaining monitor FX
→ output
```

The permanent §31 invariant remains:

> One live input sample has exactly one audible monitoring owner.

### 40.36 Dry recording with wet monitoring

Common workflow:

```text
record dry source to disk
monitor through Native Tune
```

The recorded file remains dry.

The performer hears correction.

This requires separate record and monitor authorities.

### 40.37 Wet recording

If APEX supports wet recording:

```text
dry source
+
processed source
```

should ideally remain distinguishable when product policy permits.

Do not silently destroy the only dry capture.

### 40.38 Total latency

Total monitored latency includes:

```text
input hardware/driver
input buffer
host scheduling
detector lookahead/window
pitch renderer latency
plugin chain latency
output buffer
output hardware
```

Plugin-reported latency is only one component.

### 40.39 Detector latency

A detector cannot infer a stable period before observing enough samples.

Low notes require longer periods.

Therefore “zero latency tuning” is not a universal engineering truth.

Products may use prediction, short windows, priors, or specialized methods, but measurement is required.

### 40.40 PDC and monitoring

Full PDC may be undesirable in a live low-latency monitoring path if it delays the performer to match a high-latency branch.

APEX needs explicit low-latency monitoring policy.

Playback/export still require correct alignment.

### 40.41 Bypass

Bypass must address latency.

Possible architecture:

```text
processed path
dry delay aligned to reported tuner latency
crossfade
```

An instantaneous unaligned bypass can comb or jump in time.

### 40.42 Mix control

Wet/dry mix for pitch correction must use aligned paths.

A dry path that is not delayed to match the processed path creates comb filtering.

### 40.43 Transport start

At transport start:

- reset or reconcile detector history;
- clear stale target state;
- initialize renderer latency;
- avoid first-block allocation.

### 40.44 Seek

On seek:

```text
old phrase state
must not leak into new phrase
```

For prerecorded playback, optional preroll can warm analysis/render state.

For live input, seek is irrelevant to incoming microphone time but may affect project-controlled target/scale context.

### 40.45 Loop

Loop boundaries can cause state discontinuity.

Decide whether to:

```text
reset
preroll
carry state
```

based on source continuity.

Test loops whose end and start are unrelated pitches.

### 40.46 Stop

Stop should not trigger expensive destruction on the audio thread.

Renderer state may be reset under prepared bounded rules or deferred.

### 40.47 Sample-rate changes

A sample-rate change requires:

```text
stop/reprepare
detector reconfiguration
renderer reconfiguration
latency recomputation
PDC rebuild
```

Do not preserve sample-count latency blindly across rates.

### 40.48 Buffer-size changes

The engine must support block sizes within prepared maxima.

Detector hop/state should not assume callback size equals analysis hop.

Use internal buffering if needed.

### 40.49 Realtime thread ownership

Prepare off-thread:

```text
detector objects
FFT plans
models
renderer buffers
window tables
scale tables
```

The callback performs bounded processing only.

### 40.50 Neural detector boundary

A neural pitch model may be useful.

Before realtime adoption verify:

```text
model license
runtime license
model size
first-use allocation
threading
latency
determinism
CPU/GPU dependency
offline availability
```

A model that works in Python is not automatically realtime-safe in a DAW callback.

### 40.51 Quality modes

Possible:

```text
Live
Standard
High
OfflineHQ
```

Live prioritizes latency.

OfflineHQ may use:

```text
future context
two-pass analysis
higher-quality resynthesis
```

Parameter meaning remains consistent.

### 40.52 Offline render

Offline render must not depend on live monitoring state.

It should render the project's Native Tune state deterministically under the selected quality policy.

### 40.53 Freeze and bounce

Freeze/bounce should capture:

```text
Native Tune settings
automation
key/scale state
MIDI target state
renderer quality policy
```

Unfreeze restores editable state.

### 40.54 Save/reload

Persist:

```text
key
scale
enabled notes
vocal range
retune parameters
correction amount
expressive tolerance
sustain humanization
formant policy
vibrato controls
MIDI mode
quality policy
```

Do not persist raw runtime pointers or transient detector buffers.

### 40.55 Automation

Classify parameters:

**Continuous**
- retune speed;
- amount;
- formant shift;
- mix.

**Discrete**
- key;
- scale;
- algorithm mode;
- vocal range.

Discrete changes need generation/state transitions.

### 40.56 Presets

Presets should store user intent, not hidden environment assumptions.

A preset created at 48 kHz should load correctly at 96 kHz.

### 40.57 Stereo policy

A lead vocal tuner usually operates on mono or coherently linked stereo.

If stereo input is supported:

- define detector input;
- preserve channel phase;
- avoid independently tuning L/R to different targets.

### 40.58 Sidechain/key input

A future creative mode may accept external target control.

Do not confuse audio sidechain signal with MIDI scale control.

### 40.59 Failure policy

| Failure | Realtime response |
|---|---|
| Low pitch confidence | Bypass/hold/release according to bounded policy |
| Detector unavailable | Dry/silence according to user role; surface error |
| Renderer overload | Bounded fallback; no indefinite wait |
| Invalid NaN/Inf | Contain and report |
| Scale state invalid | Fall back to validated previous state |
| Model load failure | Disable capability before streaming |
| Offline HQ failure | Abort publication; keep previous valid artifact |

### 40.60 Diagnostics

RT-safe counters can include:

```text
voiced frames
unvoiced frames
low-confidence frames
target changes
octave-rejection events
maximum pitch error
renderer underruns
detector latency
reported plugin latency
transport resets
```

Detailed text reports drain off-thread.

### 40.61 Privacy

Do not upload raw vocal audio or pitch contours by default.

Support bundles should permit explicit user inclusion.

### 40.62 Validation matrix

At minimum:

```text
44.1 / 48 / 88.2 / 96 kHz
64 / 128 / 256 / 512 sample buffers where supported
low/mid/high voices
soft/loud
vibrato/non-vibrato
slides
rap/speech transitions
breathy vocals
sibilants
silence
noise
```

### 40.63 Musical tests

Test:

```text
major
minor
chromatic
custom enabled notes
key changes
wrong-key intentional test
MIDI targets
micro-detuning
note midpoint hysteresis
```

### 40.64 Monitoring matrix

Protect all modes:

```text
MonitorDryRecordDry
MonitorWetRecordDry
MonitorWetRecordWet
```

Verify exactly one audible contribution.

### 40.65 Latency tests

Measure:

```text
reported algorithm latency
host PDC latency
physical loopback round trip
monitor path delta with tuner enabled/disabled
```

### 40.66 Artifact tests

Listen and measure for:

```text
warble
octave jump
metallic consonants
formant shift
phasiness
transient doubling
clicks at target change
zipper from parameter automation
seek contamination
```

### 40.67 CPU/deadline tests

Record:

```text
callback p50/p99/p99.9/max
xrun count
detector cost
renderer cost
first-use cost
```

Use §34 evidence.

### 40.68 Worked example — natural vocal tuning

```text
Key: A minor
Retune: moderate
Expressive tolerance: medium
Sustain humanization: enabled
Formants: preserved

Singer enters slightly flat.
Detector locks with high confidence.
Target resolver selects A.
Correction planner moves center toward A gradually.
Vibrato remains mostly intact.
Sibilant passes through unpitched path.
Output remains aligned through declared latency.
```

### 40.69 Worked example — hard effect

```text
Scale: selected song key
Retune: fastest
Correction amount: high
Tolerance: low
Sustain humanization: low
Formants: preserve or creative mode

Pitch center snaps rapidly.
Transitions become discrete.
Natural slides are reduced.
Result is intentionally synthetic.
```

### 40.70 Worked example — transport seek bug

Bug:

```text
seek from phrase on C4
to unrelated phrase on F#3
first output bends from old C4 target
```

Root cause:

```text
TargetResolver and PitchRenderer retained previous phrase state
```

Invariant:

```text
Tune state must reconcile after transport discontinuity.
```

Potential Fix Registry entry:

```text
APEX-TUNE-TRANSPORT-001
```

Regression:

```text
seek between unrelated vocal phrases
```

### 40.71 Native Tune capability decomposition

Recommended:

```text
APEX-CAP-TUNE-PITCH-DETECTION
APEX-CAP-TUNE-TARGET-SELECTION
APEX-CAP-TUNE-REALTIME-CORRECTION
APEX-CAP-TUNE-FORMANT-PRESERVATION
APEX-CAP-TUNE-MONITORING
APEX-CAP-TUNE-OFFLINE-HQ
APEX-CAP-TUNE-PERSISTENCE
APEX-CAP-TUNE-AUTOMATION
APEX-CAP-TUNE-MIDI-TARGET
```

Aggregate:

```text
APEX-CAP-NATIVE-TUNE
```

### 40.72 Maturity gates

`VERIFIED_PRODUCTION` should require defined scope.

Possible gates:

```text
RT allocation safety
callback deadline matrix
sample-rate matrix
buffer matrix
monitoring matrix
transport discontinuity
save/reload
automation
PDC/latency
offline export
freeze/bounce
perceptual validation
```

### 40.73 APEX staged roadmap

**Stage 1**
- realtime monophonic pitch detector;
- confidence;
- telemetry.

**Stage 2**
- scale/key target resolver;
- correction planner;
- basic pitch renderer.

**Stage 3**
- formant preservation;
- monitoring integration;
- latency/PDC.

**Stage 4**
- expressive tolerance;
- sustain humanization;
- vibrato controls;
- MIDI target.

**Stage 5**
- offline HQ;
- freeze/bounce/export;
- full persistence.

**Stage 6**
- shared deep-edit integration with §39.

### 40.74 Permanent APEX Native Tune invariants

1. Pitch detection, target resolution, correction planning, and rendering remain separable authorities.
2. Low-confidence analysis is never silently promoted to certain pitch truth.
3. Native Tune's initial verified scope is monophonic unless evidence proves more.
4. Target selection uses an explicit scale/key/custom-note authority.
5. Target hysteresis prevents uncontrolled midpoint chatter.
6. Correction speed and correction amount are distinct concepts.
7. Formant preservation and creative formant shift are distinct controls.
8. Unvoiced material is not blindly processed as voiced F0.
9. Dynamic pitch ratio changes are transition-safe.
10. No model loading, allocation, file I/O, or graph rebuild occurs in the audio callback.
11. Exactly one audible live-input monitoring owner remains active.
12. Dry-record/wet-monitor does not silently record the wet path.
13. Bypass and wet/dry mixing remain latency-aligned.
14. Transport discontinuities reconcile detector/target/renderer state.
15. Sample-rate changes trigger reprepare and latency recomputation.
16. Offline render does not depend on live-monitor state.
17. Save/reload preserves user intent, not transient runtime state.
18. §39 and §40 share canonical pitch conventions where they interoperate.
19. Capability maturity is evidence-gated in §42.
20. Successful compilation alone never proves Native Tune production readiness.

### 40.75 Laboratories

1. Build a monophonic pitch detector with confidence.
2. Implement scale/custom-note target resolution with hysteresis.
3. Implement correction speed and amount separately.
4. Add expressive tolerance.
5. Add sustained-note humanization.
6. Integrate a formant-preserving renderer.
7. Test dry-record/wet-monitor routing.
8. Measure full monitoring latency.
9. Test seek/loop/sample-rate/buffer transitions.
10. Create a Native Tune capability record and promotion gate.

### 40.76 Review questions

1. Why is pitch detection not the same as pitch correction?
2. Why does a tuner need target hysteresis?
3. What is the difference between retune speed and correction amount?
4. How can natural tuning preserve vibrato?
5. Why must unvoiced consonants be handled separately?
6. Why is formant preservation not automatic in every pitch shifter?
7. Why can low notes increase detector latency?
8. How can full PDC conflict with low-latency monitoring?
9. Why must bypass be latency aligned?
10. What state must reset after a seek?
11. Why must §40 not maintain a second canonical pitch truth separate from §39?
12. What evidence is required before `VERIFIED_PRODUCTION`?

### 40.77 Practical examination

Design APEX Native Tune for live vocal recording.

Submit:

1. Detector architecture.
2. Confidence model.
3. Vocal-range policy.
4. Key/scale/custom-note model.
5. Target hysteresis.
6. Correction planner.
7. Expressive-tolerance and sustained-humanization model.
8. Vibrato/formant policy.
9. Pitch renderer.
10. Monitoring routing.
11. Latency/PDC.
12. Transport state machine.
13. Persistence/automation.
14. Offline HQ.
15. Validation matrix and §42 capability gates.

### 40.78 Mastery rubric

| Level | Required evidence |
|---|---|
| Foundation | Explains detection, targets, retune behavior, vibrato, formants, latency, and monitoring. |
| Engineering | Implements a bounded monophonic realtime tuner and validates transport, buffers, sample rates, and save/reload. |
| Architecture | Integrates tuning with monitoring, PDC, offline render, §39 shared pitch identity, and §42 capability gates. |
| Research | Compares detectors/renderers, measures perceptual artifacts and latency, and distinguishes public product behavior from unknown proprietary internals. |

### 40.79 Primary sources

- [Antares Auto-Tune Pro 11 Help Page](https://help.antarestech.com/hc/en-us/articles/41117380615188-Auto-Tune-Pro-11-Help-Page): current official support entry linking the product guide and release/help material.
- [Antares Auto-Tune Pro 11 User Guide](https://antares-web-frontend.sfo3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/documentation/pdfs/Auto-Tune_Pro_11_User_Guide.pdf): official public documentation for Retune Speed, Flex-Tune, Humanize, vibrato, MIDI-to-notes, and related product behavior; do not infer private algorithms.
- [Antares AutoTune 2026 FAQ](https://help.antarestech.com/hc/en-us/articles/42855736822932-AutoTune-2026-FAQ): current public behavior descriptions for Retune Speed, Humanize, Flex Tune, Modern/Classic modes; Time-sensitive.
- [Antares AutoTune 2026 Best Practices](https://help.antarestech.com/hc/en-us/articles/42858099043092-AutoTune-2026-Best-Practices): current key/scale, range, and retune workflow guidance; Time-sensitive.
- [Mauch and Dixon — pYIN](https://qmro.qmul.ac.uk/xmlui/bitstream/handle/123456789/6040/MAUCHpYINFundamental2014Accepted.pdf?sequence=2): monophonic probabilistic F0 reference.
- [aubio](https://github.com/aubio/aubio): open pitch/onset analysis reference; license and maintenance must be evaluated before adoption.
- [WORLD vocoder](https://github.com/mmorise/World): open F0/spectral-envelope/aperiodicity/synthesis reference.
- [Rubber Band Library](https://breakfastquay.com/rubberband/): open/commercially licensed time/pitch backend reference; verify exact current license.
- [Rubber Band integration guidance](https://www.breakfastquay.com/rubberband/integration.html): documented realtime dynamic-pitch and formant-preservation recommendations.
- [RubberBandStretcher API](https://breakfastquay.com/rubberband/code-doc/classRubberBand_1_1RubberBandStretcher.html): public dynamic pitch/formant option semantics.

## 41. Autonomous Repository Engineering, Debugging, and Validation Agent

### Section 41 guide

#### Section 41 prerequisites

Before starting this section, the learner should be able to:

- Explain the DAW Brain authority hierarchy and evidence taxonomy.
- Trace repository truth, build identity, runtime evidence, testing, diagnostics, persistence, and release provenance from §§9, 14, 17, 27, 28, 34, 36, and 37.
- Understand Git working-tree state, commits, branches, diffs, build configurations, symbols, native debugging, crash dumps, and test execution.
- Distinguish a hypothesis, diagnosis, patch, successful build, passing test, verified fix, and release-ready result.
- Explain why a realtime audio defect may require source inspection, runtime traces, debugger evidence, crash artifacts, audio measurement, and regression tests rather than one textual log.
- Understand that an AI agent is not an authority merely because it can read or modify code.

The implementation laboratories assume repository access, a deterministic build path, native debugger availability, test execution, and permission to create non-production engineering metadata.

#### Why this domain matters

AI-assisted coding can accelerate APEX development, but speed without authority boundaries creates new failure modes. An agent can produce a plausible patch that compiles while changing the wrong subsystem. It can “fix” a symptom while violating a historical invariant. It can interpret an old log as current truth. It can confidently claim a crash is solved after one successful launch. It can modify production code without understanding the audio callback path.

The purpose of an autonomous engineering agent is not to replace engineering discipline. It is to automate that discipline.

The desired loop is:

```text
understand task
→ read relevant Brain contracts
→ inspect repository truth
→ establish baseline
→ reproduce
→ gather evidence
→ diagnose
→ patch minimally
→ build
→ run affected regressions
→ reproduce original scenario
→ compare before/after
→ publish evidence
→ update living memory
```

The agent must be able to stop at `DIAGNOSED` or `BLOCKED`. Producing code is not always the correct result.

For APEX, this matters especially because the product includes native audio callbacks, JUCE, plugins, drivers, project persistence, realtime monitoring, export, and complex UI. A visually small change can have deep execution consequences.

#### Section 41 learning outcomes

By the end of this section, the learner should be able to:

1. **Define** the authority boundary between Brain knowledge, repository truth, build artifacts, runtime evidence, and living memory.
2. **Design** an agent startup protocol that prevents blind patching.
3. **Capture** repository identity, dirty state, toolchain, build configuration, binary identity, and symbols.
4. **Reproduce** a defect before editing when reproduction is practical.
5. **Use** debugger, dump, sanitizer, trace, test, and audio evidence without confusing any one tool with complete proof.
6. **Trace** native crashes from process failure to symbolized source location.
7. **Select** regression tests from modified files, architecture dependencies, capabilities, and historical fixes.
8. **Separate** patch authority from verification authority.
9. **Define** task states such as `DIAGNOSED`, `PATCHED`, `VALIDATION_PENDING`, and `VERIFIED_FIXED`.
10. **Prevent** high-frequency unproductive agent loops and repeated noncompliant actions.
11. **Coordinate** multiple agents without allowing conflicting authority changes.
12. **Integrate** Visual Studio or another debugger through supported automation/protocol boundaries instead of screen-scraping assumptions.
13. **Publish** evidence and hand off verified knowledge to §42.
14. **Explain** when the agent must stop rather than “keep trying” destructively.

### 41.1 Evidence profile

**Fact:** Git exposes working-tree status and diffs. CMake provides configure/build/test presets and workflow presets. CTest executes registered tests. Microsoft's Debug Adapter Protocol defines a structured protocol between development tools and debug adapters. Visual Studio supports native debugging, attach-to-process, Just-In-Time debugging, and analysis of minidump files. Windows `MiniDumpWriteDump` creates user-mode minidumps, and Microsoft recommends writing a dump from a separate process where possible when the target is unstable. Clang AddressSanitizer, ThreadSanitizer, and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer detect different instrumented runtime defect classes.

**Synthesis:** The APEX autonomous-agent workflow, authority model, debugger bridge, regression-selection graph, evidence packet, and task state machine described here are engineering syntheses.

**Recommendation:** APEX should use a tool-facing bridge based on command-line build/test interfaces, structured debugger protocols or dump artifacts, and explicit repository state. It should not depend on an agent visually interpreting IDE windows when machine-readable evidence is available.

**Unknown:** The exact capabilities of any specific AI coding agent, OpenCode build, Visual Studio extension, or model provider are Time-sensitive until tested in the actual environment.

### 41.2 Agent authority hierarchy

The agent obeys:

```text
OFFICIAL EXTERNAL CONTRACTS
        ↓
DAW BRAIN
        ↓
APEX ARCHITECTURE INTENT
        ↓
CURRENT APEX REPOSITORY
        ↓
BUILD ARTIFACT
        ↓
RUNTIME BEHAVIOR
        ↓
TEST / MEASUREMENT EVIDENCE
        ↓
LIVING ENGINEERING MEMORY
```

The agent itself is not in this hierarchy as an authority.

It is an actor that queries and transforms evidence.

### 41.3 Brain versus repository

The Brain answers:

```text
How should a dependable DAW system work?
```

The repository answers:

```text
How does APEX currently work?
```

Before patching, the agent must reconcile both.

A Brain recommendation must never be reported as already implemented without repository evidence.

### 41.4 Agent startup sequence

For substantial tasks:

```text
1. Resolve task scope.
2. Read relevant Brain sections.
3. Read APEX_STATE.
4. Read architecture ownership.
5. Search historical fixes.
6. Search related tests.
7. Inspect current repository.
8. Capture repository identity.
9. Establish baseline build/run/test state.
10. Reproduce or characterize the defect.
11. Only then patch.
```

### 41.5 Repository identity

Capture at minimum:

```text
repository root
branch
HEAD commit
dirty state
modified/untracked files
submodule/dependency state where applicable
```

The agent must not assume a clean tree.

### 41.6 Dirty-tree safety

If the tree is dirty:

- identify user changes;
- avoid overwriting unrelated work;
- scope diffs precisely;
- do not reset or clean destructively without explicit authorization.

A successful patch that deletes the user's unrelated work is a failure.

### 41.7 Build identity

Record:

```text
buildId
commit
dirty digest or patch identity
configuration
architecture
compiler/toolchain
dependency revisions
result
warnings
errors
artifact path
artifact digest where available
symbol artifact identity
```

### 41.8 Deterministic build entry point

The agent should prefer one documented build entry point.

Possible:

```text
CMake preset/workflow
repository build script
Visual Studio solution + configuration
CI-equivalent script
```

Do not invent a new build path if the repository already has one canonical path.

### 41.9 CMake and workflow presets

CMake presets can encode configure/build/test/package workflows.

For an autonomous agent, a repository-owned preset reduces ambiguity:

```text
cmake --preset apex-debug
cmake --build --preset apex-debug
ctest --preset apex-debug
```

Exact commands depend on repository configuration.

### 41.10 Baseline before patch

A baseline answers:

```text
Does it build now?
Does the bug reproduce now?
Which tests fail before the patch?
What is the crash signature?
What is the performance baseline?
```

Without baseline, the agent can falsely attribute pre-existing failures to its patch or falsely claim improvement.

### 41.11 Reproduction record

A reproduction should capture:

```text
steps
input project
device/backend
sample rate
buffer size
plugins
transport state
expected behavior
actual behavior
frequency
build identity
```

### 41.12 Reproduction quality

Possible states:

```text
ALWAYS
INTERMITTENT
ENVIRONMENT_SPECIFIC
NOT_REPRODUCED
```

`NOT_REPRODUCED` does not mean `FIXED`.

### 41.13 Trace before patch

For engine defects, trace the actual call path.

Example:

```text
JUCE callback
→ MainComponent
→ ApplicationCore
→ AudioEngine
→ render graph
→ node
→ plugin
```

Do not patch the first class whose name resembles the symptom.

### 41.14 Authority owner

Before adding logic, ask:

```text
Who already owns this responsibility?
```

Consult:

```text
Architecture Map
source call path
persistent model
runtime graph
```

Duplicate ownership is a frequent source of regressions.

### 41.15 Root cause versus symptom

Symptom:

```text
vocal distorts
```

Possible causes:

```text
double monitoring
clipping
NaN
plugin failure
buffer underrun
sample-rate mismatch
```

The patch must target demonstrated root cause.

### 41.16 Hypothesis lifecycle

Use:

```text
OBSERVATION
→ HYPOTHESIS
→ EXPERIMENT
→ SUPPORTED / REJECTED
→ DIAGNOSIS
```

Do not publish a hypothesis as a Fact.

### 41.17 Patch scope

Prefer the smallest patch that:

- corrects the root cause;
- preserves architecture ownership;
- adds or updates regression protection;
- avoids unrelated refactoring.

Large refactors during bug repair make attribution harder.

### 41.18 Patch state

After editing:

```text
PATCHED
```

not:

```text
VERIFIED_FIXED
```

until validation passes.

### 41.19 Build success meaning

Build success proves:

```text
selected configuration compiled/linked under this environment
```

It does not prove:

```text
bug fixed
runtime stable
audio correct
other configurations correct
release ready
```

### 41.20 Validation ladder

Possible ladder:

```text
compile
→ unit
→ integration
→ targeted reproduction
→ adjacent regressions
→ system
→ performance
→ soak
→ manual/perceptual
```

Not every task requires every tier.

The required gate is capability-specific.

### 41.21 Independent validation logic

The patch author may execute tests, but verification authority comes from predefined evidence gates.

Conceptually:

```text
PATCHER
→ authors change

VALIDATOR
→ evaluates required gates

PUBLISHER
→ promotes status
```

These may be roles within one agent process but remain logically separate.

### 41.22 No self-certification invariant

> An agent that authors a patch does not acquire authority to mark it `VERIFIED_FIXED` merely because it compiled or because the agent believes it is correct.

### 41.23 Native debugger integration

Preferred machine-readable integration layers:

```text
Debug Adapter Protocol
debugger command-line interfaces
native debugger APIs
crash dumps/minidumps
symbolized stack traces
```

IDE visual UI is a human presentation layer.

### 41.24 Debug Adapter Protocol boundary

DAP defines structured messages between a development tool and a debug adapter.

An OpenCode-style engineering agent can conceptually use a DAP-capable bridge to:

```text
launch
attach
set breakpoints
continue
pause
inspect threads
inspect stack frames
evaluate expressions
receive stopped/terminated events
```

Actual supported commands depend on the adapter.

### 41.25 Visual Studio bridge

For APEX on Windows, practical options include:

```text
launch under native debugger
attach to running APEX process
JIT debugging
capture dump on crash
open dump with matching symbols
```

The bridge should produce machine-readable evidence for the agent.

### 41.26 F5 semantic boundary

Pressing F5 in Visual Studio is an IDE action.

An autonomous agent should not depend on simulated keyboard input if it can launch the executable/debug adapter directly.

The desired abstraction is:

```text
StartDebugSession()
```

not:

```text
press F5 by UI automation
```

### 41.27 Crash event

When a process crashes, collect:

```text
exception code/type
faulting thread
instruction address
module
stack
registers where available
loaded modules
build ID
symbols
recent breadcrumbs
```

### 41.28 Minidumps

Windows minidumps can preserve useful process/thread/module state.

A dump without matching binaries and symbols may be difficult to resolve.

Therefore build registry should retain symbol identity.

### 41.29 Out-of-process dump capture

Microsoft documentation recommends using a separate process where possible when dumping an unstable target.

This aligns with §34/§36 crash boundaries.

Do not execute heavy dump generation from the realtime audio callback.

### 41.30 Symbolization

A raw address:

```text
0x00007FF6...
```

is not a diagnosis.

Symbolization maps:

```text
binary identity
+
PDB/debug symbols
+
address
→ function/file/line where available
```

Never symbolize with a mismatched PDB and treat the result as authoritative.

### 41.31 Crash signature

A stable crash signature may include:

```text
exception code
top stable frames
module build identity
architecture generation
```

Address-only signatures are unstable across builds.

### 41.32 Automatic crash triage

Possible workflow:

```text
process terminates unexpectedly
→ capture/find dump
→ bind build
→ symbolize
→ search Fix Registry for similar signature
→ identify affected architecture owner
→ reproduce
```

### 41.33 Hang versus crash

Crash:

```text
process exited/faulted
```

Hang:

```text
process alive but progress stalled
```

Deadline miss:

```text
audio work completed too late
```

These are separate defects.

### 41.34 Hang capture

For a hang, capture:

```text
thread stacks
wait states
CPU usage
locks if available
audio callback sequence
worker heartbeat
```

A crash dump taken after termination cannot describe a live deadlock that was never captured.

### 41.35 Audio dropout triage

For clicks/xruns:

```text
callback timing
worker timing
xrun counters
graph generation
media underruns
plugin identity
transport event
```

A debugger breakpoint may itself disturb realtime timing.

Use §34 telemetry first where appropriate.

### 41.36 Sanitizers

ASan can detect supported memory errors.

TSan can detect supported data races.

UBSan can detect selected undefined behavior.

They are instrumented test builds, not production realtime configurations.

Passing them is evidence only for exercised paths.

### 41.37 Sanitizer routing

The agent should know which configuration supports each sanitizer.

Do not silently add sanitizer flags to production release builds.

### 41.38 Static analysis

Static analysis may identify:

```text
null dereference candidates
lifetime misuse
uninitialized values
API misuse
```

It does not replace runtime validation.

### 41.39 Test selection

Start with:

```text
modified files
→ Architecture Map
→ affected capabilities
→ historical fixes
→ protected tests
```

Then expand through dependency edges.

### 41.40 Regression collision

Example:

```text
patch modifies AudioEngine
→ Architecture Map links monitoring
→ Fix Registry reveals APEX-AUDIO-MONITOR-001
→ Test Registry selects TEST-MONITOR-MATRIX-001
```

The agent must run it even if the patch goal was “reduce latency.”

### 41.41 Serial oracle

For multicore/render changes, compare against the verified serial oracle where defined.

Different floating-point reduction order may require tolerance-based comparison.

### 41.42 Performance regression

A performance patch must compare the same scenario:

```text
before build
after build
same project
same device
same buffer
same sample rate
same plugin corpus
```

### 41.43 Soak testing

Intermittent defects require longer tests.

A five-second clean run does not close a bug that reproduced once every hour.

### 41.44 User-visible manual validation

Some DAW defects are perceptual or interaction-specific.

Manual validation may be required for:

```text
clicks
latency feel
drag behavior
focus
plugin windows
visual corruption
```

Manual tests must have explicit steps and expected results.

### 41.45 Evidence packet

A task can produce:

```text
CASE-ID
repository identity
baseline
reproduction
trace
diagnosis
patch diff
build result
tests
runtime evidence
final ruling
```

### 41.46 Agent completion states

Recommended:

```text
NO_CHANGE
OBSERVED
REPRODUCED
DIAGNOSED
PATCHED
VALIDATION_PENDING
VALIDATION_FAILED
VERIFIED_FIXED
REGRESSION_FOUND
BLOCKED
SUPERSEDED
```

### 41.47 `BLOCKED`

Use when:

```text
required hardware unavailable
required plugin unavailable
cannot reproduce
dependency inaccessible
missing symbol/artifact
legal/license boundary
```

The agent should report what evidence is missing.

### 41.48 `NO_CHANGE`

Use when investigation shows:

```text
repository already correct
issue outside APEX
duplicate report
misconfiguration
```

No code change is a valid outcome.

### 41.49 Rollback

If validation fails:

```text
do not hide failure
```

Possible:

```text
revert patch
revise patch
disable feature flag
restore LKG
```

### 41.50 Last Known Good

The agent should know the LKG for its scope.

If a new build fails critically, the LKG remains unchanged.

### 41.51 Multi-agent coordination

Agents should record:

```text
active case
branch
subsystem
files likely modified
validation pending
```

Avoid simultaneous incompatible authority changes.

### 41.52 Write permissions

Recommended logical permissions:

```text
MEMORY_READ
REPOSITORY_READ
PATCH_PROPOSE
PATCH_APPLY
BUILD_EXECUTE
DEBUG_EXECUTE
TEST_EXECUTE
EVIDENCE_WRITE
STATE_PROPOSE
STATE_PUBLISH
```

### 41.53 Publish authority

A patch-capable agent may not automatically have `STATE_PUBLISH`.

This supports future review gates.

### 41.54 Prompt-loop protection

Agents can enter loops:

```text
same failing command
same permission failure
same invalid request
```

Maintain attempt state.

After repeated identical failure:

```text
change strategy
or BLOCK
```

Do not spam tools indefinitely.

### 41.55 High-frequency noncompliant request protection

A robust agent should throttle repeated rejected actions.

Record:

```text
action
reason rejected
attempt count
alternative path
```

### 41.56 Context compaction

Long sessions risk forgetting early constraints.

Before compaction, persist:

```text
task
invariants
baseline
files changed
tests required
open hypotheses
```

to task-local engineering memory, not to unverified canonical memory.

### 41.57 Long-running session discipline

A five-hour engineering session should remain resumable.

Use:

```text
case record
task state
build IDs
test results
last verified checkpoint
```

### 41.58 Resume protocol

On resume:

```text
re-read current Git state
compare with saved task state
detect external modifications
revalidate assumptions
```

Never assume the repository remained unchanged while the agent was inactive.

### 41.59 Tool output trust

Compiler output is authoritative for that invocation.

Agent summaries of compiler output are not stronger than raw logs.

Preserve logs for significant evidence.

### 41.60 IDE output access

For Visual Studio integration, prefer:

```text
MSBuild/CMake command output
debugger protocol events
dump artifacts
test logs
```

over copying text visually from the Output window.

### 41.61 Breakpoint automation

Breakpoints are useful when:

- reproduction is deterministic;
- pausing will not invalidate the question;
- inspecting state is more valuable than timing.

Avoid breakpoints for timing-sensitive dropout diagnosis unless explicitly testing non-timing state.

### 41.62 Conditional breakpoints

An agent may use conditions to isolate:

```text
track ID
callback sequence
null pointer
transport position
```

Debugger overhead must be acknowledged.

### 41.63 Watchpoints/data breakpoints

Useful for memory corruption where supported.

They are limited hardware resources and can perturb execution.

### 41.64 Crash reproduction harness

For repeatable crash:

```text
clean launch
load exact project
perform scripted action
capture exit code/dump
```

Prefer deterministic automation where safe.

### 41.65 Plugin crash boundary

If a plugin is isolated, capture worker crash separately.

If in-process, the host may be corrupted.

The agent must follow §36.

### 41.66 Device/driver boundary

A device-driver crash or hang may occur outside APEX.

Record:

```text
backend
driver version
device
system event
```

Do not automatically patch APEX.

### 41.67 Security boundary

Do not execute arbitrary downloaded code because a build log suggests it.

Dependency acquisition follows repository and security policy.

### 41.68 Secret handling

Agent evidence must not persist:

```text
API keys
tokens
signing secrets
passwords
```

Redact logs before publication.

### 41.69 User data

Crash bundles may contain paths and project names.

Apply §34/§42 privacy policy.

### 41.70 Destructive operations

Require explicit authority for:

```text
git reset --hard
clean
delete user files
rewrite history
mass-format
dependency upgrade
```

### 41.71 Architecture migration

Large migrations should use:

```text
baseline
feature flag
dual run/shadow render
serial oracle
rollback
```

as appropriate.

### 41.72 Worked example — double monitoring

Task:

```text
vocal sounds too loud and distorted
```

Agent:

```text
reads §31
queries Fix Registry
finds APEX-AUDIO-MONITOR-001
traces both monitor paths
reproduces duplicate contribution
patches ownership guard
builds
runs TEST-MONITOR-MATRIX-001
repeats live recording test
publishes evidence
```

The agent does not simply lower gain.

### 41.73 Worked example — F5 crash

Task:

```text
APEX crashes under Visual Studio F5
```

Workflow:

```text
capture build identity
launch under native debugger
receive exception stop
record exception code
collect stack/thread
bind matching PDB
trace to source
search historical fixes
reproduce outside debugger if needed
capture minidump
diagnose
patch
rebuild
repeat crash reproduction
run regressions
```

### 41.74 Worked example — no crash under agent launcher

If F5 crashes but command-line launch does not:

Investigate:

```text
working directory
environment
arguments
debug heap
timing
debugger presence
startup project
DLL search path
```

Do not conclude the bug disappeared.

### 41.75 Worked example — intermittent audio click

Use telemetry:

```text
callback sequence 884219
p99.99 spike
worker 3 late
plugin X
graph generation 812
```

Then debugger or profiler follows evidence.

### 41.76 APEX agent startup contract

```text
TASK
→ relevant Brain sections
→ §42 state/history
→ repository truth
→ baseline
→ reproduction
→ evidence
→ patch
```

### 41.77 APEX agent completion contract

```text
build
→ regressions
→ original reproduction
→ adjacent validation
→ evidence
→ memory proposal
→ state publication if authorized
```

### 41.78 Permanent APEX autonomous-agent invariants

1. The agent never treats the Brain as proof of current implementation.
2. The agent inspects current repository truth before substantial patches.
3. Dirty user work is preserved.
4. Baseline precedes patch where practical.
5. Hypotheses remain hypotheses until supported.
6. Patch state does not equal verified state.
7. Build success alone never means bug fixed.
8. Patch authorship does not grant verification authority.
9. Debugger evidence is bound to exact build/symbol identity.
10. Mismatched symbols never produce canonical source conclusions.
11. Crash, hang, deadline miss, and xrun remain distinct.
12. RT diagnostics prefer bounded telemetry over callback logging.
13. Significant fixes produce invariants and regression protection where practical.
14. Historical Fix Registry is consulted before modifying protected subsystems.
15. Test selection includes indirect architecture dependencies.
16. Repeated identical tool failures are bounded.
17. Resume revalidates current repository state.
18. Destructive repository operations require explicit authority.
19. Secrets are excluded from evidence.
20. The agent may finish `BLOCKED`, `DIAGNOSED`, or `NO_CHANGE`.
21. §42 guides agent attention but never substitutes for source inspection.
22. Canonical memory publication requires evidence.

### 41.79 Laboratories

1. Build a repository-baseline collector.
2. Create one CMake/Visual Studio canonical build workflow.
3. Launch/attach through a debugger and capture a structured stop event.
4. Generate and analyze a matching-symbol minidump.
5. Reproduce a controlled crash and create a CASE bundle.
6. Introduce a memory bug and compare ASan versus debugger evidence.
7. Map a git diff to regression tests using Architecture/Fix/Test registries.
8. Simulate an intermittent failure and demonstrate `VALIDATION_PENDING`.
9. Run a multi-agent conflict simulation.
10. Execute full startup-to-memory completion on one real APEX bug.

### 41.80 Review questions

1. Why is an AI agent not an authority layer?
2. Why must repository truth be re-established on resume?
3. What does build success actually prove?
4. Why can a debugger hide or change a timing bug?
5. Why are matching PDBs essential?
6. What is the difference between crash and hang?
7. When is a minidump useful?
8. Why should dump capture be out-of-process where possible?
9. How does the agent select indirect regressions?
10. Why can the patch author not self-certify?
11. What does `BLOCKED` mean?
12. How does §42 prevent regression amnesia?

### 41.81 Practical examination

Design an APEX autonomous debugging agent for Windows/JUCE.

Submit:

1. Authority hierarchy.
2. Startup protocol.
3. Repository/build identity schema.
4. Baseline process.
5. Reproduction schema.
6. Native debugger bridge.
7. Crash-dump pipeline.
8. Symbol management.
9. Sanitizer configurations.
10. Audio telemetry integration.
11. Regression selection.
12. Task state machine.
13. Multi-agent coordination.
14. Evidence publication.
15. §42 memory integration.

Demonstrate one controlled native crash from launch through `VERIFIED_FIXED` without manually inventing the source location.

### 41.82 Mastery rubric

| Level | Required evidence |
|---|---|
| Foundation | Explains authority, baseline, reproduction, debugger, dump, build, test, and evidence boundaries. |
| Engineering | Automates build/debug/test workflows and produces reproducible case bundles. |
| Architecture | Integrates repository maps, historical fixes, regression selection, permissions, rollback, and living memory. |
| Research | Measures agent false diagnoses, contradiction rates, regression recurrence, and long-session reliability. |

### 41.83 Primary sources

- [Git `status`](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-status): canonical working-tree status semantics.
- [Git `diff`](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-diff): repository change inspection.
- [CMake Presets](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/manual/cmake-presets.7.html): configure/build/test/package/workflow preset model.
- [CMake command-line manual](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/manual/cmake.1.html): build and workflow invocation.
- [CMake Testing and CTest](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/guide/tutorial/Testing%20and%20CTest.html): registered test execution.
- [Microsoft Debug Adapter Protocol](https://microsoft.github.io/debug-adapter-protocol/): structured development-tool/debug-adapter protocol.
- [Microsoft — Visual Studio Just-In-Time Debugging](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/debugger/debug-using-the-just-in-time-debugger): native JIT debugger behavior.
- [Microsoft — Use dump files in Visual Studio](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/debugger/using-dump-files): dump analysis and symbol requirements.
- [Microsoft — `MiniDumpWriteDump`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/minidumpapiset/nf-minidumpapiset-minidumpwritedump): user-mode minidump API and out-of-process recommendation.
- [Clang AddressSanitizer](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AddressSanitizer.html): supported memory-error instrumentation.
- [Clang ThreadSanitizer](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/ThreadSanitizer.html): data-race instrumentation.
- [Clang UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer.html): selected undefined-behavior instrumentation.
- [JUCE](https://github.com/juce-framework/JUCE): framework source and build reference; pin exact version used by APEX.
- [pluginval](https://github.com/Tracktion/pluginval): plugin validation reference.
- [Crashpad repository](https://chromium.googlesource.com/crashpad/crashpad/): out-of-process crash-reporting reference; pin exact revision and integration dependencies.

## 42. Living Repository Intelligence and Engineering Memory

### Section 42 guide

#### Section 42 prerequisites

Before starting this section, the learner should be able to:

- Explain the DAW Brain authority hierarchy.
- Understand repository truth, build identity, runtime evidence, and regression validation from §41.
- Understand stable identity, schema migration, project persistence, and recovery from §9.
- Understand testing and validation architecture from §28.
- Understand RT-safe telemetry and evidence capture from §34.
- Understand release provenance, reproducibility, manifests, and artifact identity from §27.
- Understand that a static architecture document cannot by itself represent the continuously changing state of a software repository.
- Understand that memories derived from one build or runtime scenario must not be promoted to universal Facts without appropriate evidence.

The purpose of this section is to define a machine-readable operational-memory system that allows APEX and its engineering agents to accumulate, query, validate, and safely update knowledge about the actual repository and runtime over time.

The target system must answer questions such as:

```text
What is implemented right now?
What is only partially implemented?
What was the last verified-good build?
Has this bug happened before?
What invariant did a previous fix establish?
Which tests protect that invariant?
What architecture owns this subsystem?
What evidence proved this behavior?
Did a recent patch reintroduce an old regression?
```

The DAW Brain remains the reference architecture and educational knowledge base.

The Living Repository Intelligence layer represents the changing engineering reality of APEX.

### 42.1 Evidence profile

**Fact:** Repository commits, build outputs, test results, traces, crash packets, and runtime measurements may become repository/runtime Facts when tied to reproducible identities.

**Synthesis:** A conclusion derived from multiple repository and runtime artifacts remains a Synthesis until the relevant scope is sufficiently verified.

**Recommendation:** The registry structures, file formats, naming conventions, confidence models, retention policies, and agent workflows proposed in this section are Recommendations until implemented.

**Unknown:** Anything not demonstrated by repository inspection, build evidence, runtime measurement, or an authoritative external contract remains Unknown.

A previous agent statement is not evidence merely because it was confidently written.

### 42.2 Why living repository intelligence exists

The DAW Brain answers:

```text
How should this class of system work?
```

The repository answers:

```text
How does APEX currently work?
```

Those two answers continuously diverge and converge during development.

For example, the Brain may recommend:

```text
dynamic path-based PDC
```

while APEX may currently implement:

```text
partial fixed-latency compensation
```

The correct conclusion is not:

```text
APEX has full dynamic PDC because the Brain describes it.
```

The correct model is:

```text
Brain:
recommended architecture

Repository:
current implementation

State Registry:
current capability status

Evidence:
proof of current behavior
```

This separation prevents aspirational architecture from being confused with implemented product behavior.

### 42.3 The complete knowledge hierarchy

The recommended APEX hierarchy becomes:

```text
OFFICIAL EXTERNAL CONTRACTS
        ↓
DAW BRAIN
        ↓
APEX ARCHITECTURE INTENT
        ↓
APEX REPOSITORY
        ↓
BUILD ARTIFACT
        ↓
RUNTIME BEHAVIOR
        ↓
TEST / MEASUREMENT EVIDENCE
        ↓
LIVING ENGINEERING MEMORY
```

The final layer does not replace the previous layers.

It indexes and connects them.

### 42.4 Static knowledge versus living knowledge

Static knowledge includes:

```text
DSP principles
plugin contracts
audio-thread rules
architectural patterns
standards
mathematics
```

Living knowledge includes:

```text
current commit
implemented features
known regressions
verified fixes
performance baselines
active architecture generation
hardware-specific findings
test status
```

Static knowledge changes relatively slowly.

Living knowledge may change with every meaningful commit.

### 42.5 Core registry set

The recommended operational-memory layer contains:

```text
APEX_STATE.json
APEX_ARCHITECTURE_MAP.json
APEX_CAPABILITY_REGISTRY.json
APEX_FIX_REGISTRY.json
APEX_TEST_REGISTRY.json
APEX_BUILD_REGISTRY.json
APEX_PERFORMANCE_BASELINES.json
APEX_EVIDENCE/
```

Additional registries may be added only when they represent distinct authority.

Avoid creating multiple overlapping files that answer the same question differently.

### 42.6 APEX_STATE

`APEX_STATE.json` represents the current high-level engineering state.

Conceptually:

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "repository": {
    "branch": "main",
    "commit": "abc123",
    "dirty": false
  },
  "build": {
    "lastAttempt": "BUILD-2026-000124",
    "lastVerifiedGood": "BUILD-2026-000119"
  },
  "architectureGeneration": "AUDIO-GRAPH-V3",
  "currentMilestone": "Beta Recording Validation",
  "knownCriticalRegressions": [],
```
